have to be fenced against dairy cattle and beef cattle: 2030 for our mid -country and
2025 for our flat land. It is different if you are a dairy farmer, but the dairy boom is
over. The pressure environmentally is now coming from the beef boom.
No wonder the NGO in New Zealand that is most connected with freshwater quality,
the New Zealand Fish an d Game Council —the people who represent the tens of
thousands of New Zealanders who, every year, get money out of their own pocket to
pay for a licence to go fishing in our riverways —pulled out of the Land and Water
Forum. It was so disgusted by these cons ensual outcomes being the lowest common
denominator that it said: “We’re out of here. We’re not up for an outcome that says
we’re not even going to keep our dairy cattle and our beef cattle out of our waterways
until 2025 or 2030.”
Our rivers, after 8 yea rs of the National Government, are getting dirtier still. I see
that. I am a person who swims in rivers, I fish, and I tramp. Outside our national parks it
is a disgrace, the number of our waterways that can no longer be safely swum in
because under Nick S mith, the minimum standard that is being required is
“wadeability”—that is, clean enough to walk through, but not clean enough to swim in
and put your head under because you will get sick. That is a disgraceful bottom line, Dr
Smith, and something that you  should not be proud of as the Minister for the
Environment.
Education—do you know we have reached the parlous position in New Zealand
where the OECD says that the cause of the big tail that we have got in New Zealand of
underperformance amongst some of o ur students is caused by their economic
deprivation? The gaps have got so big in New Zealand that our kids at our poor schools
do not get ahead. I thought it was disgraceful a couple of weeks ago. I was ashamed to
live in the country where a school providi ng free swimming lessons in South
Auckland—and too few kids learn to swim these days —said that a substantial
proportion of the class were not participating because their parents could not afford
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9219
togs, and there had to be a public fund -raising effort to raise the money for them to buy
togs.
That is what is happening in New Zealand. We have got people living in cars and
garages, and parents cannot even afford togs for their kids when they are getting free
swimming lessons.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is always a pleasure to
follow David Parker, because he is a member who wants to engage in the House and he
makes a thoughtful contribution. But I would challenge him to reflect on a time when as
many of New Zealand’s core economic statistics —those vital signs that say how well
we are doing —have looked as good. I have to say, as a member of 25 years, that if I
look at those core figures of GDP —growth, in terest rates, unemployment —I would
challenge members of this House to tell me a time when New Zealand was doing better.

items.speaker: Let us go through them
items.text: economic growth—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member says: “Under Labour.” Well, let us see how
well that member is connected to the real world, because one of the issues for families is
the cost of living—how much it is going up each year. One of the reasons that members
opposite got biffed out in 2008 was that the cost of living was going up by 5 percent per
year. It is no good getting a wage increase, I say to the member opposite, of 3 percent if
your costs are going up by 5 percent. Do you know what the inflation figures are for the
last year? They are 0.1 percent, the lowest level in 23 years. That is good news because
that means that the costs for families of their power bills, their food bills, and all those
other costs are constrained and are going up by diddly-squat.
Then you look at a figure l ike wage growth—because the real gain we need to make
in our community is that wages are going up faster than the cost of living —and wages
have gone up by 2.4 percent in the last year. And, significantly, yesterday the Prime
Minister announced that the min imum wage is going up by an additional 50c per hour.
That is growth of 3.4 percent, and it is not one of those increases of 3.4 percent; it is real
because inflation is so low.
In an area that is so relevant to housing, the interest rates that families are  paying,
that businesses are paying, and that farmers are paying are at the lowest level in 50
years. Why does that matter? Well, actually, if you are a family out there in New
Zealand trying to pay the mortgage, we now have banks that are offering interest rates at
less than 4 percent. I say to members opposite: when was the last time you picked up a
newspaper and a bank would offer you an interest rate of less than 4 percent? Why does
it matter to the economy? Because if you are a business out there —and I was visiting
them in my own electorate last Friday, and they were looking at investing an extra $2
million in a processing facility for fruit, in my electorate —actually, interest rates are the
difference between investing in that additional equipment for that export industry, or
not.
Of course, I think all members would agree that one of the core economic statistics is
the level of unemployment. We know from the last figures coming down from 6
percent, down to 5.3 percent, that New Zealand has one of the h ighest labour
participation rates—the highest levels of jobs—anywhere in the OECD.
We can argue figures and quote them all we like—actually, do you know what one of
the most important signals is of how well our country is doing? It is the fact that
everybody has a choice —a choice to get on a plane and leave this country. I would
remind David Parker that if New Zealand was so great in the Labour Government years
between 2000 and 2008, why were there 35,000 bright, talented young New Zealanders
who chose to v ote with their feet and take their talent elsewhere? What we see in
contrast today is a record period of New Zealanders actually coming home. That is
9220 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
putting some pressure on my job as the Minister for Building and Housing, but I say I
welcome it. I welcom e that our country is doing so well that more migrants and more
New Zealand citizens are choosing to make New Zealand their home.
I also want to reinforce the message that this is a Government that is making real
progress on the issues that are of concern around those New Zealanders who are most
struggling. I mentioned earlier the issue of the lift in the minimum wage. I remind
Parliament that on 1 April there is going to be the first increase in core benefits in 43
years. Why can the members opposite, who plead so much, who moan and whinge as
though they are experts, not acknowledge that this Government is providing that
significant increase—not just in core benefits but even for those people on low incomes
with families, and it is giving them additional su pport? I look at the early childhood
education participation figures —the best our country has ever had. I look at the
performance of health and the best child immunisation rates that we have ever had, and
they are part of a picture of a country that is doing well.
But the responsibility of a Government is not just to deliver and do well; it is to have
a forward programme, and that is some of the things that I want to talk about in respect
of my own portfolio. I was fascinated at the questions today around t he issue of home
insulation, because, as I pointed out, in the 9 years of the previous Government an
average of 2,000 homes were insulated each year. I think we in this Parliament all agree
that insulating those older homes that were built before 1978 and did not have insulation
is a good thing. But I do have to challenge members opposite: when your record was
doing 2,000 homes per year, it is rather difficult to describe a bill that will require
60,000 homes per year to be insulated as somehow mean and ina dequate. It is simply
not credible.
I was also interested in the Greens criticising this Government and saying: “Oh, it’s
just all ‘greenwash’.” How can you describe the largest area of ocean protection in the
world, an area twice the size of the land area of New Zealand, which this Government is
committing to global marine conservation, an area of the second -deepest ocean in the
world, an area where there are over 50 different marine species and over 6 million
birds—and the legislation that we will be brin ging into this House consequential to the
Prime Minister’s announcement at the United Nations in creating that Kermadec Ocean
Sanctuary is a part of this Government’s programme that reinforces that we are a blue -
green Government. We are a Government that w ants to grow the economy but also do
the right thing by the environment.
The last point I want to make in this debate is that I have never been in a Parliament
in which Opposition parties have had so many contradictory positions. You know, we
started the year—and I remember, if we make the equivalent time —on the issue of the
Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). I say to the members opposite that I still do not quite
understand their position. I know in my constituency, where there is going to be a
reduction in tariffs on fish, there is going to be a reduction in tariffs on exports of
processed forest products, where I know there is going to be a reduction in the tariffs on
the products that we export like the kiwifruit, like the apples, like the berryfruit —
meeting with those industries, they are so encouraged about that, in the capacity for
them to be able to grow, employ more people, and pay more to people. Then why is it
that members opposite are so opposed to those fruit, those forestry, those meat, those
dairy industry gains that have been so successfully negotiated in the TPP? I see some
Labour members are in favour, some are opposed, and I cannot understand the
confusion.
Then we take a core issue —and there has been a bit of debate today about the issue
of debt. Again I have to say I am confused. I listened to Grant Robertson and he said:
“The Government needs more stimulus. It needs to borrow more and stimulate the
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9221
economy.” In the next minute I hear another Labour member, David Parker, express
concerns, and saying: “Oh, the Government is borrowing too much.” Well, you cannot
speak out of both sides of your mouth; you need to have a clear position.
And then we come to the issue of housing. David Parker in the speech that was just
given said that the Governmen t needs to go harder on the Auckland Council and make
sure that there is intensification. Well, actually, only last week Phil Twyford was saying
that the Government was interfering and bullying the Auckland Council to try to get
intensification. Well, is D avid Parker right or is Phil Twyford right, or is this just
another case of Labour being all over the paddock and not knowing what it stands for?
I equally point out the area of social housing, where I compliment the work that
Paula Bennett and Bill Engli sh are doing. I see the members opposite railing in the
House, railing in their electorates, opposed to the transfer of State houses over to
community housing providers and then standing on platforms with Phil Twyford when
he says to the community housing organisation that he supports the transfer of State
houses to those community housing providers. I know of no time in my time in this
House when we have faced an Opposition that has had such a confused position on what
it stands for. It is a party that has  lost its way. It is no surprise that it is polling so badly.
It is so far from being a credible Government because it does not know what it stands
for.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: It is always a pleasure to follow Dr Smith’s
stand-up routine. I am delighted to have the opportunity to rise to respond to the Prime
Minister’s statement, and that is partly because there is so much that needs to be
responded to—not so much about what the Prime Minist er had to say, as about what he
did not have to say.
A great deal of what the Prime Minister did not have to say concerns the primary
sector. It concerns the farming sector, the agricultural sector, the provinces, rural New
Zealand—the heartland. The Prime Minister had very little of very much use or value to
say to rural New Zealand in general or to the farmers of New Zealand in particular. That
is something of a paradox, because the National Party, this National Government, has
long touted itself as bein g the party of the farmers and for the farmers. Indeed, that was
true once upon a time, a long time ago—a very long time ago.
National has continued to trade on that old reputation and those old allegiances, even
though nowadays, and for quite a long numb er of years now, National has in fact been
the party for Queen Street, the party for merchant bankers, and, actually, the party that
does not really appear to give a damn about the farming sector at all anymore. The
farming sector is beginning to wake up t o that. It is beginning to realise that its own
party of old has abandoned it in all but name, and it is starting to look elsewhere, and
the by-election in Northland showed that. The traditionally true -blue territory of the far
north, which has been National since forever, has grown tired of being taken for granted
and tired of being marginalised. It showed that it was tired by turfing the National Party
out of its turf and installing the Rt Hon Winston Peters and New Zealand First instead.
The cracks are b eginning to show in other places as well. In Mr Barclay’s seat of
Clutha-Southland, party members and committee members are leaving the National
Party in droves, such is their disaffection with the direction that this John Key – led
“National and friends” Government is going. In the Wairarapa the winds of change are
blowing, and come 2017 they are going to deliver another body blow to the National
Party in the form of a change of member, and the new member is going to be Ron Mark.
Why is this happening? We ll, it is happening because National’s priorities are all
wrong, and people have had enough of that. Commodity prices are down, milk is down,
and farmers are hurting, and yet this National Government is steadfastly refusing to do
anything to help. Its prio rities are with the internationalists, with the bankers and the
9222 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
globalists and with its foreign paymasters —and by that I mean the people and the
institutions with links to overseas who funnel donations to National. That is where its
priorities are.
Farmers are hurting. Farmers are hurting, and rural communities are hurting, and the
Government is doing nothing to help them. We are not talking about handouts; no one is
suggesting that we go back to the days of subsidies. But there are concrete, tangible
things that this Government could be doing, and should be doing, in order to help
support farmers and the communities who depend on them at this time when things are
grim down on the farm.
New Zealand First has two bills in the ballot, which the Government co uld choose to
support, that would tangibly improve the lot of our beleaguered rural heartland and our
embattled agricultural sector. One is the Meat Industry Restructuring Bill, in my name.
This bill would see the red meat processing industry stay in New Z ealand hands. It
would see the value of New Zealand’s red meat exports stay in the New Zealand
economy. It would see returns for farmers improve, and it would guarantee jobs for
New Zealand workers in our provincial towns and service industries that suppor t the
sheep and beef farmers of New Zealand. As things stand, that industry is on the brink of
being lost to overseas ownership, and the great bulk of the value of that industry is on
the brink of being lost to the New Zealand economy.
The other bill is t he Receiverships (Agricultural Debt Mediation) Amendment Bill,
in the name of my colleague Ron Mark. This bill cuts to the heart of what has become
of the National Party, the party that used to be the party of farmers and the party of the
provinces—the party that is now being supplanted in those roles by New Zealand First,
because we still give a damn. We still give a damn. We still prioritise rural New
Zealand and provincial New Zealand, where the real wealth of this country is generated
and where New Zeal and’s income is earned. This bill highlights the way that National
has become a party that gives priority to the profits of foreign -owned banks over and
above the interests of New Zealand and New Zealanders.
There are laws very similar to the law that thi s bill would become already in place in
a number of Australian states and a number of Canadian provinces. What they do is
require banks to enter into a process of mediation, of renegotiation, before they call in
the receivers in cases where farmers find th emselves up against the odds for reasons
beyond their control. Farming is not like any other business. There are variables that do
not exist in other industries, there are fluctuations in commodity prices and exchange
rates, and there are vagaries of weath er about which farmers can do nothing. With the
best will in the world, with the best planning in the world, with the hardest back -
breaking work in the world, farmers can and do still find themselves up against the odds
when the fates conspire against them.
The banks are a part of this. They claim to be a partner for the farming sector, and
when the times are good the banks are creaming it. In fact, I have some numbers here,
prepared by the Parliamentary Library, that show the aggregate income of the 25
registered banks operating in New Zealand. For the year ended 30 September 2015,
interest from income alone was $23.5 billion.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: $23.5 billion. The profit after tax for these banks —all but
two foreign-owned—was $5.1 billion. They take their share of the spoils, but it would
seem that they are not so keen in the bad times to carry their share of the load, and that
is not good enough. New Zealand First says that that is not good enough, and this bill in
the name of my colleague Ron Mark would compel them to take a share of the load
during the lean times.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9223
National could choose to support this bill. It could choose to demonstrate that  the
welfare of our farmers and our rural communities is at least as important as the profits
of the foreign-owned banking sector. It would be nice to think that the banks might see
fit to take this step themselves, but as we are seeing, and as legislators  in Australia and
Canada have already seen and have already dealt with, they do not appear to be keen to
do that without a bit of stick. This bill provides that stick. If this Government really
cared, if it really gave a damn about the farming sector, it w ould come out and support
these two bills from New Zealand First.
Make no mistake—things are getting rough out there. Farmers are up against it, and
farmers are having a hard time. Farmer suicides are a silent epidemic, and it is going to
get worse. I hav e a paper here, a story from Radio New Zealand, saying the Reserve
Bank says that dairy farm debt alone has reached $38 billion, and a recent Federated
Farmers poll found that more than one in 10 is already under pressure from the banks
over their mortgage . One in 10 dairy farmers —that is 1,250 dairy farmers across New
Zealand. If 10 percent of our single most important export industry is in trouble, the
country is in trouble. The commercial banking sector needs to step up and become a true
partner to the f arming industry. It needs to take the rough along with the smooth, it
needs to behave in a manner that is decent and honest and ethical, and this bill would
compel it to so do.
New Zealand First drafts and sponsors bills like these two because, unlike National,
we are still in tune with the needs of New Zealand’s farmers and with the needs of the
heartland. New Zealand First recognises that the engine room of the economy is in th e
provinces, not in Queen Street, and out there in the provinces people are realising that
too. They are voting with their feet and they are giving up on National, because they are
realising that National has abandoned them. They are flocking to New Zealan d First in
droves. We are the town and country party and we are coming to the rescue of New
Zealand.
The Prime Minister makes a lot of noise; he makes a lot of statements. The Prime
Minister makes a lot of noise about a lot of things that are not importan t, like $26
million on a referendum on a flag change that nobody wants, but he has very little to say
of any actual value to the people of the heartland. But, fortunately, those people can take
great heart from the fact that New Zealand First is here to sa y it for him and to do it for
him. Roll on, 2017. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Well, it was interesting that that
last speaker finished around priorities and the flag change. I remember the New Zealand
First Party has come out with a policy that only citizens can now vote in New Zealand,
and not residents. The New Zealand First Party has an attack on our migrant
communities, saying that they are not valued members of this society and saying that
they are not able to vote. [ Interruption] Next, the Labour - New Zealand First - Green
coalition will come up with taking away—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I  regret interrupting
the member, but I think Mr Mark needs to address interjections to the member, and not
to me. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. That member, Mr Mark, has
been interjecting because he is worried that he will see that the New Zealand public will
now know that New Zealand First wants to take away the right to vote from those
people who are only residents and not citizens. Taking away the right to vote is
something that this Parliament should take ver y seriously, and it is a disgrace that the
New Zealand First Party wants to do that to New Zealanders who work hard and make
this country so strong, and that is the disgrace that is the New Zealand First Party in this
Parliament. The New Zealand First Part y will not stop at this referendum, to take away
9224 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
that right to vote. It will take that into the election, and it will take it away on other
issues where it sees that only citizens and not residents should be allowed to vote —that
is becoming the policy of the New Zealand First Party. We know that is how it works; it
has done it in the past, and it will continue to do that again in the future. That is the way
it operates, we all know that.
And all those other parties in this Parliament that will support the N ew Zealand First

items.speaker: Party
items.text: the Labour Party and the Green Party —they need to come out to make sure that
they are not supporting a policy that would take away the vote from residents in this
country, like the New Zealand First Party is intending to do. I know that New Zealand
First is led by the Don Trump of New Zealand politics, but if that is the way it wants to
do it, there will never be a wall high enough for the New Zealand First Party. It will
never build the wall as high as Don Trump can do. Its leader h as never employed
anyone, as Don Trump has; its leader would never be able to build the wall that the New
Zealand First Party would love to see in this country.
It is outrageous to see the attack from that party on our rural sector —that party that
would no t support the trade agreements of the Trans -Pacific Partnership (TPP)
agreement. Go to each of those farmers in Northland; go to each of those farmers
around the country and say to them that you come to this House and you are the
saviour—or the New Zealand  First Party says it is the saviour —of farmers, and yet, it
will not support one of the biggest things this Government and this Parliament could do
for farmers this year, and that is support a trade agreement. Why will it not support a
trade agreement when it actually will deliver for New Zealand farmers; why does it not
do things that actually matter; why do they not do something that is substantial and vote
for something that will help New Zealand farmers; why does it vote against New
Zealand farmers in t his House; why does it consistently vote against the people it says
that it wants to represent?
That is the dichotomy of the opinion within the New Zealand First Party: it does not
understand what it actually means to be a farmer. None of its members are f armers.
There are no farmers in the New Zealand First Party. There is no one there who
understands what farming is actually about. Nobody in the New Zealand First Party is
going to support farmers when they need them to have support in a trade agreement. I
want to see the New Zealand First Party actually vote for trade agreements, vote for
farmers, vote for regional New Zealand, vote for a stronger economy, and vote for
economic growth—not vote for higher walls, no voting, and taking away rights from
migrants, as the New Zealand First Party intends to do.
Things are going well in one of the biggest provincial cities in New Zealand: in
Hamilton. In Hamilton we have delivered for the people of this country. There is a
positive mood in that city, and the good r epresentation of the two local MPs Tim
Macindoe and David Bennett is part of that. Not only have we delivered new schools
for our electorates —new schools have been opened in the north of Hamilton and
Rototuna, and a new school to come in that area too with  the junior high school opening
this year and the senior high school opening next year. This is something long awaited
by residents in that area. The previous Labour Party candidates have stood on pieces of
ground in that area and said this would be a nice  place for a school, but never actually
delivered the money to build those schools. The National Government delivered the
money; the National Government built the schools; the National Government gave the
residents what they wanted. The National Government  has delivered and the National
Government has a plan for economic growth that is delivering there.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Same story with the expressway.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The other plan for economic growth in the Waikato is the
expressway, Mr Macindoe. There was a question in the House today about the
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9225
Cambridge Bypass. Ron Mark is wondering what the Waikato Expressway is. It is a
four-lane road—probably two more numbers than he can count to, but it is a four -lane
road.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Ten long years.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Ten long years, or 10 years to build a road that New Zealand
First never supported. And the Cambridge Bypass opened before Christmas, and many
residents have used that because it is an exceptionally great link between the Waikato
and the Bay of Plenty.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: And all on time and under budget.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, exactly, Mr Macindoe. What is more, there is more to
come: the Huntly bypass is now under construction. Anyon e travelling south from
Auckland and coming to live in the fine Waikato region, which is a great opportunity
for all Aucklanders, will see the Hamilton bypass that has been started to be
constructed: a $450 million project delivering for regional New Zeala nd—$450 million
spent in regional New Zealand; spent for regional New Zealand, and spent to build
stronger provincial cities in our country. Not only that, we have the sod -turning on the
next part of the Waikato Expressway: the Hamilton bypass —$800 million
approximately for that bypass, including another $100 million on top for the
Longswamp four-lane road. That $800 million is going to be spent in Hamilton, going
around the boundary of Hamilton to provide a bypass there that will create the modern
city that will be the economic growth hub of the Auckland -Hamilton-Tauranga growth
triangle: the golden triangle.
That is something that this Government has come into Parliament and delivered for
provincial New Zealand; it has delivered for our city, and it has de livered for our
country. At the same time we have seen unemployment reducing through this country,
and that is something that I think many New Zealanders have been looking forward to
for many years. We have seen the minimum wage increasing substantially in  New
Zealand; we have seen average wages increasing substantially in New Zealand; we are
seeing low inflation; we have seen low interest rates, which means that New Zealand
households are in a much better position. The New Zealand economy grew by 2.3
percent in the year to September 2015. That is great growth when you consider the
world economy and how delicate it is out there. That is all part of good economic
management; of prudent economic management; and delivering the infrastructure —just
as we have seen in Hamilton—for it to grow our country and our city.
New Zealand is in great shape. Hamilton is in especially great shape. Hamilton has a
strong future ahead of it. It is a provincial city that knows where it is going, that is
getting the investment, and  delivering. We welcome all people to the city of Hamilton,
and we are not intending to take away their voting rights like the Opposition parties will
do when they get a chance at some point to put in front of this House bills in their
names in their members’ bills.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Sit down.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The Labour Party says to sit down. Well, the Labour Party is
supporting the New Zealand First Party. They are mates; they are together in this. The
Labour Party is again st migrants as well. It has shown that time and time again, by
wanting to reduce immigration into New Zealand as part of its policy. Its policy is to
reduce immigration —that is how it is good bedfellows with the New Zealand First
Party. Next it will be tak ing away voting rights, and that would be a disgrace to this
Parliament. Thank you.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: Labour supports an
economy that works for e verybody, not an economy that works only for the privileged
few who gather from time to time at Skycity Casino to pat John Key on the back for
9226 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
ensuring that the New Zealand economy delivers for a narrower and narrower group of
people, as it has done in the  last 7 years under the National Government. Under a
Labour Government, New Zealanders will be able to have hope that they will be able to
get a job—a job that pays well, a job that has secure hours, a job where they know from
one week to the next how much  they are going to earn so that they can pay the
mortgage, they can pay the power bill, they can buy the groceries from the supermarket,
they can put food on the table for their kids, and they can put a roof over their heads.
That is the hope that we have for New Zealand; that is the Kiwi Dream that we believe
in on this side of the House —the Kiwi Dream that has been slipping ever so further
away from the grasp of ordinary New Zealanders every single one of the 7 long years
that the National Party has been in power.
On this side of the House, we are interested in what is happening with the future of
work. We are interested in ensuring that the future of work delivers for working people.
On the other side of the House they laugh at us for having a Future of W ork
Commission. They laugh at us for bringing people like Guy Standing and Robert Reich
to New Zealand to actually talk about the challenges of the future of work, the
challenges of greater automation, the challenges of a greater number of people working
in contracting situations rather than in employment situations, the challenges of
ensuring that the future of work actually delivers for people, that it results in higher
wages, that it results in stable incomes, and it results in people being able to live the
Kiwi Dream—being able to own their own home, being able to have a life outside of
work. Those are the sorts of things that we are focused on, and that is what National
members laugh at us for. Well, they can laugh as much as they like; we will continue  to
focus on the Kiwi Dream.
David Bennett can say as much as he likes that more people are employed. Actually,
the number of people unemployed is still higher today than it was when the National
Government came to office. The few people who have been able  to pick up extra work
are picking up part -time work, or casual agreements, or zero -hour contracts—insecure
work that does not pay the bills and does not give people the security they need to be
able to lead a decent life—and National is happy with that. W ell, we are not happy with
that on this side of the House. We are unsatisfied with that. We think New Zealand can
do better. Just because National has given up on the Kiwi Dream does not mean that the
rest of us have to give up on the Kiwi Dream. So, yes, we are looking at the future of
work. We are looking at how we ensure that productivity gains and the wealth that this
country generates can be shared fairly, so that a hard day’s work does result in a good
day’s pay and actually means that you can have th at Kiwi Dream and you can feed your
family and you can live a reasonable life. That is what people expect from living in New
Zealand, and it is slipping away under the National Government.
So we will look at things like how we ensure that people who are i n contracting
situations get the minimum rights that we should expect for everybody who works in
New Zealand, like getting the minimum wage. The Government can crow about putting
the minimum wage up by a meagre amount —it has finally hit $15 an hour, 6 or 7  years
after the Labour Party first said that we should have a minimum wage of $15 an hour.
That is great, except for the fact that there are thousands of people who work in New
Zealand who do not get the minimum wage because they are not employees and the y
are not entitled to those basic minimums. There are thousands of New Zealanders who
do not get all the other basic rights that ordinary working people should be able to rely
on in New Zealand —and do you know what? National is OK with that too. Well, on
this side of the House we think we can do better.
So our Future of Work Commission will look at things like how we expand
collective bargaining so that people who are in contracting arrangements can get the
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9227
benefits of joining a union and bargaining collect ively, and using their collective power
to get fair wages and a fair income, so that they can live a decent life. Those are the
sorts of things that we are interested in on this side of the House. Those are the sorts of
things that National laughs at.
One of the things that we believe should be part of the Kiwi Dream is being able to
rely on our health care system to deliver when we need it. When you go to hospital you
should be able to expect to get the care that you need. I am hearing overwhelmingly
from people in my electorate and from people across the country, actually, that our
health system is failing. That is what we get when National fails to fund the health
system properly. OK, the Prime Minister can stand up and say that the health budget has
gone up every year. That is true. But the question is: has the health budget moved
sufficiently to cover the costs of inflation and population growth? No, it has not.
In fact, $1.7 billion is missing from our health system, and that shows up in events
like the one I experienced a couple of weeks ago when I drove for 2 hours to take my
father from Palmerston North to Wellington Regional Hospital for an appointment that
was pre -arranged—only to be told when we walked through the doors: “No, your
appointment is no t going ahead.” Why did we not hear about the fact that that
appointment was not going ahead before we left Palmerston North and drove all the
way to Wellington? Because the booking clerk was so tired of calling my father and
cancelling his appointments that they were too embarrassed to make that phone call, and
they put it back on whomever it was who made the decision to cancel my father’s
appointment one more time, and that phone call never happened.
That, to me, demonstrates a health system that is sick,  and it has become sick under
this National Government because National refuses to fund health care. It refuses to pay
our health professionals properly, and it refuses to provide the resources so that our
health system can absorb one or two urgent cases a nd still provide the routine cases —
which they had booked people in for, written to them about, told them to come to
hospital, and make a 2 -hour journey, or longer in some cases —and when people walk
through the door, they are told that “No, your appointment  is not going ahead today,
because we don’t have the resources to provide that appointment that we promised you
were going to get.” That broken promise is delivered to us by National and Jonathan
Coleman refusing to fund the health system properly.
I received a letter that one of my constituents got from our local primary health
organisation. This constituent had been referred to the primary health organisation by
their GP and the referral was for a mild to moderate mental health condition. They were
told that they did not meet the criteria, not because their condition was not sufficiently
acute for the primary health organisation to take them on —no, they did not meet the
criteria because the primary health organisation has the resources to provide for only
mild to moderate mental health treatment for Māori, Pasifika, community services card
holders, and people between the ages of 10 and 24. I will give the organisation credit —
it was absolutely honest about that. It did not say: “You don’t meet our crite ria because
you are not acute enough, because you don’t have an illness, because we don’t think
you need to be treated.” They said: “You don’t meet our criteria because you’re not
Māori, Pasifika, a community services card holder, or a person between the a ges of 10
and 24.”
Our health system is sick if we cannot respond to the people who need treatment.
This person could very well have received low -level treatment for a mild illness and
saved the health system a lot of money. My concern is twofold: this per son will become
sicker because they are not getting the treatment they require, and that bothers me
greatly. But another thing bothers me, and that is that they may very well end up in the
mental health ward at the hospital with a more acute condition that  is more detrimental
9228 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
to them and also more costly for our health system. That is what is wrong with our
health system—it is short-sighted, it is under -resourced, and it is underfunded, and that
is thanks to this National Government.
None of this lives up to the Kiwi Dream. None of this lives up to what it means to be
a New Zealander. It is certainly not how I was brought up as a youngster in New
Zealand—I was led to believe that this was the best country in the world to grow up in.
But now it is a country where it is almost impossible to find a job, and when you do find
a job you are likely to be underpaid and to have too few hours to make ends meet. It is a
place where the Government laughs at people who say we need to focus on the future of
work and we need to make sure that people are prepared to engage in the future of work
to get a decent income. And it is a country where you get turned away from the hospital
even when you have an appointment. That is not the Kiwi Dream. That is the nightmare
of John Key’s National Government.

items.speaker: Dr SHANE RETI
items.text: The Prime Minister’s statement of 9
February outlines the current and future initiatives as this Government looks to continue
to build a resilient and competitive economy and do a good job for New Zealanders.
The underlying fiscal strategy that was enunciated is to have a tight rein on spending, to
pay down Government debt, and then to return excess revenue to taxpayers. In return,
we expect results in efficiencies from our public services. This strategy is giving us
projected economic growth of 2.7 percen t over the next 5 years, and this position does
well against GDP growth in other major OECD countries like Australia, the US, and
Japan.
At a national level, then, the economic outlook is stable, with steady hands on the
tiller. Where we can policy influe nce key local drivers, such as interest rates, the
Consumers Price Index, and inflation, we do so in the long -term interest and with the
best information we have to hand. By definition, then, we have less influence on
offshore factors, and this is where a resilient and multifaceted economy provides the
best solution, yet, at the same time, recognises the not insignificant contribution by New
Zealand to mitigate some of those global risks through our voice in forums such as the
United Nations Security Counci l. At a macroeconomic level, then, the positive growth
in a steady and stable economy is good.
At a regional level, this Government recognised the importance of the regions, and
the regional growth programme specifically focuses on five regions to identif y growth
opportunities: Northland, the Bay of Plenty, the East Coast, Manawatū -Whanganui, and
the West Coast. This programme is a collaboration between the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment and the Ministry for Primary Industries, together with local
businesses, iwi, and councils. Last year in Northland we had the regional growth
strategy at the beginning of the year, which identified the scope of the opportunities,
and this year, a few weeks ago, we had the regional action plan identifying 58
opportunities for Northland.
Why Northland? Well, you know, we acknowledge the challenges. We are not afraid;
we do not avoid them. We acknowledge the challenges that are currently confronting
dairy, and we are working hard to do what we can about that. We also acknowledge the
challenges that Northland has in underperforming compared with other regions. So we
are not afraid to address those issues. In fact, the action plan, with its 58 points,
identifies and prioritises what those actions might be.
I would like to look at two of the significant actions in that plan for Northland. First
of all, there is the road of national significance. The road of national significance is
absolutely critical for Northland. It is part of a nationwide investment in roading  for
roads of national significance at $4.5 billion. There are projections of 35,000 jobs as
part of that package. Northland was very pleased to hear the scoping out of the four-lane
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9229
highway from Auckland to Northland, the “Northland corridor”. That is rea l progress
and, even better, it is an example of regional investments moving off the blackboard, off
the plan, and becoming real and tangible.
In fact, Northlanders can see how real and tangible this investment is right now. As
they come over the top of the Brynderwyns there is probably a kilometre of cones as the
north side of the Brynderwyns is straightened out and the safety profile improved.
Another 15 to 20 minutes’ drive on, you will come to the Kensington roundabout,
which is about to commence —a significant piece of work on State Highway 1, which
will also improve feeder roads into that area. Another 15 to 20 minutes on, on State
Highway 1 at Hikurangi there are several hundred metres of cones where the highway is
being upgraded, there and many other areas of roading investment as well.
I would like to take one other example from the action plan: Hundertwasser Art
Centre. It is another example of actually deploying an action —taking it off the
blackboard and making it real. There is $4 million for the  Hundertwasser and the
Wairau Māori Art Centre. In 1973 Frederick Hundertwasser came to New Zealand. He
was an established international artist when he did. He gained New Zealand citizenship,
lived in Northland where his artwork was prolific and was influe nced by living in
Northland, by living in New Zealand, and by living with Māoridom. I challenge a
search for any other international artist who came to New Zealand with that reputation
and has done the same. Stan Semenoff, Phil Halse, and others have led t he
Hundertwasser challenge and over many years others have contributed. It is a real
example of this Government contributing to the regions, actually putting its hands in its
pocket—$4 million of proof and evidence right there. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I would like to take a leaf out of Bill
English’s book, actually, and spend just a moment reflecting on some of the Opposition
response to the Prime Minister’s stateme nt and particularly to its members’ discussion
on the future of work. One of the things that I would like to draw out is how they
particularly reinforce that the future is going to be a period of unprecedented change; we
are going to have significant globa lisation, technological connectivity and disruption,
and massive turmoil. In fact, it is a huge opportunity for both capital and labour —and
they talk about a huge free flow of ideas and talent and investment.
So with that as a basic premise, I find it extr aordinary that the policy response of the
Labour Party to that future is to contract out of the very trading bloc that has been
established to maximise the opportunity for this country to be able to participate in this
future. It is a trading bloc that har dwires innovative businesses to over 40 percent of
world trade: 800 million consumers. It is a trading bloc that creates a framework to be
able to deal with the issues of intellectual property and services and investment into the
future that other countrie s are lining up to join. It is a trading bloc that will exceed the
expectations of the national investment analysis. That is a future that this Government
wants to be a part of and the Opposition wants to withdraw from, and I think it is very
flawed thinking indeed.
The other policy that Opposition members then put on the table is one that increases
the subsidies for those who want to retrain. I respectfully put forward that that is
precisely the wrong question to be asking. The real question here is wheth er we are
teaching the right vocational and tertiary courses to enable people to have the skills and
resilience to be able to be successful in that future economy. In my view, this
Government has a fantastic track record in investment, particularly across vocational
and tertiary areas both in terms of their prioritisations of ICT graduates, STEM funding,
the lifting of engineering students, and the like.
In fact, I believe that when we talk about resilience and the capacity to deal with a
changing world, lo oking out 5, 10, 15, 20 years, it is as much about attitude as it is
9230 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
about technical competency. In my opinion, a party that—as we do—talks to that future,
is keen to embrace the world of tomorrow, the one that sees globalisation as a
significant generational shift and an opportunity to connect us with world consumers, is
the way of the future and is a party that has the right policy settings to be able to deal
with that reality. In my view, that future is particularly exciting and challenging, and our
success as a country will be measured on how connected we are to the world. It will be
measured on how direct the pathway is for our innovation to the consumers of
tomorrow, and it will talk to how technically competent we are as a nation and how
resilient we are as individuals and communities.
As I have reflected over the last couple of weeks and listened to the various
responses to the Prime Minister’s statement, I firmly believe that on this side of the
House we have a framework that is focused on preparing New Zealand for that future
and what we have on the other side of the House is a party that is captured in its 1980
student president and political rhetoric. I was with its members at that time. I was in the
New Zealand Union of Students’ Associations and Waikato Student Union with Grant
Robertson. I heard his speeches. They are the same today as they were 25 years ago, and

items.speaker: Bill English is right
items.text: they are caught in a policy response that is 25 years old. They do
not understand how they talk about this futur e of globalisation. They talk about the
forces that are changing the world rapidly, but their policy response is inadequate, it is
weak, it is poor thinking, and it is the reason why they are 25 points behind in the polls.
It is the reason why the community of the Bay of Plenty and Tauranga are so supportive
of John Key, so supportive of this Government, and I am very proud to be a part of it.
Thank you.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: The Kiwi Dream —it is not too m uch to ask. I think
that the National Party has forgotten about the basic needs of New Zealanders:
somewhere safe to live; hopefully, a place that you can call home, that you can own.
That is not too much to ask. Basic needs include security for the people  we love, a
chance to enjoy the outdoors and the environment that we care about, and a job —a
decent, secure job—that gives us the time, the money, and the safety to lead a fulfilling
life with those we care about. It is a simple concept —the Kiwi Dream —but for an
increasing number of New Zealanders it is getting completely outside of their reach
under this National Government.
I was hoping to hear something inspirational from the Prime Minister’s statement
that might change that situation, but a couple of weeks after the Prime Minister stood up
and gave his statement, you know, I cannot name one exciting thing that he said, and I
do not think any New Zealander can. What was the transformational thing that the
Prime Minister came out with in his speech that w ill improve people’s lives? That is
what we are charged with: we are charged with improving people’s lives, not handing
out the same old misery that is stopping thousands of New Zealand families and
children from achieving that simple Kiwi Dream. That is w hat we are here to try to
secure. It is out of reach for far too many New Zealanders under this Government.
My generation of parents is facing the sad situation of being the first generation ever
to look at our children and know that they are going to be worse off than we were. That
has not happened before. I think all parents aspire to know that their children’s lives are
going to be better than theirs. But we are facing down the barrel of being the first
generation who will not be able to look our childr en in the eye and say that, because
they face increasing housing costs and their chances of actually owning their own home
are becoming a distant, distant memory. They face increasing debt for everything that
they are engaged with—for their education, and for just simply being allowed to live on
this planet and participate in life in New Zealand. They are under growing amounts of
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9231
debt. The life expectation of the generation below us is below the life expectation for
my generation.
That is a dreadful situat ion for any parent to have to contemplate. Also, our children
face increasingly insecure jobs. That is what they are facing under this National
Government. It is only the Labour Party that is concerned enough about that prospect
that we are doing the hard work and the thinking and the policy making around what the
future of the workforce needs to look like, to actually make it more secure for people, to
ensure that the workforce and the labour market work for people.
I listened to the sad contributions from the last couple of National MPs. Todd Muller,
who has just resumed his seat, said that our entire success is going to be measured on
how connected we are to the world. No, Mr Muller, our success will be rated on how
people’s lives are. We have an economy  to serve the people; not the people to serve the
economy. They have got it completely the wrong way round. That is what I think was at
the basis of the Prime Minister’s statement that was so disappointing and did not bring
forward any of the inspiration, any of the vision, that New Zealanders are desperately
crying out for.
Under National, the Kiwi Dream is slipping away. National members are too
distracted on working out how to get rid of our flag, for goodness’ sake! They are so
distracted on how to get rid of our flag that they had a crisis meeting about it. They had
a crisis meeting on how to get rid of our national flag when they should have been
having a crisis meeting on how to lift out of poverty the increasing number of children
who are slipping i nto poverty under National’s reign. That should have been what the
crisis meeting was about; not about getting rid of our flag. So the Government has
completely got its priorities upside down.
On this side of the House we are connected to the Kiwi Dream, and we are
determined to deliver that. I want to talk about a few aspects that we are taking charge
of. Extending paid parental leave is one aspect. If the Kiwi Dream starts anywhere it
starts in those first early days and months of a child’s life. Getting  that right, getting the
support, getting the security, getting the attachment between parent and baby —there
should be no greater priority than that. That is where the Kiwi Dream starts. If it goes
wrong in those early months, what all the research and evi dence tell us is that we as
taxpayers will pay for that, over and over and over again. When that child cannot learn,
when that child ends up in hospital, when that child is not going to school because of
health problems, when that child is disconnected from their caregiver, from their parent,
then we all pay, over and over again, for the bad outcomes of that.
On this side of the House, and with the support of other wise parties, what we know
is that this sort of investment is the type of thing that the Pri me Minister should have
been talking about. He should have been agreeing to extend paid parental leave to 26
weeks. But was he doing that? No. Instead, he is talking about putting a veto on it, to go
against the will of this Parliament and to go against th e will of the majority of New
Zealanders, to put a stop to getting the start to the Kiwi Dream. That is what the Prime
Minister is focused on; not on dealing with the issues that matter to New Zealanders.
Decent jobs—that is what this side of the House is  focused on. We know that having
a decent job is fundamental to being able to secure the rest of the Kiwi Dream. It is
fundamental to that. But under this Government, zero-hour contracts are what have been
going on. People have to put their lives on hold, just sit and wait for a phone call that
may never come, to give them a little bit of extra money so that they can put food on the
table. For far too many of our families those jobs mean not only that can they not
participate in their community but also tha t they cannot do the basic thing of putting
food on the table. We are a food-producing nation, and 27 percent of our children live in
poverty. Too many of our children go to school hungry, in a food -producing nation.
9232 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
How can we get it so wrong? How can tha t be? Did the Prime Minister address that at
all in his statement? There was not one measure —not one measure —to reduce child
poverty. There was not one measure to secure decent jobs. There was not one measure
that actually deals with the day -to-day pressures that New Zealand families are facing,
and it is very, very disappointing.
Another part of a decent job is the good old Kiwi adage that you get a fair day’s pay
for a fair day’s work. There was never a rider put on that—I have never heard one—that
says “but only if you are a certain gender, or only if you are a certain race.” What I am
talking about is equal pay. We need urgently to address equal pay as well. This
Government cannot even talk about equal pay. It talks, instead, about getting women to
go off and do jobs traditionally done by men. That seems to be the Government’s only
idea that it has got in this space. Well, it is not acceptable and it needs addressing.
In the final part of this speech I want to talk a little bit about transport and its r ole in
the Kiwi Dream. I can tell you that sitting on the Auckland motorway for hours on end
is not part of the Kiwi Dream. That Government has presided over increasing volumes
on the Auckland motorway, without people getting anywhere. It has spent $2.3 bi llion
on the Waikato Expressway. That was money, funding, set aside by a Labour
Government to do exactly that. We agree with the Waikato Expressway, but what the
Government has managed to do is to squander that $2.3 billion. It now takes longer than
ever to get from central Hamilton to central Auckland. It now takes longer than ever. It
used to take an hour and a half
Hamiltonians now have to put aside 3 hours to get from central Hamilton to central
Auckland, and that is after the Government has spent $2.3 billion on the Waikato
Expressway. Why? Because it did not do the public transport part that needed to go
alongside that, to make it work. The Government has ignored the needs of public
transport in Auckland, and now what we are doing, with the Waikato Exp ressway, is we
are feeding a greater volume of traffic faster to get to the “great southern car -park” and
sit there for longer. That is what the National Government has managed to achieve. It is
not good for productivity. It is not good for family life.
Because of the housing crisis in Auckland, which the Government has failed to fix,
we have got people moving to Hamilton, living there, but returning to their jobs every
day in Auckland. They are going on that motorway, sitting there for hours on end, doing
a full day’s work, and doing it again at the other end of the day. They are becoming
unsafe on the roads, and when they get home they are feeling stressed with their
families. That is not the Kiwi Dream. It is not working under this Government.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Ā, kia ora e Te Mana Whakawā; tuatahi, ka
maumarahatia Te Rakatira Tākuta Ranginui Joseph Isaac Walker. Nō reira, e Te
Rakatira o Te Whakatōhea, e Te Rakatira o Te Iwi Māori, e haere at u rā, haere atu rā ki
Te Pā o Te Whakawairua, e takoto mai, takoto mai, takoto mai, e moe mai, moe mai rā!
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. In the first instance I reminisce about the noble
Dr Ranginui Joseph Isaac Walker. Therefore, to you, esteemed one of Whakatōhea and
Māoridom, depart and move on to the spiritual place. Lie there, lie down, and lay there.
Rest and slumber on.]
I stand to take this split call to support the Prime Minister’s statement. I want, first of
all, to highlight the work of this Government to improve Māori well -being of
individuals and communities. We continue to resolve the historical Treaty of Waitangi
claims settlements and we have the whakaaro—the idea is that we do want to settle with
all those iwi that are willing and are ab le, by 2017. Also, there is Te Ture Whenua
Maori Bill, which will unlock the revision of that Māori land legislation, which has
huge potential to unlock the huge economic potential existing in Māori land.

items.speaker: Kelvin Davis
items.text: Which version? There’s been 18 rewrites.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9233

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Well, wait for it. When it comes to the Māori Affairs Committee,
you will see it. I also want to reflect on the debate surrounding Waitangi this year.
Waitangi, our national day, was hijacked by opponents of free trade. It was hijacked. Up
and down the country, we have seen Māori being fed misinformation about the Trans -
Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement. We have seen this right across the country. Two
major things that they have been fed: the first one is consul tation and the second one is
this idea that the TPP agreement would infringe on their rights under the Treaty of
Waitangi.
Let us look at the consultation process, because the truth is that the consultation
process for the TPP agreement actually started i n 2008, and for Māori there were
specific consultations with the Federation of Māori Authorities, individual Māori
businesses, and also iwi. Throughout the process the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and
Trade actually updated iwi and Māori businesses every 6 months, so this
misinformation that they were never consulted—that is misinformation. The next part of
it is about this infringement of rights—

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: Were you there? I was there. It’s not consultation.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I just ask the member
to take a seat for a second while I remonstrate with one of my colleagues. I was not
there, and the member should know not to address the speaker in that way.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Kia ora. Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. The misinformation
around the TPP agreement actually infringing on the Treaty of Waitangi —nothing in
the agreement prevents the Government from honouring the Treaty; nothing in the
agreement. When we look at the trade agreements that have been negotiated since 2001,
all of those, in those trade agreements since then, they’ve always had those provisions
in it that there would be no infringement under the Treaty of Waitangi.
Finally, at the beginning I  acknowledged Dr Ranginui Walker. In one of his books,
Struggle Without End —he was a man who saw there was far from doom and gloom
regarding the development of iwi Māori —he called Māori development “the most
powerful cultural renaissance […] of a colonised  people in the world.” One of those
cultural achievements he highlighted was Māori entrepreneurship. Māori own nearly 30
percent of our primary industries and stand to be the biggest beneficiaries of the TPP
agreement. Māori care about the same things that  other New Zealanders care about.
They want jobs, they want better wages, and quality public services.
That is why the Government has pursued and will continue to pursue the TPP
agreement and other opportunities for economic growth. We are about wealth cre ation
as opposed to about wealth redistribution. Kia ora.

items.speaker: MAUREEN PUGH
items.text: It is a privilege for me to stand and take this my
first call in the House. For the benefit of my colleagues, I am based in West Coast -
Tasman, and I am very proud to stand here today in support of the Prime Minister’s
statement—a Prime Minister who has taken it upon himself to recognise the importance
of the tourism industry in this country and has placed himself in charge of that particular
portfolio. Tourism is directly contributing $10.6 billion to the national economy. We are
experiencing a very buoyant tourism sector at the moment, and my recent visit to South
Westland, just last week, encourages me that the industry is in good heart and the
country is in good heart.
The Prime Minister’s statement touched on several items that affect the people who
live in the area of West Coast - Tasman in a very positive way. One of those is the
changes that are proposed for ACC that will be coming in this year. A total of $450
million will be saved in levies paid by businesses and employees —that is $450 million
that stays in the pockets of those people. That is a huge contribution back to this nation.
9234 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
When I was campaigning in 2014, the Government pledged that it would replace one
of the bottlenecks in the tourism sector, on the roads in between Greymouth and
Hokitika, and that is the Taramakau road -rail bridge. Although quite quaint in its
design, where you share the road and the bridge with a train, in this day and age it is no
longer satisfactory. The Government plans to spend $15 million to $20 million on
replacing the Taramakau road-rail bridge. This project is expected to start later this year,
and delivers on that pre-election promise. I am very proud that we were able to promise
that to the electorate and also deliver. This is part of the Accelerated Regional Roading
Package.
Also part of that programme is the realignment of what is called the Mingha Bluff,
and for those of you who have ever travelled State Highway 73 from the West Coast to
Christchurch, you will know that it is one of the remaining narrow sect ions of road —
very windy. If you have ever had the misfortune of being stuck behind a transporter,
you will know that if two trucks meet on that particular section of road, there is simply
no room to pass—they literally touch wing mirrors. In this day and a ge, with the tourist
volumes that are making their way across that road, it is very heartening indeed to see
this work progressing at such a great rate and —I have got to say —too, without too
much disruption to the traffic flows along that road. This is a $ 22 million project being
invested into the area and, all going to plan, it will be finished at the end of this year.
This will significantly improve the safety of locals and visitors visiting and travelling
across that road. It is also very important for our freight transport operators.
Another item in the Prime Minister’s statement that is of particular interest to me is
the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement. The industries that benefit in the areas
of West Coast - Tasman—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: Huge on the Coast. Huge.

items.speaker: MAUREEN PUGH
items.text: —huge—dairy, meat, fruit and vegetables, forestry, and
fisheries. By the time the TPP is fully implemented, the tariff savings alone will value
$259 million. That is $259 million nationally that  is staying with the growers to grow
their business, to employ more workers, and to benefit their industries. This is great
news for New Zealand.
There is an example on the West Coast at the moment of the central -local
government partnership. I spoke about  this in my maiden speech, where working
together produces greater results for Kiwis. This Government has pledged $300
million—sorry, I wish —$300,000 to help with the employment opportunity in Buller,
and that is a partnership, one -to-one, with the Buller District Council. That is going to
see workers being able to be retained in the town so that other business opportunities
can grow and take up their employment at a later date. Thank you.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. I rise to take the final
call for the Greens on the Prime Minister’s statement, and I want to address the four
priorities that he outlined. They were to responsibly manage the Government’s finances,
to build a more competitive and productive economy, to deliver better public services to
New Zealanders, and to support the rebuilding of Christchurch.
I applaud the Government’s small army of public relations and communications staff
for being able to spin this Government’s appalling record on these issues into some kind
of achievement. National has promised to responsibly manage the Government’s
finance. The reality is that it has increased New Zealand’s public debt to $120 billion. A
legacy of National’s poor economic ma nagement is tax cuts to its rich mates and
giveaways to dodgy corporates. It promised to build a more competitive and productive
economy; instead, it built an economy that was built on property speculation —ask
anyone in Auckland —and on casino capitalism an d on unsustainable practices. It has
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9235
failed to meaningfully diversify the economy and implement a vision towards a greener
and more sustainable economy.
Our trading fortunes seem to rise and fall with the dairy prices, and we see, as the
result of this, f arms carrying nearly $60 billion in debt, with dairy farms carrying $40
billion of that debt. Nearly one in 10 farmers is under financial stress. The
Government’s single -minded focus on bigger, more intensive farming endangers our
fragile ecosystems. It pr essures farmers into intensifying, and it undermines New
Zealand’s No. 1 strength: our “clean, green” reputation.
This Government claims to have provided Better Public Services. It has certainly
been very good at delivering public services to further priv ate interests—to places like
Serco, Skycity, and, let us not forget, charter schools —and it has certainly been very
good at replacing democratically elected bodies in favour of appointed cronies. We see
this with the Southern District Health Board and gove rnance in Christchurch. But the
facts speak for themselves. National’s approach is not working.
Currently there are 129 days of waiting time to get a State house if you are in urgent
need. One in three people needing a house is turned away and taken off t he waiting lists
to help the Government fudge the books with its creative accounting. The Government’s
hard-line ideology is pressuring our hard -working public servants. Our nurses and
doctors are having to cope with nearly $2 billion —$2 billion —in underfu nding, our
universities are slipping in the world rankings, and our Department of Conservation is
struggling to fulfil its core responsibilities due to budget cuts.
The reality on the ground was exposed a couple of weeks ago by the Salvation
Army’s report. In it, it says—and as we know—that there are still 220,000 kids living in
poverty, there are still 150,000 notifications for potential child abuse this year, and there
are over 55,000 food parcels being provided by the Salvation Army. Only on “Planet
Key” can the number of kids remaining in poverty increase despite the economy
growing 12 percent since 2010.
The reality about our Public Service is that it cannot continue to struggle with
underfunding. Political reporter Andrea Vance was correct: instead o f having Better
Public Services, we have “Bitter Public Services”. Despite the Government’s glossy
public relations, our hard -working teachers, nurses, doctors, and police are bearing the
cost of having to do much, much more with less, and that means that our most
vulnerable—our kids, kids living in poverty, regional New Zealand, and our new
migrants—are bearing the costs of these stealth cuts.
Let me just talk a little bit about Christchurch and the promises there. My colleagues
from Christchurch have already touched on this, but allow me to ask the question once
more: how can the Government be listing its rebuilding of Christchurch as an
achievement and then, several days later, slash the funding for mental health services in
the area? Rebuilding is more than replacing bricks and mortar. It is about supporting
people who have been hurt and are facing losses, it is about wrapping support around
the vulnerable and vulnerable communities, and it is about acknowledging that the loss
of friends, family, businesses, and ways of life can be painful and difficult and that it
requires help. I pay tribute to the incredible resilience, courage, and fortitud e of the
people of Christchurch, and I condemn this Government, which by its actions is failing
the people of Christchurch and the people of New Zealand.
The Government has repeatedly promised a brighter future for New Zealand, but it
has always talked a better game than it has been prepared to deliver. For ordinary
working New Zealanders, we have gone backwards in terms of rights at work, we have
gone backwards in terms of the work climate where lots and lots of public servants feel
bullied and fearful, a nd we have gone backwards about zero -hour contracts. The Prime
Minister promised a brighter future for New Zealanders, but, actually, he has left every
9236 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
New Zealander in the dark. The recent increase of the minimum wage to $15.25 an hour
and the gap between  that and the living wage of $19.80 reflect that reality. Since 2009
the highest-paid third of New Zealanders have seen their incomes increase eight times
as much as the lowest-paid third.
Last year the Government promised to outlaw zero -hour contracts, b ut instead of
moving on that, what it is doing is attempting to legalise them. Last year the
Government promised a gold-plated Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement, but we
are being sucked in and stuck with an agreement that will cost 5,000 jobs and l eave us
open to being sued by big corporates. There is a better way—there is a much better way.
It is interesting to note what the Prime Minister did not talk about. Not once did the
Prime Minister mention the word “inequality” or the word “poverty”, not once did the
Prime Minister address the growing gap between the haves and have -nots in this
country, and only once did he mention climate change —and then only in passing. A
progressive Prime Minister would have talked about child poverty and supported
measures to fix it, like our breakfast in schools bill —the Government could have
supported that —and like, maybe, decent incomes for families. A progressive Prime
Minister would have talked about how climate change is the greatest challenge we face,
but it is a lso an opportunity for New Zealand to become world leaders in a new, high -
value, cleantech, low-carbon economy. A progressive Prime Minister would have talked
about how we can have an economy that works for everyone, not just the very rich, and
a progressive Government with the Greens in it would do more than just talk and spin.
We would act on these issues and make sure that every single child in New Zealand
is cared for and lives in a warm, dry home. We would make sure ordinary New
Zealanders would get a  fair deal at work and a fair share of the benefits of a smart,
thriving green economy that works for everyone. We would make sure that we have
rivers we can swim in and vibrant green cities and townships with fast, affordable, clean
public transport. An Aotearoa with the Green Party at the heart of Government will be a
much kinder place, and certainly we would deliver a lot better than what this
Government has.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak on the Prime
Minister’s statement. If you are listening to this debate, you would have heard a lot of
slogans, but, actually, when I read the Prime Minister’s statement, I see a very clear
vision for New Zealand. It is ver y clear, and it is very clear that there is a very big
contrast in this House between the Opposition and the Government. The vision is an
open, democratic nation that is connected to the world, where we live in a place where
every young person has the abil ity to have access to decent health and education
services. Let us look at what has actually happened over the last 7 years, and where we
are going.

items.speaker: Let us take the first issue
items.text: our economy. We hear a lot from the Opposition about
how much it cares about business. Those members turn up, they have the cocktail
functions, but when it comes to the crunch —one of the biggest things that will affect so
many of our exporters —where are they? They have gone. They have ditched our
exporters. Because the reality is t hat the emails that were coming in to me in Auckland
Central—yes, there were those people who were opposed, but there were a whole lot of
exporters who understood the basic concept of a deal that would reach 800 million
people and 11 nations, that would le ad to, if not signed, a whole lot of businesses small
and large having tariffs on them that other countries would not have. It was
inconceivable to them that we would not sign it. In fact, I think it was one exporter who
said to me: “We would literally have our hands tied behind ours backs.”
So the Labour Party talks a good game, but when it comes to the crunch, it cannot
sign the deal and, actually, it is all over the place. We know where former Prime
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9237
Minister Helen Clark sits on this, and I do want to ac knowledge her. You know, she
quite clearly understands the issue for New Zealand if we were to not sign this thing.
We understand where Phil Goff sits on this. He is a former trade Minister. He quite
practically understands a $2.7 billion deal for our coun try and what that means. We
actually understand where David Shearer sits on this, but he has been muzzled by his
leader. The reality is that half of the Labour caucus support this deal, but because of
petty politics they have not been able to step up and do the right thing for New Zealand.
We are a Government that has a Prime Minister who is outward -looking and who is
walking the talk and signing deals like the Trans -Pacific Partnership. I want to
acknowledge the Hon Tim Groser. When it comes to the economy, we are a
Government that was hand ed billions of dollars of a hole in the ACC books. I am the
Minister for ACC. We now have a situation where we have been able to put $1.5 billion
back in New Zealanders’ pockets. We have got $450 million coming back. That is from
motor vehicle levies being  cut, that is businesses levies being cut —that is actually real.
In contrast, we were handed a complete shambles in terms of the books.
When it comes to other areas of the economy, the reality is that —if you listen, again,
to the Opposition you will hear a completely different level of slogans and a completely
different world —the average wage in New Zealand has gone up $10,000 under our
Government. It is now at $57,000. But, again, our vision is more than that. It is not just
about the economy.
When it co mes to infrastructure, we were handed a massive deficit. I am Associate
Minister of Education. Let me walk you through the numbers. We were handed leaky
buildings and we were handed old buildings. More than 60 percent of the buildings in
New Zealand were o ver 60 years old. What happened? There were $2.7 billion in 7
years under Labour; we have put $4 billion in. We are literally fixing these schools all
across New Zealand more than ever before. No Government has undertaken such a
social infrastructure upgra de of our schools as this Government has. So if people want
to talk about a Government that cares, that is one example.
Let us talk about the other examples. When it comes to health, we have a whole lot
of young people who we want to ensure get access to the doctor. Which Government
was it? It was our Government that said: “Right, we’re going to give free under -13s
visits to young people in New Zealand.” We have delivered that. When it came to the
issue raised by the Green Party of breakfast in schools, it  was our Government that has
put in millions of dollars, enabling those schools that want it —not compulsorily, not
making sure that every school has to have set times for their particular breakfasts. We
actually said to schools: “It’s up to you if you want  it, but we will enable those young
people to get access to breakfast.” When it came to insulating houses —we are now
