350,000 insulated houses later. Again, this is set out in the Prime Minister’s clear vision
for New Zealand—a country that is focused on op ening up our many businesses to the
world, having access to those markets, having access to decent incomes, but also
enabling some of our most vulnerable to get better support. And our record in those
areas that I have just outlined is very clear.
When it comes to infrastructure spend, let us look again in Auckland. Again, we hear
a lot of slogans from the Opposition about the Kiwi Dream and all of these things, and
we hear a lot of slogans about the fact that we should not be investing so much in roads,
but here are the facts around rail in Auckland. It is our Government that has put $1.5
billion into the electrification of rail, and I was very pleased to be with the Prime
Minister when we confirmed that we are looking to bring forward the City Rail Link.
What is that about? That is actually about Prime Minister John Key being responsible
for delivering the vital artery in Auckland’s rail system. That is a project that will lead
9238 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
to not just the people of central Auckland benefiting; it is the people of west  Auckland
and South Auckland who are literally going to have their journey times slashed in half.
That is a compassionate Government. That is a Government that is investing not just
in roads but also in public transport. Again, we are spending billions of  dollars ensuring
that our young people are connected to the world and that it is a connected nation.
Whether it is the ultra -fast broadband programme, which has been a couple of billion
dollars, we are one of the only countries in the world —and this is so mething that I am
most proud of and when I leave Parliament, this is one of the things that I will be most
proud of. We said when we came in that we were going to do everything we could to
connect New Zealand schools. And we have not only said that we are going to put the
fibre in the ground, we are going to enable every school that wants it to have access to
fast connections, reliable connections funded by the Crown. We are, we believe, one of
only a couple of countries in the world that are delivering tha t. We are roaring ahead
with that programme. More than 90 percent of New Zealand schools have been
connected to that, and that is paid for by us because we believe in a nation that is
globally connected where every young person gets that opportunity.
So, again, we hear a lot from the Opposition about the Kiwi Dream. The Prime
Minister’s statement was very clear: an open nation connected to the world, where every
young person gets better access to equality of opportunity. And it is our Government, in
so man y areas —from education to insulating houses, to free under -13s visits, to
investing in infrastructure and catching up with the massive deficit that we have been
left in areas like rail, in transport, and in ultra -fast broadband. That is incredibly
significant. And we have done this at one of the most difficult times, in terms of our
history, with the global financial situation, but also with the Canterbury earthquakes.
As the Minister of Civil Defence, can I say this. There is a lot of talk around the
Canterbury rebuild, but I have had the good fortune of meeting Ministers from across
the world, and I do want to say this about the Hon Gerry Brownlee: it is one of the most
complex processes to basically try to rebuild a city. I think that we have not only th e
Prime Minister’s leadership on pretty much day one in saying “We will rebuild that
city.”—and we have spent $17 billion on doing that —but also the dedication and the
huge amount of work that the Hon Gerry Brownlee does every day to ensure that we are
rebuilding that city. But the reality is that there are many situations across the world
where we can see that this does take a bit of time, and we acknowledge the people of
Canterbury and their patience through this period. But, at the end of the day, we hav e
put up the money and we are absolutely committed to working through that.
This is a Government that not only has compassion and has the right policies from a
fiscal perspective but, actually, is walking the talk when it comes to the Kiwi Dream.
Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. The
Hon Clayton Cosgrove—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: If you look at Kiwi society, Kiwis do not
ask for much from their Government or from their nation. They ask for a fair go, they
ask for a future, they ask —and they want —some hope; not just for themselves but for
their families, for the future generations, and for their loved ones. New Zealanders know
what they are about.
The last speaker, Minister Nikki Kaye, talked about the Prime Minister’s statement
and the vision and the great words and the great slogans that were in it. She talked —and
I wrote it down —about “a Government that cares”. She talked about “a compassionate
Government”. But there was one word and one phrase that did not appear in the Prime
Minister’s statement yet was evident today, and that was the word “Keytruda”. We had
a display today in Parliament where members of the public presented a 45,000 -person
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9239
petition. People sat in the gallery watching the to -ing and fro-ing of question time, and
they are people who are fighting for their lives, quite literally. We had a couple of
individuals come to our caucus meeting this morning to talk about the fact that, in both
cases, they were, effectively, told it was lights out —they were not coming back. As my
colleague said, to go home and die was the message: “There is nothing that can be
done.”
And we had people on the front lawn of Parliament: people who have done sausage
sizzles; people who have raised money through Givealittle websites and on Facebook;
people who have mortgaged houses for their families —not because they have a choice
to do so but because they have to, literally, in the case of the melanoma disease, try to
keep their loved ones alive because the Government refuses to fund Pharmac to
produce, literally, a lifesaving drug.
As Annette King has said, there is no first -line or fro nt-line treatment like
chemotherapy or radiotherapy for this disease. These people require a lifesaving drug to
survive, and this is not, you know, the old green -lipped mussel, sort of magic potion
stuff that we had a few years ago. No, these are people wh o were told “Go home and
die.”, who funded this medication themselves and are now living today. So when that
member talks about compassion and when she talks about a caring Government, she
should reflect on those folks who sat in the gallery today and who were on the front
lawn of this Parliament begging, in many cases, for this Government to save the lives of
their family. That might sound a bit dramatic over there, but it is a medical fact. It is a
medical fact.
The Prime Minister talks about aspiration. Well, it is hard to have aspiration if you
are dead. It is hard to have aspiration if your whole life as you move to retirement is
about mortgaging your home, going on Facebook to beg the public for some money,
going and running galas and other things, because that is what you literally have to do to
ensure that those you love who are victims of this awful disease can have their lives
saved. I am told people are dying daily from this disease, and these are people whose
lives can be saved. I ask the Minister  of Health—as he says “Pharmac might get some
more money”, or the Prime Minister, as he says “We’ll have to wait and see until the
Budget”—to act. And every day that we wait and every day that we procrastinate, or the
Government procrastinates, people literally die.
So when we talk about vision and when we on this side talk about the Kiwi Dream,
and the Prime Minister talks about aspiration —and when we hear 10 minutes of lofty
speeches about roads and all sorts of other infrastructure and the wonderful
opportunities available to New Zealanders, who do not ask for much —those New
Zealanders sitting in the gallery and out on the front lawn will never be able to exercise
those aspirational goals because they might not be here.
Government inherently is about choi ces. Ministers make choices every day. They
choose to fund a flag referendum at 26 million bucks. They choose to fund charter
schools and Novopays that fail. They choose all these things, and today is an
opportunity for them to make a choice and literally —literally for those people —save
their lives.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Stuart Nash—5 minutes.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: What I would like to talk about is equality of
opportunity and the Kiwi Dream in the 21st century. Nikki Kaye stood up and she talked
about an aspirational Government and what it was doing, but the facts speak for
themselves. At the moment in New Zealand there are over 300,000 Kiwi children living
in poverty, our jail numbers are at a record high, and there are over 150,000 New
Zealanders who are unemployed. The world that Nikki Kaye speaks about is the world
of people who have succeeded; they have had o pportunities, and I celebrate them and I
9240 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
say: “Well done. Good on you. You’ve worked hard. You’ve got to where you are by
getting out there and really making it happen.” But I have grave concerns for those
without hope, without opportunity, or without aspiration.
Equality of opportunity is my reason for getting into politics and my underlying
philosophy. Equality of opportunity means it does not matter what your postcode is,
what your parents’ income is, where you live, or what your last name is. It is about
allowing Kiwis to reach their full potential, and it starts with education.
Education allows people to reach their potential —to be as good as they possibly can
be. We are not talking about everyone becoming Oxford dons, but what we are talking
about is people achieving and becoming part of society. A generation ago, if you were
not so academically inclined there were jobs in the freezing works, in the wool stores, at
the forest service, at the ports, in the Ministry of Works, and in the post office. T here
were jobs for everyone. In fact, they used to joke in the 1950s that the Minister of
Labour knew the name of every single unemployed person because there were only
about 11 of them. That has changed.
These days, if you want to be even a grunt in the a rmy, you need National Certificate
of Educational Achievement level 2. Education is where it starts and education is a way
forward. It is the way that Kiwis can reach out and make that Kiwi Dream a reality. It
has never been so important in providing young  Kiwis with the right to a life that we
have had and that our forebears have had, but at the moment it is just out of reach of a
generation coming through because they have not got that ability. Education is so
important that it cannot be underestimated. I t was why the Labour Party, a Labour
Government, and Andrew Little have really trumpeted education as a way forward, as a
transformational policy to allow Kiwis to achieve to their potential.
We are going to enter into a referendum on the New Zealand flag.  Sir Roger
Douglas, in this House —you know, we disagree on certain fundamental philosophy —
said that he had never ever seen a Prime Minister come into power with so much
political capital as John Key and completely waste it. I simply cannot understand, for
the life of me, why Mr Key is burning so much political capital on something like the
New Zealand flag when there are so many things that he could go incredibly hard on
that would change the lives of good, hard -working Kiwis and that would transform this
country from one where we have begun to almost accept that child poverty is just the
way it is.
When you think that this is a country founded on such egalitarian principles that
people moved from London, from the UK, and from around the world to come here, to
have a fresh start, and to start again in a society that valued everyone. The thing is that a
Labour Government has always been the Government of transformation, of social
evolution that is not social revolution, and it will be again. There is a differe nt way. I
know this; New Zealanders know this. There is an alternative. We cannot keep going
the way we are. If you are doing really well life is good, but for more and more and
more Kiwis life is a struggle and life is a challenge. As mentioned, I celebra te those
who have done well—good on you—but for those for whom life is a challenge, we also
need to work hard for them. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: The previous speaker, Stuart
Nash, was talking about the time when somebody said there were 11 unemployed
people in the country. I can remember that time, back in the mid -1970s. It was just
down on Pipitea Street, not far from this Parliament, where I watched a gang f rom the
Ministry of Works dig a hole. There were 13 workers there. Each had a spade or a
shovel, and there were 12 watching and one digging.
Back in the 1970s this country was very wealthy because we had a great relationship
with Britain. We were able to sell all of our goods, no questions asked, but then Britain
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9241
joined the EEC and suddenly our markets evaporated and disappeared, and this country
has to live in a different way than it did in that period of time. We have to be far more
productive, we have to be sharper, we have to be leaner, we have to be competitive, and
we have to be productive on the world stage. That is what this Government has brought
to this nation —productivity edge competitiveness on the world stage. That is why this
country, this nation, and this Government are respected all around the world.
Back in 2008 National became the Government with 45 percent support. We went
into 2011 and we won with 47 percent support. We went into 2014 and we won again
with 47 percent support. In October 2015 we were receiving 47 percent support and at
the beginning of this year, once again. So what that shows is that there has been
consistency of support because there has been consistency of policy and consistency of
output and achievement for this countr y. After returning to Taranaki in 2008 —after
living for 22 years in Auckland —what I have witnessed is the credibility and
consistency of this Government in its support for the people of Taranaki and regional
New Zealand. It is a good thing.
What we receiv e from members of the Opposition is a continual —as would be
expected—undermining of the achievements of this Government. I remember when the
Leader of the Opposition commented and was quoted in September last year on the
number of visits to New Plymouth by  Government Ministers. He said “When the town
was booming, there were Ministers here every couple of weeks. Now you can’t see
them for dust.”, referring to the time of challenge and hardship that two particular
sectors in the Taranaki economy were facing —obviously, dairying and the petroleum
sector. He said: “It’s not enough to stand on the sidelines cheering during the good
times, then turn your back when times are tough. Taranaki and the rest of New Zealand
deserves more than that.”
So he said they were there every couple of weeks. I went through the list of Ministers
who came to my electorate, my region, and I wanted to find out the level of support this
Government gave regional New Zealand, particularly in my electorate. I went through
and I counted the m up. There were 18 ministerial visits in 27 weeks, which is a visit
every 10 days. So we were very much on the map, and I think what regional New
Zealand appreciates and understands about this Government, and about our Prime
Minister, is the fact that the re is commitment and consistency. So that was the
September comment.
Last week on 23 February the Leader of the Opposition accused the Government of
abandoning Taranaki. He said during the oil boom Ministers touted Taranaki as the
golden province. He said : “Now they’re nowhere to be seen. It’s not good enough to
turn their back when the going gets tough.” So, once again, I went through and I looked
and counted the number of my colleagues who had come through to support not only
myself but the people of Tar anaki, and the people of New Plymouth. At the end of last
year the Prime Minister was there. Nikki Kaye, the Associate Minister of Education,
came to look at school buildings. Paula Bennett came at the end of last year to open the
new Novotel hotel and to look at areas of economic development in our region.
Just over a week ago Amy Adams came to celebrate the completion of the roll -out of
ultra-fast broadband in my city. Steven Joyce came last week. Judith Collins came last
week to support the business com munity and to visit the New Plymouth police station
and the Department of Corrections, where there is fantastic collaboration taking place.
Maggie Barry was in town. So even in the last month, since Parliament has been sitting,
we have had a considerable n umber of ministerial visits, with them coming to our
region every 4 to 5 days.
So what I am saying is that regional New Zealand continues to be on the agenda and
to have the attention of this Government, but we would be told differently. In fact, the
9242 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
people of my region shake their heads, they scratch their heads, and they wonder at
what they hear being so different to what they see. This is why, despite the rhetoric, this
Government and our Prime Minister continues to receive support from New
Zealanders—nearly one in every two. What they see is consistency. What they see is
consistency, and a tremendous gap between us and the Opposition, obviously, as well.
Then, of course, we have —I will not tell you what is happening and coming up. But
the previous spea ker came and visited Taranaki, not just recently, but let me just talk
about his visit last year —when he came with a number of his colleagues to visit the
Stratford power station. I think this is a great example of why people question the
validity of the m embers opposite to govern. My colleagues across the way, Mr Nash
and Carmel Sepuloni and, of course, Mr Grant Robertson, came and they had a good
look at some of our assets. There was an article in the Taranaki Daily News  that was
quite perplexing. So I wr ote a letter to the editor because I wanted to know the answer
about the difference between what they said and what I saw. I think New Zealanders all
the time want to know the difference between what they see and what the Opposition
says.
So I wrote a let ter to the editor. The article on 8 October by Hannah Lee is titled
“Labour Bigwigs”—that is, you, Mr Nash —“Visit on Regional Outreach”. It has Grant
Robertson, Labour’s finance spokesman, saying “there was an increased interest in the
Stratford power stat ion now that Contact Energy had shut down their Ōtāhuhu power
station for good, on 30 September … It’s a bit of a boost for Stratford.” So that is pretty
good. He knows Contact Energy is permanently closing the Ōtāhuhu power station,
therefore, Contact Ene rgy’s other assets, such as the Stratford power station, are going
to be in higher demand and higher need. I can see why Andrew Little made him finance
spokesman. Then he went on to say: “However, the power station, like other regional
infrastructure, was in need of desperate upgrades to bring it into the 21 st century.” If I
was Mr Nash at that point in time, as the energy spokesperson, I would be saying to Mr

items.speaker: Robertson
items.text: “Grant, please don’t say that. Don’t say that.”
So needing to understand his sublime co mmentary on energy generation and
infrastructure, I wrote a letter to the editor seeking the paper’s wisdom. In terms of
Grant Robertson’s referring to regional infrastructure needing a desperate upgrade, I
was not sure which of Contact Energy’s power stat ions in Stratford he says needs
upgrading. Could it be the 377 -megawatt station that Contact Energy describes as a
large, efficient and modern plant being one of the largest gas turbines in the world
housed in a single building? Could it be that one? Or pe rhaps it is the other power
station needed to be to be brought into the 21 st century, Contact Energy’s 200-megawatt
gas-fired station, the one that Hekia Parata, Chester Borrows, and I accompanied the
Prime Minister to, which he opened on 31 May 2011?
Just as I close, what I want to say is that credibility is the most tradable commodity
in politics. Just last week we had Mr Little telling all of Taranaki that the Government
has abandoned them. Just 2 days before, the Minister for Economic Development, the
Hon Steven Joyce, was there meeting with all the civic leaders of the whole region,
putting his finger on the pulse, finding out what is going on.
This is why this Government is credible and can be trusted. We have not
abandoned—in fact, we are committed a nd we work hard to support —regional New
Zealand, and we work hard to ensure that the economy of this nation continues to be
strong and will continue to grow even in places such as Taranaki, where the
commodities of milk and oil are receiving far less than they used to. What we see is a
region that is resilient, working hard, pulling together, and that is going to come through
this with flying colours. Thank you.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9243

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. The
Hon David Cunliffe—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: The member Jonathan Young,
who has just sat down, was half right. The Labour caucus committee was in Taranaki
this last week, and here is what the good people of Taranaki told us about National’s
regional development efforts: they are arrogant, they are o ut of touch, they have lost
their way, and they are a tired, third -term Government that needs to be retired. They
gave us three specific examples, and I will mention them.
The first one was the so-called regional growth studies. They are nothing but studi es.
People told us that the studies simply recite and package what the locals are already
doing. There is study but no money, study but no action, study but no plan, and people
are deeply cynical about National—a waste of space in regional development. It is like a
New Year’s resolution that you are going to go on a diet: “We’ll have regional
development this year.” Well, it does not happen under National because it does not do
action and it does not do a strategy.
The second example that comes to mind is the famous Ōpōtiki harbour development
in my colleague’s East Coast area. It is an economic and financial no -brainer. It has
been proven to officials and Ministers multiple times. What happens? The Government
does a kind of public relations sham and gives $3 million out of $30 million for yet
another study, maybe to announce a grant in an election year. The people of the Eastern
Bay of Plenty are not that stupid. They know when there is a con under way, and that
con was Steven Joyce.
The third example that  the member actually raised is the problem with white gold
and black gold —oil and dairy. Well, we cannot control the oil market and we cannot
control the global dairy market, and that is the problem. We have got all our cows in
one basket. Labour has been saying for the last 6 years: “We need a plan for economic
development. We need a plan to diversify our economy. We need a plan to add more
value in science and innovation, through research and tertiary education, to the God -
given natural resources that we do so well in.” What did National do? It converted
everything into dairy farms and then it wondered why things looked pretty ropey when
the price collapsed from 8 bucks to 4 bucks, and now, of course, there are calls to
socialise the problem after it priva tises the profit. You just watch this space, because
there will be a lot of farmer pressure to say “Well, we need a free pass from the banks.”,
the same banks that are announcing record profits—billions upon billions of dollars.
Let us talk about the Kiwi  Dream. You know, half of New Zealand is enslaved to
mortgages, making those Aussie banks really, really, rich with those record profits. The
other half is trapped in a rental poverty trap, struggling to keep up and struggling to get
their kids through ter tiary education, but not getting ahead —middle-class Kiwis never
getting ahead —of the fortnightly or monthly pay check. A country of aspiration, we
used to be.

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: Like leadership.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: A country of winners, we used to be. Oh, ho! There is
Judith Collins, arising from the crypt, talking about leadership aspiration. Pots, kettles—
yeah. The Kiwi Dream is worth campaigning for. The Kiwi Dream is not about lofty
goals. It is not about spin.  It is about the absolute basics: a roof over your head that is
warm and dry, whether you own it or you rent it; some security of tenure for people
who are renting.
The Kiwi Dream is about having a good job and the education available to keep up
with the changing workplace. That is why Labour’s Working Futures Plan gives 3 years
of free tertiary education for any type of training from apprenticeship to PhD at any
time of your life, from post-school to pre-retirement. Our children are never going to do
9244 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
one job all their lives; they might do 10 jobs, and they are going to need to move into
and out of the workforce. Here is the choice. When you boil it all down, we have got a
choice between two futures: a dumb economy that is vulnerable to those commodity
price cycles, or a smart economy, where we invest in knowledge and invest in each
other, close those widening equity gaps, and protect our environment. If we do that, that
is a dream worth making real. That is what a Labour -led Government is going to
deliver, with our colleagues here, for a truly better future for all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Clare Curran, 5 minutes.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: The Prime Minister’s statement is
an opportunity to get a bit philosophical about why we are politicians and about why we
are all here, why we are all committed to a set of values, what we actually came  in here
to do, and whether or not we have managed to achieve any of it. So I am going to start
with a quote from A A Milne, who, as you all know, wrote Winnie-the-Pooh: “Pay
attention to where you are going because without meaning you might get nowhere.”
Well, this National Government has not only lost its way, but it is turning our political
system into a fake democracy —a fake democracy, where there is no Kiwi Dream and
where there is not much meaning.
Just a month ago, New Zealand slipped down again in the global transparency
rankings. We are no longer the least corrupt country in the world. Transparency
International’s 2016 Corruption Perceptions Index ranks us behind Denmark, Finland,
and Sweden. This is our worst ranking since 1998, which was the year  before Helen
Clark became the Prime Minister. Our Public Service works hard to be open and
impartial, but this Government is doing damage to our reputation, whether it is through
the Saudi sheep saga, whether it is the Oravida scandal, whether it is handi ng out
payments to MediaWorks, or whether it is cronyism and dodgy deals. But, of course,
that is not all.
Jonathan Young talked about the Opposition undermining the achievements of this
Government. Well, what has really been happening since 2009 is that we have seen a
steady erosion of democracy in this country. There are some glaring examples of this.
Some of the most glaring include the freezing of funding and the gutting of public
broadcasting in this country, the stifling of reasoned debate —public deb ate—and the
scoffing at, and belittling of, those who have attempted to keep debate alive in this
country. As I said, we have been embroiled in scandals around handouts to MediaWorks
and editorial interference in Māori Television. We have seen questionable  appointments
to the board of Radio New Zealand, the freezing of funding to Radio New Zealand,
New Zealand On Air, and Māori Television, the killing off of TVNZ 7 —I could go on
and on. It is just the tip of the iceberg, but there are more. There are increa sed central
government powers at the expense of elected regional and local government—of course,
the suspending of the elected council at Environment Canterbury is the glaring example
of that.
There is the withholding of information under the Official Inf ormation Act —
delaying or releasing documents that are mostly redacted. This is not a Government that
is committed to transparency and openness, which we saw late last year when the
Ombudsman released a report into the Official Information Act that showed
Government departments being encouraged by Ministers’ offices to withhold material
for political reasons. It was incredibly disappointing. That report also contains some
disappointing information from the Ombudsman, with her suggestion that media and
politicians could be charged for information, which would set a dangerous precedent. It
is a longstanding convention that agencies do not charge media or politicians because it
would stifle the free flow of information that is in the public interest. So what
happened? In January we had the first sign that agencies are charging for Official
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9245
Information Act requests, with the Reserve Bank charging a Fairfax business journalist
as part of that policy.
Then we have got hard evidence of Government inaction on transpa rency and
accountability, with the Open Government Partnership report released just a couple of
weeks ago—New Zealand is part of an Open Government Partnership consisting of 69
Governments—which found a huge lack of consultation and ambition in opening up the
Government and an action plan that consists of programmes that are already under way
and are not designed to improve Government practice. That report does not practise
what it preaches.
We are seeing a lack of openness and transparency. What New Zeala nders want is a
sense of meaning from their Government; instead, we have a Government that has lost
its way.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki): I am not sure whether one would call
that last speech philosophical or just sort of a litany of woes that really just have not, I
think, got any impact whatsoever. I have to say, when I go around my electorate and
other parts of the country, it is funny t hat nobody, but nobody, raises or mentions those
issues at all. In fact, if you are talking to people out in the electorates, what they talk
about is very much what we heard in the Prime Minister’s statement, and I will come to
some of those bits later.
I thought, though, to start —I just want to very briefly touch on Cyclone Winston.
The primary reason for that, having lived and worked in Fiji and, in fact, gone through a
cyclone a few years ago there, is to just speak, I suppose, in solidarity somewhat wit h
the people there, to say to them: Ni sa bula vinaka na kai viti, e vanua viti. Having been
through a cyclone —it literally came up the driveway where I lived and blew the place
apart—I can say that the people of Fiji are incredibly resilient. We often att ribute great
smiling faces to them as a people and, despite this adversity, I am pretty sure those
smiles will still be there.
The one thing about cyclones is —obviously, you have a few hours of terror, if you
will, but it is the damage that continues to be  done afterwards. I suppose, in using a few
minutes of this speech, it is to encourage New Zealanders and Kiwis to continue to be
generous. The cyclone itself might destroy the buildings but it also rips up the crops,
particularly the dalo plant. It turns it into a little helicopter and literally pulls it right out
of the ground. So the first week you would actually go, as we did, and harvest some
food and eat. But in the weeks after, it begins to rot and, of course, you begin to run out
of food. Where we w ere, we were cut off for about a month, and so your food supplies
begin to run very low. The other thing —and those who have lived in the Islands will
know—is that all the sea salt gets blown up on to the land and actually scorches the land
and the trees, a nd everything goes brown. It is not actually that they have been ripped
out of the ground in that case, but, again, scorched.
So an encouragement to those listening and to New Zealanders as a whole, and to
this House—continue to support the people of Fiji . The cyclone is not just simply an
activity of a few hours but is something that goes on for weeks and months. In fact,
even after I had left, after a couple of years, the damage of the particular cyclone that I
went through was still being felt. Again, t o the people of Fiji, I want to wish them well
and strength at this time.
This remains a very strong and positive Government. As said in the Prime Minister’s
statement, there has been a whole list of activities where we have performed incredibly
strongly. We have heard everything from the increase in wages, unemployment, which
is falling and is expected to fall even further, and, of course, an area of interest to myself
is around health care —an incredibly positive story to be told there. I think that is
reflected in a couple of ways. First and foremost, we know that more elective surgeries
9246 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
are being done. I note that a couple of constituents this week, sadly, have had to go to
hospital. I am thinking of Valerie, in particular —if she is listening in —who wrote in
and told me: “Six days in hospital, but a remarkably excellent experience through the
Auckland DHB.” So we know that not only are surgeries going up but also the quality
of surgeries is seen as very positive.
We know that extra funding is being put into the likes of palliative care. I think that it
is particularly good to acknowledge the good people of the Eastern Bays Hospice. Once
again, those from Tāmaki will know the Eastern Bays Hospice, or at the very least the
Dove shops, which raise an enormous amount of money for hospice care in our
community. One thing that I always like to stress to the House is that hospices like
Eastern Bays Hospice are actually about where people are able to be at home and be
supported. It is not like this little mini -hospital filled with morphine and other drugs; it
is actually a life-giving dynamic, and I want to thank all of those who work in hospices,
particularly those within my own electorate. We have got a whole lot of these new pain
management teams out now. There is  a lot of support, particularly for people with
orthopaedic pain. Again, a really good news story.
I think that is somewhat reflected in the work of the Health Committee at the
moment. It is, and remains, an incredibly, incredibly busy Health Committee. Ov er the
last year—and, again, I think it is indicative of just how well the Government is doing—
we have seen more funds made available to assist carers. There was a bill we just passed
2 weeks ago in this House with unanimous support —a bill under a National
Government—to actually pay those providing care for the cost of transport, for the first
time. We are also updating the Radiation Safety Act, and I think later today, actually,
we may have a chance to complete that piece of work. Last year we updated legi slation
around health practitioners. In other words, we are looking at the health industry in New

items.speaker: Zealand and saying
items.text: “How do we increase the scope of practice for various
professions?”. The best example is things around death certificates or sick leave
certificates, which are primarily the purview of medical practitioners, but we are saying:
“Actually, scopes of practice have changed now, so why not see nurses and others being
involved with that?”. We have also modernised elements around health protection.  This
was around regulation of sunbeds, but also dealing with how we, I suppose, monitor
infectious diseases. So, again, it is a busy select committee, but I think it is indicative of
actually what is a very positive Government making positive changes.
I say though that it is busy —it was something I was sharing with some members of
my constituency last week around the select committee, because petitions often come
up. I thought I would give an indication of just some of the topics that the Health
Committee is looking at at the moment and acknowledge those who have put these in.
There are quite a number of petitions before the committee. We are dealing with
everything from surgical mesh to transgender operations, female prophylactics to tube -
weaning—so that i s for young people, babies mainly, who have to be fed by tube and
how you wean them off that. It is quite a difficult process. We are looking at adrenalin
autoimmune-injectors, or EpiPens, if you have an anaphylactic shock. We have been
looking at petition s around public health and disability, pharmaceutical waste, assisted
suicide, and the district health board in Northland. And services —pathology services.
We are looking at maternity services and smoking, and —just when you think that we
had not actually c overed all the topics, moral, ethical, medical, and otherwise —we are
also looking at the whole element of cannabis, Sativex, as well. So, it is a rather busy
and, I would like to think, hard -working committee, with all members —but I certainly
say that of our Government members—working incredibly hard.
So, for me, we are a Government that remains incredibly focused, a Government that
is incredibly busy, and I think one that remains very much in touch with New Zealand.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9247
One of the best gauges for me is being i n the electorate. It is where I derive most of my
strength and energy, working with the good people of Tāmaki, and they continue to talk
about the things that matter. Most of what we have heard from the other side today is
really just superfluous in many w ays. It is not what really impacts on people: health,
absolutely; education, for sure; and crime, and law and order are incredibly important —
knowing that they are safe in their homes. And, of course, the economy is something
important, too.
But the people of Tāmaki have also understood that the Government is behind them,
and so, in the last year in particular, we have had a number of successes, again, building
on the good work of the Government. So there has been money for a cycleway. I know
the member for Auckland Central is very proud of her —I think—bright pink cycleway.
Ours is not going to be pink, I understand, but we have a wonderful cycleway going
from Glen Innes through to Tāmaki Drive. We have had about 45 new classrooms for
our schools promised, and more money for Mandarin teaching.
So there is, I suppose, a positive amount of real positive work going on, particularly
in the education field. I am very conscious that today in the gallery there is a young lady
who is now out of school but was formerly  of Glendowie College here to grace us, and
that, actually, we have got amazing young people who are in our communities. I see that
day after day, and I certainly see it when I go to the high schools and colleges in my
electorate, be it Selwyn, Tāmaki, Gle ndowie, or Sacred Heart —remarkable young
people doing remarkable things. This Government is behind them, it is behind our
education system, and also—as I was indicating earlier —it is really strongly behind the
health sector.
So I think we have a very prou d record as a Government. I think the Prime Minister
himself has articulated things very well and clearly in his statement. We are a
Government that talks about the things that matter. We are a Government that remains
very much in touch with the people of New Zealand. We are a Government that is going
to continue working hard because we are doing that listening. And if we need no better
proof, it is just to look at the polls of where we are, and where the Opposition is.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: What a pleasure to be able to
take a call on the Prime Minister’s statement. I must say I am so delighted to be back as
the Minister of Police and the Minister of C orrections as well as, obviously, being the
MP for Papakura. I have to say, in the last couple of months when I have been coming
back into the role, it has been so good to go and visit the police and the Department of
Corrections and also to have a look at  some of the other work that is going on but also
to be back helping to make decisions around where we go to from here, because we
have had some amazing achievements in the whole justice sector in the last 6 or 7 years.
When I think about the fact that we are now at the lowest recorded crime rate since
1978, we have reduced the number of offences —“we” as in the whole of Government
and all of the wonderful agencies working with us —by 100,000 over the last 5 years. It
is a tremendous achievement, and I would just like to sing out, basically, a bit of praise
for the police, the Department of Corrections, and all the other agencies and NGOs, as
well as the Government agencies working together to bring that about. We have crime
rates down. We have youth crime dow n. We have all of those areas down, but one area
that I think we have all felt the need to get better progress in is family violence.
If we look at family violence—and I know that this is a real topic in our entire justice
sector. The reason is that famil y violence actually leads to more violence. One of the
things that we have done today is to make some announcements —my colleague Anne
Tolley and I —around gangs. In my particular announcements around the Gang
Intelligence Centre, which is based in the polic e but works across a whole raft of
agencies from the Ministry of Social Development to the Department of Corrections, to
9248 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
Immigration New Zealand, to the Customs Service, and to others as well —what the
centre does is it really goes after and targets gangs.
You might ask why we would do that —why I am saying that in the same breath as I
am talking about family violence.
Well, actually, there is a very good reason. Sixty percent of children who grow up in
gang homes are the victims of family violence —so that is 60 percent—so much so and
so violent that Child, Youth and Family are involved. We are not talking about a smack
on the hand; we are talking about children being abused and/or neglected, so much so
that Child, Youth and Family is involved. That is a pre tty staggering thing to say, is it
not?
I go to the prisons and talk to the prison directors —who used to be called prison
managers but they are prison directors now, and I did that just the other day —they say
to me that they believe that 90 percent of all  of the prisoners in our jails have
themselves been victims of family violence as children. When I was first the Minister of
Corrections and I went and visited the women’s prisons, I found out a little bit about
some of the prisoners there, and I realised—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable Minister. The time has come for me to leave the Chair.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Tēnā koe e Te Whare, tēnā koutou e te whānau o Te
Pāremata. Kia ora mai tātou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[Greetings to you, the House, and to the family of Parliament; thank you and
acknowledgments to you all.]
Members, when we adjourned for the evening meal break the Hon Judith Collins was
speaking. She has 6 minutes and 30 seconds remaining to speak.

items.speaker: Pita Paraone
items.text: She was in her stride too.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yes, that little break can actually stop the flow, but let us
get back into it. I was speaking I think, from memory, about visiting our two women’s
prisons and realising, after discussing some matters with some of the prison staff as well
as the prisoners, that actually what they had in general —and obviously there are always
exceptions—were some of the most abused women in the country. They are abused
because the vast majority of them are gang women and they live in a culture of abuse.
Yes, some of them have gone on to commit dreadful crimes against their own child ren
and some of them have been involved in the methamphetamine trade —they are not
there just because they were abused; they are actually there because they have
committed very serious crimes —but there is a huge relationship between abuse of
children and those children choosing at a later stage to go on to abuse others.
That is not to say for a moment that all people who are abused, children who are
abused, or victims are going to then become perpetrators, but there is a very serious
connection between abuse and that person going on to become an abuser. I think one of
the issues that we have learnt is that the abuse of children, the abuse of people, can lead
to trauma. If it is not recognised as a trauma and it is treated as “Well, this is what
happens in th is family. This is what we do. I know, let’s put them back with the
grandparent, who, by the way, used to abuse the parent.”, we are going to continue to
have kids being killed in their own homes.
In my electorate in Papakura we are a very diverse elector ate. There are a lot of
gangs, there are a lot of really great people, and there is a lot of every mixture you could
think of, but what I also know too is that there are some kids who never get a chance.
They never get a chance in life because their own fa milies are so dysfunctional that
dysfunctional is simply a word and is basically a platitude, because the families are so
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9249
bad that for their kids, home for them is the least safe place that they could ever be.
There is a reason that these kids are out on t he street at 2 o’clock in the morning as 9 -
year-olds, or whatever. Primarily, it is because home is so unsafe. It is not because mum
and dad are at work. It is not because something is happening there. It is because home
is unsafe, and that is what we are dealing with.
So when Anne Tolley and I today were discussing and announcing some of the
initiatives being put together and announced on the gang initiatives, it is not about
cracking down, it is not about banning, and it is not about whatever, but it is actually
about these kids. If we can try to stop these kids being abused, if we can try to stop
some of those behaviours, we will actually make a difference when it comes to those
kids growing up and becoming violent, angry people —but mostly angry men —and
going on to commit further acts of violence.
I also heard tonight that someone said that methamphetamine is not a problem now.
That is piffle. Last year, in 2015, 334.3 kilograms was seized by customs and police.
That is three times more than the year before, in 2014, when it 98.8 kilograms. We have
got a big problem here, and this trade is being fuelled by, and fuels, gang activity. In
prisons, they say it is more dangerous now for staff because gangs are now working
together and they are working together against corrections staff.
What I would say to this House is that we have done really well in the law and order
area. As a Government, we have done great work. Our agencies have worked together.
We have worked together for some common goals for the peopl e, but I would also say
we have got a long way yet to go, and we have not solved the problem and we will not
solve it until kids can be safe in their own homes and men and women can be safe in
their own homes. That is a really sad thing to have to admit—that we have kids growing
up in homes where there is no such thing as safety unless dad, or mum’s partner, is
actually put in jail, and that that is the best that we can do for some kids. That is just not
good enough. We do have a big issue there and we are taking steps to address it.
We have dealt with issues before that have been hard. When we first came into
Government, illegal street racing was a big issue. In 2009 we had six people die, 49
people were injured, and we had a total of 69 crashes involving illegal street racing. We
brought in the laws around vehicle confiscation and crushing. In 2014 there were no
deaths, 23 injuries, and 33 total crashes for that year. This problem has been hit on the
head. Yes, it still occurs, but not anything like it did occur.
I would love us to be able to say as a Parliament that we took some steps one day and
we actually sorted out family violence in this country. It is a big ask. It is not easy. If it
was easy, it would have been done. It is a really hard job, and I would like us all to work
together on it. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: It is a split call on behalf of the Labour Party —5
minutes, Poto Williams.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Kia orana. That is a really
good note on which to start my contribution, because I do want to respond to some of
the comments that the Minister has made around family violence.
Much of what the Minister has said, I agree with. In fact, most of what she has said, I
agree with. I agree that family violence is a huge, huge problem in this country, and I
agree that many people in New Zealand will concur that dealing with the issue of gangs
and gang families will go so me way to dealing with the issue of family violence.
However, when you have the situation where you have over 100,000 family violence
call-outs by police in a year, the gang portion of that statistic is minor —is minute —
compared with the impacts that it has  for every single community in this country.
Whether they are low socio -economic communities or whether they are in the leafy
suburbs, every community is impacted by family violence.
9250 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
Although this measure goes some way to addressing a portion of it, here w e are, yet
again, debating the use of targeting resources to a particular group versus taking some
universal steps to address the issue across the country. A hundred thousand family
violence call-outs by police: that would mean that there were at least 95, 000 families
who are not gang affiliated who are still going to be impacted by family violence, and
whom the measures that the Minister has announced today will not touch—they will not
touch. There are 62,000 family violence investigations where at least o ne child is
resident or present in a home where violence has occurred. The measures that have been
announced today will not impact 60,000 of those children.
The Minister did touch on a very important point, and that is about the trauma that is
experienced by these children. It may not necessarily be that they are experiencing the
violence themselves in the sense of being physically abused; the fact that they are in a
home where violence is present, even if they are not physically abused, is traumatic
enough for them to be damaged and to have huge impacts on their future life
outcomes—negative impacts.
The Minister, I want to reiterate, was also the Minister who reformed the Family
Court, and the impacts of that reform have had a negative impact on family violence. It
is now harder to obtain a protection order to keep yourself safe. The reductions to the
threshold for legal aid mean that fewer and fewer women, in particular, are able to
obtain those protection orders. How are they able to keep themselves an d their children
safe when the key legal mechanism with which to do that is withdrawn from them
because of changes that that Minister made to the Family Court? Also included in that
reform was the reduction in access to Family Court counselling, where many  issues for
families were resolved before they became major concerns for the country.
So although I concur with much of what the Minister says, yet again this country is
headed down a very, very dark passageway for when we are dealing with targeting
small groups of people and when the problem is so epidemic. I was not going to speak
specifically about family violence; I was going to address some other issues of trauma
that exist in my community in Christchurch East. But I must respond to what the
Minister has said in this regard.
Family violence is a scourge on our society when 100,000 incidents are reported and
they are only a fifth of what occurs. We need to be looking away from targeting, and to
doing some specific work with those NGOs, with the refuges, with the police, and with
Child, Youth and Family to contain this epidemic and not just look at specific and small
targeted areas. I think that is not a good use of our taxpayer funding. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A second 5 -minute call for the Labour Party —Louisa
Wall.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora e Te Māngai o Te Whare, tuatahi,
aroha ki te whānau o Dr Ranginui Walker, moe mai rā e te rangatira.
[Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. Firstly, empathy to the family of Dr Ranginui
Walker. Sleep, esteemed one.]
I am actually really pleased to take a call in the debate on the Prime Minister’s
statement and I really want to focus on two points that he made . The first was that he
said there will be a $17 billion hole in the economy —so the Government is already
anticipating that our revenue will be short $17 billion. The other point that he made,
which I just find incredible, was that in spite of that this Go vernment is 100 percent
focused on tax cuts.
The fact that it is 100 percent focused on tax cuts as part of its fiscal strategy got me
thinking about what that means. What that actually means is that there will be spending
cuts and, as such, there will be  service cuts. So I was thinking about the services that
will be cut because of the Government’s obsession within that context to give tax cuts to
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9251
the people they have traditionally given them to —wealthy New Zealanders, who, quite
frankly, do not need them . So what does that do to undermine our public service: the
provision of hospital services, social services —services that New Zealanders need,
actually, to keep them healthy and to keep them well.
I found it really interesting at the beginning of the year , on 9 January, actually, that
there was quite a big write -up and media focus on the rheumatic fever prevention
programme in South Auckland, which is now is in its fifth year. It is actually a $45
million investment because this Government, rather than pro vide houses so people did
not get sick, actually said: “What we’ll do instead is we’ll go and test the kids.” So they
are working in 61 South Auckland schools, and last year 20,000 cases of group A
streptococcus were detected through that programme. That i s incredibly commendable
because what that meant is those kids could get antibiotics. Why? Because if we could
prevent group A streptococcus turning into something else —that is, rheumatic fever —
then that was the Government’s solution to addressing this who le issue of poverty and
the lack of quality housing provision in South Auckland.
So I was incredibly surprised to see on 9 January this year that the funding that
Counties Manukau District Health Board is receiving for this programme is going to be
cut by 50 percent. On 1 July 50 percent of that $9 million annual investment will go, so
it is the district health board’s responsibility to keep funding that programme that has
proved effective and has found 20,000 children who need access to antibiotics to stop
them from getting rheumatic fever. Wow!
The Counties Manukau District Health Bo ard is one of all district health boards
around the country, except for the Southern District Health Board or one of the boards
in the south, that does not have to cut funding. But, actually, Counties Manukau District
Health Board is part of the $138 milli on—what would I call it? The hospitals are being
directed to save money —$138 million —this year. Counties Manukau District Health
Board has to save $20 million. So not only does it have to save $20 million it is also
going to lose $4.5 million for an initia tive that this Government has been trumpeting
and has been very proud about because it is stopping South Auckland kids from getting
rheumatic fever. Those are the challenges and those are some of the decisions that it has
made because of the obsession of this Government to cut taxes.
It has meant cuts in mental health services in Canterbury, and I know that my
colleague Denise Roche talked about this earlier. Within the context of the increased
need of people in Christchurch calling out for help —we know th at the helplines for
young people have been oversubscribed for 5 years —what has the Government decided
to do? It is going to cut funding for mental health services in Canterbury. It is ludicrous.
It is ridiculous. We are supposed to govern in the best inte rests of all New Zealanders
and meet their needs —and this Government, supposedly, has put Canterbury as a big
priority—but, actually, its obsession with tax cuts means that it is cutting funding for
rheumatic fever, it is cutting funding for mental health services, it has cut funding for
Women’s Refuge, and, actually, the list could go on and on and on.
I think that this Budget, actually, is a dark day—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: It’s not a Budget.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: The Prime Minister’s priorities, which actually will translate
through to the Budget, will be incredibly interesting to see. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5 -minute call on behalf of the National Party —Paul
Foster-Bell.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER -BELL
items.text: E Te Mana Whakawā Tuarua, tēnā koe; tēnā
koutou katoa e ngā mema o Te Whare. I take pleasure in speaking in support of the
Prime Minister’s statement in this debate on his statement in the House. I will be
sharing my call with my colleague Ian McKelvie, the honourable member for the
9252 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
Rangitīkei, so I plan to cover the town issues and I will leave it to Mr McKelvie to
cover the country.
Here in Wellington we have enjoyed a wonderful summer. Not only has the weather
been superb and allowed us to enjoy some great cricket on display, but we have had
some extraordinary events here. The hotel beds have been full. In fact, we have had a
record year for tourism in Wellington and everything from that Sir Pete r Jackson
Gallipoli exhibit at Te Papa through to The Great War Exhibition at the National War
Memorial museum—and I want to pay tribute to Christopher Finlayson and the input he
had into that wonderful attraction —has been awash with tourists and visitors spending
their money here in the capital. Similarly, Weta Workshop —when I had some relatives
staying over the summer I decided to take them out to Weta Workshop to see the
Thunderbirds Are Go exhibit, where they can see the sets used to recreate that iconi c
1960s TV series —also enjoyed large numbers of visitors. Wellington has benefited
from record tourist numbers.
We have also seen significant Government investment into the capital. I would point
to the ICT Graduate School, which will upskill our workforce  with those modern
technical capabilities that they need to be able to earn those good incomes. That will be
implemented here in Wellington, hosted by Victoria University over the coming year.
If I can turn to another issue, it is that this year is the 30 th anniversary of the
legalisation of homosexuality in New Zealand. I want to put on record that I enjoy
working cross-party with colleagues, including the member who just resumed her seat,
Louisa Wall. We will be hosting an event here at Parliament on Satu rday that kicks off
Pride Week here in Wellington, and I am looking forward to doing that. But later on this
year there will be events, I think, in the parliamentary precinct to commemorate the
decriminalisation, which was a significant event in New Zealan d’s history. I am proud
to be a member of a Government that also looks out for the interests of all members of
our community, not just the majority.
I had an interesting discussion recently with a constituent here around refugees, and I
would point, in the Prime Minister’s statement, to his comments around the threat posed
by Islamic State of Iraq and Syria and also the refugee problem that the world is facing.
This person with whom I was chatting was a Polish migrant—one of the Pahīatua Poles.
She was an o rphan who, after her family was treated horrendously by the Soviets —she
and her mother were deported to a gulag in Siberia —then came to New Zealand via
Iran, actually, of all places. They stopped there for a few years on their way to New
Zealand. In the discussion with this constituent, a very clear point came across. She was
pointing out that, actually, the last thing that the refugees who are coming to New
Zealand need is pity. Pity is not what will help them to integrate into our community. It
is not what will help them to get jobs, to become educated, and to make a contribution
to their new home, New Zealand.
I am proud to be part of a Government where there will be an additional number of
refugees accepted into New Zealand, but that is being done in a c ontrolled way, unlike
what we are seeing in Europe. We will have the health facilities, the transport, the
housing, the social development, and the educational services in place to make sure
those people are properly looked after. I look at the approach ta ken by some of the
parties in this House and by some of the lobbyists in the community, who are promoting
either what I would describe as the hard -hearted approach—that is, to reject all, even
those who are fleeing from some of the worst atrocities in the world; fleeing for their
very lives—or the soft-headed approach, where we want to open up the doors in such a
way that we would take numbers that we are not able to properly support. I am proud to
be part of a Government that is actually taking the right c ourse of action, which will be
looking after those who are escaping from real danger, but we are not opening the
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9253
floodgates to New Zealand. I fully commend the Prime Minister’s statement to the
House.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5 -minute call on behalf of the National Party —the
honourable member Ian McKelvie.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I am like the off -course substitute, Mr
Deputy Speaker. For those wh o do not know what that was, in the old days at the TAB
the off-course substitute was the one that replaced the one that was there before —Jami-
Lee Ross, thank you.
I come from the Rangitīkei, obviously, and I have always prided the Rangitīkei on
having the most intelligent part of New Zealand in my electorate. Of course, the piece
of Palmerston North that has got the most intelligent people is in my electorate.

items.speaker: Iain Lees -Galloway
items.text: No, they live in my electorate —they go to work in your
electorate, but they live in my electorate.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: You can imagine my absolute amazement when I read, the other
day, that Whanganui is one of the world’s most intelligent cities. In fact, it is in the top
seven in the world.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am not surprised.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I immediately thought of Mr Deputy Speaker —well, that is
where he comes from, of course. Just to appease the member for Palmerston North, the
Rangitīkei electorate also has more sheep than any other electorate in New Zealand, just
as a matter of interest, including Southland.
I want to talk briefly about the Trans -Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement and its
effect on an electorate like mine. It will have a positive impact on our challenged
communities, and the reason it will is that as we move into the increased incomes as a
result of our trade agreements and the TPP agreement, the trickle -down effect will
significantly impact on those electorates through things like dairy,  sheep, beef, and
timber. I want to talk particularly about timber in the Rangitīkei electorate and around
New Zealand because the change that I envisage coming, and I think we all envisage
coming, as a result of the TPP agreement in the timber industry, f or example, will be to
encourage a lot more manufactured products to leave New Zealand. That will be good
for the New Zealand timber industry.
The other point about the timber industry, of course, is that we have so many pine
trees in New Zealand we probably do not have the infrastructure to get them all out in as
quick a form as we might need to. So that will be a challenge for the future, and of
course it is going to moderate the number of trees that are cut down at any one time, just
because we need to get them processed and out of the country. So that is an interesting
issue.
The Government, over the last 7 years, has moved to significantly improve our
tourism opportunities. Of course, the north end of my electorate has a great reliance on
tourism. The Whanganui River and the changes that have happened to the ownership
and the development of tourism opportunities around the Whanganui River —what is
going on with cycle tours, river tours via jetboats, canoes, and other means. They are all
very busy. Recre ational walking, cycling, fishing, and climbing are attracting people
from all around the world to our country, to our region. The critical thing that will
enable this to continue, of course, is our work with the environment. I think it is really
important that Minister Smith, who has worked very hard on a lot of the issues around
our environmental stuff, is now moving again to further our opportunities to clean up
our waterways. I think that that is a challenge, and I guess in a way it is a nervous
challenge for many in rural New Zealand, but none the less it is a challenge that we
need to face up to. It is hugely important for our tourism and agricultural industries that
we take that opportunity and make sure it works.
9254 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
The policies of this Government are now creating jobs in regions and areas that for
years have struggled. This is evidenced by the much-improved unemployment figures—
a 3 percent turn -round in 12 months in my region —and the fact that 175,000 new jobs
have been created in the past 3 years. Ove r the last 7 years the average wage has
increased significantly, and the announcement just yesterday of the new minimum wage
of $15.25 an hour will again make another difference to those people who are paid at
that end of the scale.
It is a challenge for our rural towns to survive and to continue to grow, but it is
important that we do. I think this Government is supporting them in a manner that will
enable more jobs to be created and will enable more young people to stay in those areas.
I think in the fut ure we are going to see significant growth, particularly around the
tourism industry, and particularly in the north of the Rangitīkei electorate and in many
other parts of New Zealand, as we move further down the path of developing our
environmental opportunities and developing our tourism opportunities.
Our challenge as a small trading nation is to sell more to the rest of the world than
we do now. We need to go into these trade agreements and move ourselves along as
quickly as we can. We need to create n ew products and we need to create new
opportunities for the producers of those products, and I think this Government’s policies
are moving those along pretty quickly. So I have a great deal of pleasure in supporting
the Prime Minister’s statement. I think we are on the right track, and I look forward to
the next 12 months of our Government working very hard for New Zealanders. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5 -minute call on behalf of the National Party —
Parmjeet Parmar.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: It is with great pleasure that I take this call
to support the Prime Minister’s statement. I would like to start by congratulating our
Prime Minister on his strong commitment to New Zealand and on keeping on delivering
what he promised to do. This year, just like the last year, is going to be a great year,
under the leadership of the Rt Hon John Key. I am saying it is going to be a great year
because wages are rising faster than inflation. In the last year the average wage grew by
3.1 percent and inflation stayed at 0.1 percent. My hands cannot demonstrate the scale,
but the difference is obvious —3.1 percent versus 0.1 percent. Business confidence is
high and t here is strong activity in all sectors, including the manufacturing sector. We
know we have come through significant challenges, and we have stayed on top of our
spending. That is evident from us receiving a surplus for the 2014-15 year.
This is a Governm ent that is a sensible manager of the Government’s finances. But
the Opposition has started coming out with some irresponsible spending pledges. Its
education policy shows that it lacks fiscal understanding. It lacks the understanding of
what New Zealander s want. I am saying that is an irresponsible spending pledge
because Kiwis do not need a reminder about the significant challenges that we have
come through. That is why on this side of the House we are focusing on the economy.
We are focusing on growing o ur businesses so that they can invest more, create more
jobs, and create higher-paying jobs so that we can continually keep investing sensibly in
different sectors.
To support our economy we need free -trade agreements. The Trans -Pacific
Partnership (TPP) agreement is in the best interests of New Zealand. As the Prime
Minister, the Rt Hon John Key, keeps saying in very, very simple words, we are a
country of only 4.5 million people. Our businesses cannot grow by just selling goods
and services to each other . We need access to bigger markets. What has shocked me is
the Opposition members’ stand on the TPP agreement. It has shocked me that they are
unable to comprehend the importance of the TPP agreement, even when explained in
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9255
such simple words. It is a pity that they do not see the importance of the TPP to our
businesses and households. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is always ironic to note that female members
from the Opposition always talk the loudest while a female member of the Government
is on her feet. I suggest to  members to take a breath and allow the member to complete
her speech.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Thank you. This side will continue to focus on—

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I take offence at that remark.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The member may well take off ence. I do not believe that
the observation of the Speaker in respect of that is a matter that the member can take
offence to. I look to the Clerk —I am sorry if the member has taken offence; I will not
withdraw the comment.

items.speaker: Iain Lees -Galloway
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think this raises an
interesting issue, and I appreciate the Clerk’s advi ce that there is no Standing Order
relating to when a member takes offence to something that the Speaker has said, but I
think that on this side of the House we would appreciate it if you would, perhaps, give
some thought to this and come back with a rulin g. Clearly, a member has taken offence
at a comment you made relating to interjections that were being made. There seems to
be a gap in the Standing Orders, and I think it would be helpful to the order of the
House if we had some ruling on what members sho uld do if the Speaker has caused
offence.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The member will be pleased to know that I have
reflected in the time that he has been making his point of order, and in the spirit of
cross-House collaboration I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: On this side, we will continue to focus on getting free -
trade agreements. We have achieved a free -trade agreement with Korea, and we have
started negotiations with the EU. Now, in the second year of our t hird term, as per the
Prime Minister’s statement, we will continue to invest in our families and households.
And we are seeing results. Unemployment figures have dropped to 5.3 percent. There
were 21,000 jobs created in the December quarter, and that figur e carries a very
important significance because, after working for the whole year, people evaluate,
analyse, and see whether they want to change jobs. So 21,000 jobs being created in the
December quarter is very good news. There were 175,000 jobs created i n the last 3
years.
To support that kind of growth, we need investment in our infrastructure, especially
in Auckland, because Auckland is our largest commercial centre. That is why the Prime
Minister has already announced bringing forward the start date o f the City Rail Link.
And, of course, we have our roads of national significance. Victoria Park Tunnel is a
great tunnel, and riding through that tunnel is a great experience. Commuters are saving
a lot of time going through that tunnel. We have finished d igging the Waterview tunnel,
and when the boring machine, Alice, finished boring that tunnel, I was there, just next to
the Mt Roskill electorate’s boundary, with our two Ministers, the Hon Simon Bridges
and the Hon Paul Goldsmith. I can tell you that the excitement there was huge.
We will continue to invest in our transport system and our motorway system to make
it reliable, safe, and efficient. We have accomplished a lot, yet we will continue to
invest more in our infrastructure in different sectors. We will continue to listen to the
people of New Zealand, and we will continue to create opportunities for our current and
future generations. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: It is a real pleasure for me to rise in support of the
Prime Minister’s statement, which will be of no surprise to the House. It has been an
interesting debate thus far. A comment that I heard from the other side of the House
9256 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
referred to the thinness of t his statement. I thought it was only appropriate for me to go
back and have a look. I suppose, from a distance, this does look like a rather thin
document but, when I looked at it, it has got quite small type, to be honest. But it is 10
pages long, and, on average, there are about 10 paragraphs per page.
There are a hundred —at least—different things that this Government proposes to do
over the next year. This is not a tired Government; this is not a Government that in its
third term is running out of ideas. This is a Government that is working hard for all New
Zealanders. It is working hard to ensure that New Zealand is the kind of place that we
all want to live in.
I am proud to be associated with a Government that puts people and families first.
This is a Government that over this time period has increased the minimum wage —as
the Minister of Finance said today—I think by 27 percent, while inflation has been only
11 percent over that time period. There have been significant increases in minimum
wages. We a re increasing the amount of paid parental leave, and we have decreased
ACC levies. We have been the first Government in 43 years —43 years—to actually put
up the real amounts of benefits to families with children.
This is a Government that puts jobs, the economy, and increasing opportunities at the
centre of economic development. We are moving forward; we are moving on with new
ideas. We are taking an innovative approach to solving some age-old problems over this
time period, over recent times, and we are going to continue to do this, as outlined in the
Prime Minister’s statement. We are going to continue our investment approach to public
services.
This is a Government that cares enough about the poor of our communities, those
who are most vulnerable in our communities, to ensure that we are looking at the causes
of those things that will, potentially, lead them into long -term benefit dependency and
other things. If we just simply say we are going to throw money at this or we are going
to continue doing thin gs the way we have always done and somehow expect to get a
different result, we will be fooling ourselves. And so what we are doing is ensuring that
we take innovative approaches, an investment approach, to ensure that those people who
are at most risk of long-term welfare dependency, who are at most risk of suffering
harm, those who are at most risk of not achieving educational standards —we are going
to provide better, more targeted services to them to ensure that their needs are met.
We are doing it thro ugh the social housing reforms. We were debating them last
week. It was good to see some of those bits of legislation go through that will ensure we
can provide better social housing for our people —that we are not sitting back and
simply saying that becaus e someone came up with an idea in the 1930s that that is the
only good idea you could ever have about social housing. No —we are moving forward,
we are trying to be innovative, and we are looking for new ways to do even better things
for the people of New Z ealand. But this document is, I think, particularly good because
it is not a narrow -focused document. The Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament for
this year is wide ranging.
I have just talked about our social investment strategy. We are also committe d to the
regions of New Zealand. We are committed to a regional growth programme. We have
seen regional growth studies across a number of communities in New Zealand, and that
is going to keep happening to others as well. This is about setting a blueprint f or
regional development and regional growth. I am privileged to live in a community
where we can take by -products from animal slaughter and turn them into
pharmaceutical products—it is fantastic to see the innovation that is happening there —
that can take N ew Zealand’s pāua crop, the majority of it, and can it and export it to
places around the world.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9257
We are moving forward economically, we are moving forward socially, and we are
moving forward environmentally. We are committed, as a party, to continue to cl ean up
New Zealand’s rivers. That is why we have got our new freshwater consultation
document out. There has been great work done, I know, in my own backyard, in the
Manawatū, where $5.2 million from the Fresh Start for Fresh Water Clean -up Fund has
been invested. The community is working together, alongside the Government, to clean
up the Manawatū River. We know that the progress is slow in these areas but we are
going to see progress. This is a great statement from our Prime Minister, it outlines
exactly what we want to do over the next year, and it will be better for New Zealand.

items.speaker: PITA PARAONE
