items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker. Engari, i mua i te
haere tonu o tēnei wāhanga, e tika ana kia tū  ake tēnei ki te tautoko i ngā mihi i
mihingia e tēnā o ngā rōpū tōrangapū ki a Whakatōhea, ā, me Te Waka o Mātaatua, i te
hingatanga o tō rātou rangatira, a Ranginui Walker. Ko ia te tangata hei tauira mō tātou
o Te Ao Māori puta noa ki te iwi whānui o Ao tearoa. Mēnā e hiakai ana koe ki te kai i
ngā mātauranga o te ao, kāore kau kē koe e hinga atu. Nā reira, e kara, e Rangi, haere,
haere hoki atu. Takahia e koe i runga te ara whānui, i kawe atu i a koe ki te
kāpunipunitanga o ngā wairua. Nā reira, kua ea t e wāhi mā koutou e noho nei i roto i te
ao wairua, ka hoki mai ki a tātou nō te ao tūroa, nā reira, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, huri
noa ki tēnei o tātou Whare.
[Greetings, Mr Deputy Speaker. But before this session continues, it is fitting that I
rise to support the tributes accorded by that one of the political parties to Whakatōhea
and the Mātaatua canoe at the death of their esteemed elder, Ranginui Walker. He is the
person who is a model for us of Māoridom and for the public throughout New Zealand.
If you crave to feast on worldly knowledge, you will never perish. So to you, dear friend,
Rangi, depart, farewell. Walk upon the broad path that will take you to the gathering
place of the spirits. Our part in regard to the spiritual world is therefore fulfill ed, and I
come back to us of the real world to acknowledge, greet, and salute you throughout this,
our House.]
Can I say that just listening to the comments emanating from the other side of the
House, I wonder sometimes whether I am in the same country, gi ven that those
members continue to extol the virtues of their Government and of their leader and how
they have addressed things like housing, health, unemployment, and education, and yet
where I come from, in the electorate that I am responsible for at thi s time on behalf of
the New Zealand First Party, Whangarei, the statistics, particularly in terms of Māori,
are not that good. That is in spite of the Government extolling the virtues of having the
Māori Party sitting at the same table. So I need to ask myself: is this is another world, or
am I just imagining things?
Can I say regarding Māori in the labour market that national Māori unemployment is
still sitting at 12.6 percent. Findings from both the 2014 and 2015 surveys identified the
exact same issues within Māori unemployment. Māori unemployment may have fallen
marginally in both 2014 and again last year, but it still remains twice as high as the rate
for all ethnic groups. I have not heard from that side of the House what the Government
has done in th at regard. I look at education. In 2015 Māori with degrees or higher
qualifications had the highest employment rate, 86.3 percent. Māori with no school
qualifications had the lowest employment rate, 42.4 percent. So it does pose the
question whether in fact the education that has been provided for our people is relevant
to them getting a job. There used to be a time when they would get their qualifications
and head off overseas. However, it is not so good now, particularly in Australia where
they used to go, because of the mining industry and the decline in work in that area.
I want to touch on something that I have had to face year in, year out, and that is the
question of Waitangi Day. As the chairman of the organising committee that puts
9258 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
together a progr amme for that day, we can always, as a committee, ascertain before
Waitangi Day whether the dust will fly, using a Māori paraphrase, or whether it will be
calm and everyone will enjoy themselves. Unfortunately, the Government chose to sign
the Trans -Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement 2 days out from Waitangi Day. One
should not be surprised at the reaction, not only from Māori but from people across the
nation. Although we might say that we have trade agreements that are good, I think the
nub of the protest is, essentially, about what the detail is in those agreements. Although
we have been assured by the Government that the Treaty will not be infringed on, we do
not have any evidence that in fact that is the case. So one should not be surprised:
although i t has been said that Māori do not know what they are objecting to, they
certainly know that they have not been told the detail. Likewise for the rest of the
country.
Can I suggest to the Government that, in spite of the comment about consulting the
people, the very people who were at Waitangi who protested certainly were not
consulted. The Government may have consulted some of its friends from the
“Browntable”, who are , in fact, behind driving a lot of the amendments to legislation
that will help strengthen their position at the “Browntable”, but the ordinary Joe
Bloggs—they have not been consulted. So one should not be surprised.
The other thing I am a little bit anno yed about is that every year we have a large
number of protesters who come to Waitangi, do their protest, and leave their crap
behind for those at home to have to deal with. To have a former leader of the National
Party and the ACT Party say that the perso n was not charged because they were Māori
is an insult, because the person certainly was not a Māori. The person was from
Christchurch, and I would like to tell her what she has caused at home and the fact that
we are now becoming a laughing stock of the w orld because of such activities. We
should be concerned.
The other thing is the question of the flag. Again we have people protesting about
that, and probably there may be a need for change, but did the people of New Zealand
ask for it? How often have we from this side talked about the need to have more funding
for particular social programmes, and been told that there is not enough money? Yet at
the whim of the Prime Minister we can find $26 million to try to make a flag change
that the majority of people do not want. The question has been asked: why should Māori
not ask for a change? Well, can I just remind this House that part of the present flag
includes the Union Jack, and if we go back to the Treaty of Waitangi, who was that
covenant between? Māori and Queen Victoria. So the Union Jack is a reminder to all of
us that the Treaty of Waitangi does have a part not only in the history of this country but
in the future of it as a whole. I just want to say those things and to say that in spite of
what Governm ent members have said about how good their party is, how good their
Government is, the facts certainly do not show that.
The member from Whangarei, Shane Reti, made comment about the different
roadworks, and he started off by listing the roadworks on the Brynderwyns. Can I tell
you that what has been done is not roadworks; it is probably more earthworks. It is
creating four lanes going into one lane at the top. So what about the other side of the
hill? He also used the Hikurangi bypass as an example. Can I  remind the member that it
was only a few years ago that that bypass was put in, so already either it is out of date or
the work that was done at the time has become irrelevant. So let us not get carried away
with what we think we might have done, given th at there is still an unacceptably large
number of our population, our fellow citizens, who are living in poverty. Nā reira, tēnā
koutou.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Maggie Barry—a 5-minute call.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9259

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.role: Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage
items.text: Kia ora, Mr
Deputy Speaker. Just a couple of weeks ago, I was with many of my esteemed
colleagues who are gathered aro und me here tonight at the Bluegreens Forum in
Tekapō. It is a wonderful part of the country, and I think it is good for politicians to get
out of the rarefied atmosphere of the Beehive. Having heard several of the calls from
Opposition members tonight, I think it would behove them well to get out and about a
little bit more into the community, because, far from sitting braying about what might
have been and fantasising about what they are not doing, it would be useful if they got
together, as we did a few weeks ago. My colleague here, Alfred Ngaro, is, of course, an
ardent Bluegreen, as are many of my colleagues here, because what we tend to do as a
Government is unite behind our Prime Minister, behind our leader, in stark contrast to
Labour. We do more for  the environmental and conservation movements than the
Greens would ever imagine, and I also think David Seymour made a couple of excellent
points.
There seems to be a bit of braying. Maybe some of the people across the other side of
the House might have had a little bit too much sun in the dinner break. They are a little
flushed and unreasoned. I have heard tonight about the struggles some of my colleagues
have had to be heard above the cacophony, so I am going to rise above it because I do
feel that ther e are some important things to say about the vision that we have around
conservation, in particular. I am sure David Seymour will be paying close attention,
with his new -found love for sanctuaries and eliminating pests and ensuring that the
things we love—the taonga species—are protected.
Let me talk to you about a broad, big, hairy, stretch vision —that is, a predator -free
New Zealand. I am not talking about the Opposition at this time. I am focused instead
on rats, stoats, and possums, primarily. Aerial d rops of 1080 are working and will
continue to be used. I would request that the Greens stand up and actually come out a
little bit on this one and support—

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: We have.

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: —1080 in an obvious way. Keep up the work then, Ms
Sage. It would be really useful if you joined the chorus of approval rather than carping
from the sidelines. We will leave carp to another time, of course, in their substance.
The thing about having a predator -free New Zealand is  that what you need to do is
kill the things that are killing the things you love. So we take pre -emptive strikes. We
have the technology to rid a valley or a peninsula of pests, as at Zealandia here and in
other parts of the country, but we do need to hav e a longer -term vision that really is
about eradicating these exotic pests. They have come here from different lands, made
this place their own, and now, of course, they need to be dispatched. It is costing the
economy $3.3 billion a year, the eradication of these exotic pests. I hope I am not
disturbing any of my colleagues who are a little squeamish about extermination, but I do
think it is important to address these issues.
The vast habitats our native animals need will be heightened and they will be sa fe,
and the regions will also enjoy better tourism, if we can embrace this vision. Take
Taranaki—the Project Taranaki Mounga partnership, which was announced in
December, is an example of how big goals can be achieved, region by region, and you
need to involve several partners. The Department of Conservation is contributing about
a third of the cost of the $24 million project in Taranaki. I was there on Thursday for a
very exciting launch, along with my colleagues the Hon Chester Borrows and Jonathan
Young—if he is here —as well and Barbara Kuriger and others. We were talking about
biodiversity in Taranaki. It is a very important thing to think about collaboration —an
unknown for the Opposition, of course. Project Taranaki Mounga, with its biodiversity
vision, has the ability to change the face of conservation in New Zealand. I think that it
9260 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
is incredibly encouraging, and it will be the start of what we hope to roll out over the
next few years.
Wilding pines—and I commend my friend and colleague Nathan Guy on this. The
Ministry for Primary Industries is leading the charge, and we are very focused on
getting rid of these wilding pines because we cannot afford to back away from the
problem. The Government, regional authorities, community groups, businesses,
philanthropists, and the forestry sector itself need to combine forces. Wildings, for those
of you who are not up to speed with it, already cover about 1.7 million hectares of land,
and they are advancing at a rate of around 6 percent a year. If we sit back and  do
nothing, wildings will cover about 22 percent of our country within the next 20 years,
and that is totally unacceptable. Most of the land that they would colonise is arable land.
It is good, productive farming land and it is land that we need to use for other things.
The wilding conifers do not respect the boundaries. They seed widely and freely—up
to 20 kilometres, in fact, with some of this very fine pollen —so we really need to be on
top of this issue, and the New Zealand Wilding Conifer Management S trategy is
something that we, as a Government, have bought into. We, at central government level,
will take a leadership role in this, and we will work with others to achieve the goals.
That is what this John Key - led Government is all about: fine leaders hip, a strong,
united caucus and Cabinet, and strong, united thinking and philosophies that will deliver
a vision.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: That got leaked, eh, Maggie?

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Again, the Opposition members are incredulous. These are
unknown territories for them.
War on Weeds is another element of our vision that is not to be underestimated. It
seems to me that while we focus on the birds and while we focus on our creatures —a
very important part of our biodiversity —we cannot  forget the plants. The War on
Weeds, which we declared about 6 months ago, has rolled out the dirty dozen, which are
common or garden plants that have got away on us a bit and we need to pull them
back—“a bit” is actually understating it. We spent somethi ng like $1.2 million from the
Department of Conservation Community Fund to help community weed control groups,
with Weedbusters and the Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust, and I commend a
lot of these smaller groups. Up and down the country they are united.
I was visiting a place in Taranaki on Friday, as the Minister for Senior Citizens, and I
would have to say that it was incredibly heartening to see a group of about 40 people in
their 70s getting together to weed, to plant, to destroy pests, and to create habitats for
our creatures. It gets them together, doing something with great purpose and meaning,
and it is good exercise. That is another of our programmes, which we call Healthy
Nature, Healthy People, which is where you get people into the great outdoors. They are
doing something for themselves but also —in the case of the people in Taranaki, and so
many groups up and down the country I have seen in the last year —they are working
for the good of our nature. They are working together in a cause that they believe in. We
help them out with funding.
We also encourage, through the Kiwi Conservation Club and a successful bid for
new money that we got across the line in last year’s Budget of over $11.2 million —we
have invested that in the future of ou r national bird. The number of our national birds is
declining at about minus 2 percent a year. That is a decline that we need to reverse. We
have a target, we have a name, and we have a vision. That is how you measure what you
do and that is how you manag e the problem —again, unknown territory to the
Opposition members, who have fallen very silent because they are completely at sea
with these notions.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9261
When it comes to Kiwis for Kiwi, the turn -round has begun. We are working with
New Zealander of the Year n ominee Rob Fenwick to help community groups to protect
the birds and protect their habitats. We are boosting the Department of Conservation’s
own funding by more than $6 million a year —and that will be from 2018 onwards —
expanding breeding programmes such a s Kiwi Creches, Kōhanga Kiwi, and pest
control, as well as monitoring all of the existing populations. The whole game, really,
around this is to protect the birds —the kiwis, in particular —so that they get to a stage
where they can help themselves, and at t he time when they are about a kilogram in
weight, they are then able to. They can fight off anything actually, kiwis. That is why
they are our national bird, I think. They are fierce. They may not look the most elegant
birds. They do not fly, but they have  commendable character. They are extraordinary
birds at looking after themselves, but they need a bit of help along the way.
So if we turn that minus 2 percent decline into a plus 2 percent increase, we will have
about 7,000 more birds, and that means the y will be able to proliferate in the wild. My
dream is to ensure that they are audible —that they keep people awake at night in the
suburbs around New Zealand. We want the bird numbers to go up. We need to be able
to work with the tools that we have in nature and conservation.
Just going through some of the issues that we have been dealing with in the arts,
culture, and heritage area, tonight I signed a co -production agreement with the Israeli
Government so that we can have films and television —shared proje cts and shared
collaboration between our countries. That is the 17 th co-production agreement we have
signed over the past few years, and it means that the ties that bind the countries that we
have cultural links with will only increase at a stronger level.
The Ministry for Culture and Heritage is working with a lot of different regions to
mark the anniversary, as well —WW100. This year we are moving away from Gallipoli
and into commemorating the battle sites of Europe, and we are opening plinths and
telling the New Zealand story internationally.
I would like to finish my call tonight on seniors, which is the third portfolio
responsibility that I have. Leading the fight against social isolation —which is a
newfangled way, maybe, of describing loneliness —we need to get rid of that corrosive
element and stop the lead and decline of loneliness and social isolation into elder abuse,
which is a big problem in New Zealand. Around 2,000 cases are reported currently, and
that is probably a real underestimation. There ar e closer to 18,000. So the challenges
continue, but I think this Government, under John Key’s strong leadership, is well up
for the programme.
You will see that I am wearing the alternative flag on my lapel. I will be voting for
that, and I would urge others to look beyond the—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the member. Her time has expired.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I just want to spe nd 5 minutes —but I
want to pick up where that woman, Maggie Barry, has just left off. I spent my holidays
in Northland this year, and I did not hear the birds. I did not hear the birds, and I will
tell you why—because pest control in Northland is so abysma l that the birds are being
killed off. The conservator up there in Northland did not even have the guts to be able to
ask for any more money —which is less than $1 million a year —to ask the Government
for more money to preserve those birds, because she knew  that she was going to get
turned down. That is the legacy of this Government. The legacy is that it has got no
money, it has cut the budgets, and now our forests—certainly in Northland—are at risk.
So that is where I wanted to start off, but I want to talk about a meeting that I had
yesterday with a young guy called Sudhvir Singh, who is from Generation Zero. He
spoke at the Auckland Council meeting a few days ago. He talked about pulling up the
ladder. What he meant was that while he was trying to get things that we all want —a
9262 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
house, a job, and everything else —the well -heeled people and everybody else around
the Auckland area were pulling up the ladder. He was booed and hissed at as he gave
evidence to the Auckland Council about the need for more housing in Auckland.
We all want the same things —the same things that I want, he wants. He wants to be
able to have a piece of that Kiwi Dream that I have, which is about getting his own
house. But inequality in New Zealand has grown wider and wider. I am talking not just
about the inequality between the rich and the poor; I am talking about the inequality
between young and old. Today the younger people come out of university with a huge
student loan. They have to pay that off, and then they are confronted —if they are living
in Auckland—with average house prices of $900,000 -plus. Who could possibly afford
that? These people are being priced completely out of the market.
I want to say that this Government does  not look forward. It does not look to those
people who need their help. It is not like the Labour Party, which has just recently put
up its proposal to have 3 years’ free tertiary education. At least there is a plan there to
address the intergenerational inequality that exists in this country. Not only that, but this
Government will not address —will not even look at —the issue of superannuation.
Right now, this year, we are spending more money on superannuation than our entire
education budget, and it is st ill going up. That is something that is a legacy, once again,
that these younger people are going to have to pull up.
Sudhvir Singh is wanting what a lot of other young people have been asking for, but
this Government defends the people who booed and hiss ed. Basically, those people are
desperate to hang on to their privilege and desperate to keep their property prices high—
desperate to pull up the ladder so that young people do not get a chance any more. That
is something that we in the Labour Party detest—we detest unfairness. We want the best
for everybody.
We do not want to see the inequality gap growing in terms of poverty and also in
terms of intergenerational equity. So we are willing to put our money where our mouth
is. We want to see people going on to tertiary training and getting it for free, so that they
are not burdened down with great big loans and so that they get a proper leg -up and a
proper chance in life, and we want to see them get affordable housing. That is why we
have always supported t he building of 10,000 affordable houses a year. Those are two
bold initiatives about addressing what we need to be doing in the future, and that is
something that this Government has nothing to say about because it allowed the
property price to go to an av erage of $900,000 in Auckland. It has nothing to say to
those younger people who want to get a chance in life.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5-minute call—Rino Tirikatene.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: I am pleased to respond to the
Prime Minister’s statement, and, naturally, I am standing to oppose the statement. But
before I launch into that, I would like to just join with my colleague Mr Shearer there in
responding to Ms Barry’s waxing lyrical on the big goals of biodiversity in her
portfolio. I always pause —because Mr Shearer said that he could not hear the birds in
Tai Tokerau, and that is a sad fact —and I think of the slaughter by the Deerstalk ers
Association of the four takahē on Motutapu Island under this Minister’s watch. That is
another reason. It is not only about underfunding but we had an incompetent Minister
bring in amateur deerstalkers who wiped out 30 percent of one of the most endang ered
species there in one fell swoop. So that is the great achievement from that Minister right
there.
But I would like to switch to the Prime Minister’s statement. If people sitting at
home are confused as to what was in that statement, they have got a v ery good point,
because we have got a chorus line here waxing on with their pre-scripted lines, but what
I would say is that the Prime Minister gave two speeches. There is a very thin document
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9263
that is the actual statement, but what he actually delivered in  the House was just his
normal court jester routine. So no wonder the public at large are confused by this
Government.
I think there is so much spin going on that we need to really break through. We need
to break through the spin from this National Govern ment. We hear things like “a better
Public Service” and “a sharper, leaner, more competitive Public Service”, and what that
really means is —and I want to give an example from my own portfolio area. In
customs, what that really means is understaffing, under -resourcing, and a front line in
disarray at our border. That is what that really means, and I can give examples. We are
seeing front -line customs officers taken off duty. They are actually there to screen
passengers, but what we are seeing is hundreds of passengers coming through Auckland
Airport and only seven customs officers are there to process 2,000 passengers an hour.
That is an example of mismanagement not only from the department but also from the
Minister.
But it gets even worse than that, becaus e what is happening —and we had Mrs
Collins talking earlier on about the great achievements in the law and order arena now
that she is back on deck. But what that actually means is that not only are we under -
resourced at the border but we are seeing a flood —a flood—of illicit drugs coming into
our country. Mrs Collins herself said that 330 kilos of methamphetamine was
intercepted last year. What is actually happening is that that is what was caught, but,
actually, only one in 10 is actually caught at the border.
So we could extrapolate that number out and say that there were 3 tonnes of
methamphetamine that came into the country, and we can actually back that up —true.
So that is an actual failure of this National Government. National came in after
campaigning in 2007 about how it wanted to crack down on P —crack down on the
scourge. Well, that is an actual failure there, and the Government itself has admitted it.
The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet has admitted that the availability and
the usage and the purity of P is on the rise, so there is a complete failure there, and the
Ministry of Health is also saying that the usage among average Kiwis has not changed.
It is right up there, and it is above the international average. So there is a failure r ight
there from the Government, and we are seeing that.
What that does, though, is it cuts across and it is damaging to our communities. It is
prolific, and that is one more thing that is hurting our communities at large. People want
to feel safe and peop le expect to have the Kiwi Dream of being safe in their
communities and safe in their households, but what we are seeing is actually the
opposite from this Government. It does not care about the communities at large. It does
not care about the people who a re struggling to buy a house. People are being turned
away by our health system, which is overstretched. The thousands of children who are
in poverty —that is really a sad indictment on this Government, and that is what our
country is subjected to today. I oppose the Prime Minister’s statement.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5-minute call—Andrew Bayly.

items.speaker: ANDREW BAYLY
items.text: I was going to talk about a number of
things tonight, but I just thought I might respond to some of the speeches, particularly
the last two that we have had from Rino Tirikatene and David Shearer. They followed
an excellent speech by my colleague the Hon Maggie Barry, who was talking about
what we are doing in the area of conservation, and then I heard the two speakers talking
about the lack of birds up in Northland. Well, I would just like to invite both those
speakers to come and visit me in Hunua, becau se we have got a wonderful programme
around the kokako, in the Hunua Range.
In 1974 there was only one breeding pair left in New Zealand, but thanks to the good
efforts of the Auckland Council and also the Department of Conservation we now have
9264 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
66 breedin g pairs in the Hunua Range. This is a wonderful achievement in bringing
back a bird from the brink of extinction into something that is viable, and, what is more,
I am raising $10,000 to go towards that programme. I would like to challenge those two
former speakers to put up some money and come and help our programme and come
and join in and see how these birds live in our wonderful part of this country.
I heard a couple of other things mentioned. I heard a little debate about
superannuation. I just wish t hese speakers would actually spend 5 minutes looking at
some facts and figures. I heard Mr Shearer saying that our superannuation is dreadful
and it is out of control. Well, actually, the facts are that currently we pay 5 percent of
our total Government spend on superannuation every year. When you compare that with
most OECD countries we are well below the average. Most are about 9 percent and up
to about 15 percent. Even stretching it forward many, many years up to 2050, we will
ultimately hit about 8 percent of our total spend. Just to put that in context, over the last
8 years through the good efforts of our Minister of Finance we have reduced
Government spend by near on 4 percent. When you are spending nearly $70 billion a
year, that works out to be roughly about $9 billion to $10 billion of savings a year. That
alone is going to offset a lot of that increased cost.
But what we are also doing is growing an economy and reducing debt. So even now
our debt is at 27 percent of GDP, which will be half of Austr alia’s by 2020, and
England and the EU will be four times ours. The US will be five times ours by 2020.
We will have modest debt. That is all about preparing ourselves so we can meet these
future commitments.
Finally, housing —I heard that magic word about  housing. Again I invite the
members to come to Hunua. Come to Hunua because 12,000 sections are going to come
to market over the next 5 years —12,000. And I heard someone saying we need 10,000.
Come to my wonderful electorate and you will see it. The issue  we have got is we need
to continue to invest in infrastructure and that is what we are doing —$4.25 billion into
roading into Auckland alone over the next 3 years, and all those other good things like
schools that our new mayor will be able to come and ope n over the next few years. I am
looking forward to doing it. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: A very robust act to follow
there—well done, Mr Bayly. I would just l ike to talk in support of the Prime Minister’s
statement. I will start off by talking about a remark made by Mr Shearer with regard to
the Labour Party’s free tertiary education policy. It is probably fair to say that I am the
probably closest to that spac e of policy in this House. I have actually just recently paid
off my student loan. But one of the things that I think is important to remember is that
the Government already, effectively, carries the cost of about 75 percent of student loan
payments. When you look at it in that context, you see that 25 percent of that loan is
still being paid for by the student. It is still quite considerable as part of their salary, but,
actually, the cost of appreciating that is considerable as well.
I do not think that there is much in life that you get for free, but if you do receive
something for free, many people do appreciate it. But if you are receiving a free
education, the ability or the incentive for you to actually work hard and study to try to
get the best results that you can are not there if there is not a cost to you and there is not
an incentive to complete your education. And I can tell you about that first -hand. I think
that what the Government is doing with regard to tertiary education already is a very
positive move. We are already incentivising students enough to study but not making it
unaffordable for them to do so. If you come from a family, or if you are in a position
where you cannot afford to pay for accommodation or some course -related costs, ther e
are payments through the accommodation supplement and payments for course -related
costs. There are subsidies there to assist people into education.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9265
Just regarding the Prime Minister’s statement, New Zealand is in good shape, and I
say that with strong c onfidence as someone representing a large rural electorate at the
bottom of the South Island. That progress is actually due to the hard work and positive
attitude of New Zealanders, but it is also because of the stability and cohesion and
confidence that c ome from having more than 7 years of strong and stable Government
under John Key’s leadership.
We have got a busy agenda in 2016, carrying on from 7 years of hard work and
consistent policy development. We are pressing on with social housing reforms to do  a
better job for our tenants. Many residents in Invercargill will, hopefully, benefit from
that as those discussions progress over the coming years, and I am sure that if my
colleague Sarah Dowie was here she would be remarking on that.
We are also maint aining a strong focus on law and order. To that end I want to
compliment and acknowledge the hard -working police officers in my electorate.
Particularly, I want to name three people, and they are the area commanders responsible
for the Queenstown-Lakes area, the Clutha area, and a large part of the Southland area.
They are Alastair Dickie, Richard McPhail, and Olaf Jensen.
I also want to acknowledge the hard work of the staff of the Otago Corrections
Facility, and the manager, Jack Harrison. It is an impor tant part of our electorate. It is
Milton’s largest employer. It has created opportunities for that town, for employment,
and for other staff to move on. The reason why I mention those areas is that they are
often thankless jobs, but there are a lot of peo ple who go out every day and protect and
serve our constituents right across the country.
I want to touch a little bit on some of the things that we are doing. In New Zealand
we have to focus on the things that we can control. We are a small Island nation  at the
bottom of the world. Things that we can control are our own competitiveness and our
economic performance, and we are also well placed to meet external challenges in so far
as we can, as well.
Otago and Southland, as I have already mentioned, are p rimary industry - driven
communities, and as well we have got Queenstown, the Catlins and Milford Sound,
which are largely driven by tourism. We cannot forget that New Zealand is performing
very well compared with most countries in these areas. Just in ter ms of tourism, last
year there were over 100,000 visitors who travelled to the Catlins, and there were over
600,000 visitors who travelled to Milford Sound, which is back up near pre -global
financial crisis numbers. Queenstown was No. 1 for the internation al visitor spend, with
14 percent market share of international expenditure. So these parts of the economy are
doing very well.
We had the southern field days a couple of weeks ago where 13 MPs came down,
including the Prime Minister, the Minister for Pri mary Industries, Nathan Guy, and the
Deputy Prime Minister, Bill English. That has provided a lot of support for our farmers
down there, and I just want to acknowledge that. In closing, I have no hesitation in fully
commending the Prime Minister’s statement and supporting it. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Melissa Lee—5 minutes.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: I would like to take the opportunity to speak to our
Prime Minister’s statement to the House for 2016 and to commend it. I fully support his
statement. We are incredibly fortunate in this country, I think, to have such a great
leader who is working for fa milies and supporting the needs of ordinary New
Zealanders. I think it is well recognised that the people in New Zealand, the public,
actually also recognise that in the Prime Minister.
The great work this side of the House is achieving can be seen throug h fantastic sets
of policies, and I would like to kick off with the tourism portfolio, which the Prime
Minister has been responsible for. Since 2008 this Government has invested $700
9266 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
million in tourism and tourism promotion. In the year ended December 2015  we saw a
huge rise—a more than 30 percent increase —in international visitor spending. That is
up to $9.7 billion —not $9.7 million, but $9.7 billion —in international visitor spending,
which is an increase of more than 30 percent.
I would also like to talk  about the great achievement of our finance Minister, Bill
English. He got the books back in the black, and that is not a small achievement
considering the fact that we have had a huge global financial crisis and that New
Zealand was faced with a lot of is sues, including the Christchurch earthquakes that
devastated the economy. We recently marked their fifth anniversary.
In 2015 this House saw the successful completion of the free -trade agreement with
Korea, my birth country. Many members have already exto lled the virtues of free trade.
Last month we saw the signing of the Trans -Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement, one
of the biggest free-trade deals in the world and a deal that will bring huge benefits to all
regions of this country and to many people in p overty and hardship in developing
communities around New Zealand.
It is a real shame that there are people in this House who do not actually recognise
the amazing opportunity that exists for New Zealanders in this deal —a view that even
the previous Labour  Government saw with China. That free -trade agreement has
actually boosted this economy. I see that the Hon Phil Goff is sitting over there. We
know for a fact that he supports free trade, and there are other members in his caucus
who actually do recognise the benefit of free trade, as well.
This partnership is going to revolutionise our markets and the way that New Zealand
companies can engage with the global market. Whether they are squash and
fruitgrowers on the East Coast or deer velvet suppliers in th e South Island, we on this
side of the House recognise their need for the reduction of tariffs and an end to trade
barriers when we are dealing with international markets and we are actually selling to
those markets. I recently saw, and actually posted on my Facebook as well, cherries that
are being sold to Asia. We are seeing a huge openness in the market. Looking at Korea,
for example, the tariff that it actually had was 25 percent —it is gone. The 25 percent
tariff that it used to have is gone, and it mea ns that it actually gives access to the market
without tariff.
We will be able to send our world -class wines and other luxury goods to Japan
without tariffs and restrictions. We also will see many New Zealanders export to our
free-trade agreement partners tariff-free. This will greatly improve our market access in
those countries, and support more New Zealand industries across our country. I think
free-trade agreements —the likes of the Korea free -trade agreement and TPP —are
something that we should all support and actually welcome.
The Prime Minister’s statement also shows what a fortunate nation we are to have
strong leadership and the economic opportunity this country actually has. This year
benefits for families with children will increase on top of inflation. This week actually
saw the minimum wage rise to $15.25 a n hour. We are getting more support for after -
school care, and more cutting of red tape to give small businesses the tools that they
actually need.
I am here to support the Prime Minister’s statement. This Government is in good
spirits and is doing great work.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Alfred Ngaro, 5 minutes.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Prime Minist er’s
statement in the House, but before I do so —I have only just returned back to the House
this evening and heard the news that Mr Twyford’s mother had passed away. Though
we may be in opposition in the House and candidates and contenders in our
communities, the fact is that we are still people, and so I do want to acknowledge the
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9267
passing away of Mr Phil Twyford’s mother. I give my condolences to him, and his
family and his whānau as well, at this time.
I was away from the House because I was at the orient ation week at Auckland
University. I was there yesterday. I know that I saw Mr Cunliffe hiding under an
umbrella, heading to the school. I saw Mr Clayton Mitchell —he was there as well. He
was on the other side. He did not quite have his three -piece suit on, but he still had the
suit and tie. He was out there talking to the students at Auckland uni. One of my sons is
actually there at Auckland uni. It was quite interesting yesterday, in having these
conversations with a lot of the students there and talking about what the Government is
doing. They wanted to know what direction the Government is going in.
I had one student come up to me, and I could see by his body language that —he was
looking like he was coming for a fight. He came there and he stood at a di stance, and he
said: “Oh, yeah, National Party, eh? National Government.” I said: “Yep, that’s right.”

items.speaker: Then he said
items.text: “Yeah, well, what are you doing? What are you doing for our people?”.
He spent the next 3 minutes telling me about all the things that we a re not doing —not
caring for the poor, not doing enough for Māori, not doing enough for Pasifika —and he
just went on and on and on. So I said “Oh, that’s great. Well, why don’t I start by just
introducing myself to you?”, and he said: “Oh!”. I said: “Maybe you don’t know where
I come from. Look, I’m a first generation —born here. My parents came from the
Pacific. My mum was a cleaner, my dad was a labourer. I come from a working -class
family. That’s where I come from.” He looked at me and he goes: “Well, and what are
you doing in the National Party?”. And I said: “Well, because of this: the values that my
parents gave me as a working -class family were these —and my grandmother as well,
and others who turned around and said this to me. They said ‘You know, we’ve  come
here for the same opportunities. We don’t want to have anything more special than
anyone else, but all we ask for is this: we want the same opportunities as anyone else.’”
One thing I also told this young man was the fact that I am a tradesman. I th ink I am
one of the few tradesmen who may be in the House here, in Parliament, of 121 MPs. I
am an electrician by trade. I started off as a Māori Affairs pre -apprentice, and went to

items.speaker: Domett Avenue Hostel. I said to him
items.text: “The fact is that I too come from a t rade.” He
said: “I was a painter before I came here to Auckland University, and now I’m doing
law.” So I said to him: “So here’s the thing, right? In my background”—I said—“I don’t
have political science, but the thing that I like about where this Governme nt is going,
and when we’re talking about our Prime Minister, is this: that we basically don’t talk
about stuff all the time. We get on and do the job that needs to be done.” I said: “You’re
a painter. You sit here. If you look at a building over days and days—you can talk about
it till the cows come home, right—it won’t go anywhere.” In other words, you’ve got to
say “Here’s a job. It needs to be done.”, and fix it and make it happen. That is the
pragmatism of this Government.

items.speaker: So he said to me
items.text: “Give me s ome examples. Let’s talk about this.” He talked about
“What are you doing for Māori? Let’s talk about this.” I asked him “In 9 years of a
Labour Government, OK, how many Treaty claims were completed?”, and he said: “Oh,
I don’t know.” Well, you can count them on just two hands—it is called six. Right? In 6
to 7 years of a National Government —Peeni Henare will know what it is —it is 43. So
what is it? We can talk all the days that we can, but we just get on and do the business
that needs to be done.

items.speaker: He said to me
items.text: “What about housing? What are you doing for housing in our
communities?”. He said “Labour’s doing a lot more.”, and I said: “In 9 years how many
houses do you know that they actually retrofitted to make warm and dry?”. He said: “I
don’t know.” It wa s 2,000 a year, 18,000 over 9 years. I said: “Do you want to know
what we’ve done? I’ll tell you this: over 40,000 Housing New Zealand homes; under the
9268 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
retrofitting programme Warm Up New Zealand, over 300,000; if we do the Residential
Tenancies Amendment B ill, it will be over 180,000 by 2019. That will come to
500,000.” I said to this young man: “What I stand for —I don’t have a political science
degree. I’m a tradesman at heart. I come in here to do things that make a difference for
our communities, for young people like you and your family. In other words, we just get
on with the business. But”, I said, “I tell you what. Don’t just take what I say for
granted. How about you let the facts speak for themselves? That’s the evidence.”
I commend the Prime Minis ter’s statement, because it is pragmatic, it is practical,
and it gets on with doing the business, the things that Kiwis respect and have voted for
in the last two elections. Thank you.

items.speaker: PEENI HENARE
items.text: Tēnā koe, e Te Māngai o Te
Whare. Ko Tūtāmure te tupuna, ko Te Whakatōhea te iwi. E te ahorangi, e Ranginui
Walker, e te tohunga o te whakaiti, e te ahorangi o te ao mātauranga, tēnei e tangi
apakura atu ana ki a koe, otirā, koutou kua ngaro atu ki Te Pō. Ka tāpiri atu ko te māmā
o taku hoa mahi a Phil Twyford ki a ia, ka tāpiri hoki ko tōku tupuna 2 wiki ki muri, i
mahue ake ki te pō. Nō reira, koutou e te hunga wairua ki a koutou, e moe, e moe,
okioki!
Ka noho ahau ki roto i Te Reo Māori. He aha te take i pēnā ai? Kia kite tātou me te
whakamātautau i tēnei Kāwanatanga me wā rātau manawanui ki tō tātou Reo Māori, tā
te mea, aianei tata ake nei ka uru mai Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori ki roto i tō tātou Whare.
Nā, ka kite tātou mehemea e manawanui ana tō tātou Kāwanatanga ki tēnei taonga o Te
Reo Māori. E rua ana ngā take, pū ana ki a tāua Te Māori. Ko te mea tuatahi i tēnei wā,
ko Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori, ko te mea tuarua, ko Te Pire Whenua Māori. Ka whakaaro
ake Te Iwi Māori, ko ēnei mea e rua, he taonga. He taonga Te Reo Māori, he taonga anō
hoki te whenua ki a tāua Te Māori.
Nō reira, ka whakaaro ake ahau ki ngā mahi nanakia, ngā mahi māminga o tēnei
Kāwanatanga. Ka whakaaro ake ahau ki ngā kōrero a Ranginui Walker i ro to i tana
pukapuka e mea ana: “Me hui ngātahi Te Kāwanatanga me Te Māori ki runga i te
marae. Me kaua Te Kāwanatanga e karanga hui ana ki roto i ngā hōtēra, ki roto i ngā
wāhi Pākehā. Me tae atu ki te marae ki te āta kōrero i ngā take e pā ana ki Te Iwi
Māori.”
Nō reira, ka tukuna atu te pātai ki tēnei Kāwanatanga: he aha te take i tū ngā hui e pā
ana ki Te Pire Whenua Māori ki roto i ngā hōtēra o te Pākehā? Ko reira katoa te wairua
o Te Māori? Kāhore! Kāhore! Kāhore! E pātai atu ana ki tēnei Kāwanatanga e i a rātou
e huri haere ana i te motu whānui, i whakaae mai Te Iwi Māori ki ngā nekehanga o Te
Pire Whenua Māori? E kāhore! E kāhore! E kāhore!
Nō reira, ka tukuna atu tēnei pātai ki tēnei Kāwanatanga: ko te aha koutou mō Te Iwi
Māori—ko te aha koutou ki Te  Iwi Māori? E tika ana te kōrero o taku hoa mahi, a
Nanaia Mahuta, e mea ana: “Nō reira, he aha te painga mō tāua Te Māori?”. Ka kite
tātou ki roto i ngā tatauranga e mea ana: e pōhara tonu ana Te Iwi Māori; kei te ngaro
haere te whenua Māori; kei te mimiti haere Te Rēo Māori. Anā, kei te mauhere. Ā, ko te
nuinga o ngā mauhere ki roto i ngā whareherehere, ko Te Māori. Anā, ko ngā tatauranga
o te ao hauora. Ānā, ko Te Māori e pēhi ana ki raro. Nō reira, ki te whakautu i te kōrero
a te mema kātahi anō kua noho ki roto i tō tātou Whare, ā, e hoa, he aha nei te painga ki
a tāua Te Māori? Ka kī atu, horekau! Horekau! Horekau!
Nō reira, ka tū au ki te whakahē i te kōrero a Te Pirimia i te tīmatanga o tēnei tau tā
te mea, kua kōrero ahau mō ngā tatauranga, kua kōrero ahau mō ngā nekehanga
māminga o tēnei Kāwanatanga. Ka whakaaro ake ahau mō te kōrero ā tōku tupuna e
mea ana: “I r ongo ēngari, kīhai i rongo! I kite ēngari, kīhai i kite.” Koi nā te mahi o
tēnei Kāwanatanga ki tōku Iwi Māori. Kua kōrero ahau mo te pōharatanga. Kātahi ano
au ka mutu i ngā huihuinga ki roto i te tāone nui o Tāmaki -makau-rau, ā, ko te nuinga o
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9269
ngā kōrero e mea ana, e pōhara tonu ana rātou. Ka whakaaro ake ahau ki Te Wharekura
o Manurewa, kua roa rawa e tatari ana mō Te Minita Take Mātauranga, kia whakaae,
kia tū te wharekura ki roto o Manurewa. He aha te take? Ko Te Reo Māori te take. He
aha te take? Ko t e oranga o tāua Te Iwi Māori! Hei whakakapi ake kua kite ahau i ngā
māngai o te Kāwanatanga e kore aro mai nei ki tō tāua Reo Māori. Hei whakakapi ake,
tukuna te poi, kia rere! E hari koa ana kua tatū te whakatau mō te mahi poi a te tāne ki
roto i te ahure a kā tū ki roto i ngā mārama e tū mai nei, e Te Māngai o Te Whare, tēnā
koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. Tūtāmure is the ancestor and Te Whakatōhea is
the tribe. To you, Professor Ranginui Walker, professor of humility and profes sor of the
world of education, I lament here for you, but at the same time for all of you lost to the
void. I add to him the mother of my parliamentary colleague Phil Twyford, and an
ancestor of mine 2 weeks ago who was left behind in the void. So, to all of you spiritual
ones, sleep, slumber, and rest.
I will remain speaking in the Māori language. And why do I do that? So that we can
see and test this Government and its stout heart in regard to our Māori language,
because not too far away now the Māori Lan guage Bill will be introduced into our
House. We will see then just how stout our Government’s heart is to this treasured
aspect of the Māori language. There are two matters that we of Māoridom place
emphasis on: the first one, at this point in time, is th e Māori Language Bill, and the
second one is the proposed Te Ture Whenua Māori Bill. Māoridom consider these two a
treasure. The Māori language is a treasure and so is the land to you and me, the Māori.
And so I think about the crafty and devious actions o f this Government and the
statement made by Ranginui Walker in his book, which stated: “Government and Māori
must meet together on the marae. Government must never convene a meeting in hotels
and non-Māori settings. They must go to the marae to really talk  matters through that
relate to Māoridom.” So the question to this Government is: what is the reason why
meetings for the proposed Te Ture Whenua Māori Bill were held in non -Māori hotels?
Was the Māori spirituality all there? Not at all, not at all, not at  all! I ask of this
Government whether, as it went around the country at large, the Māori people agreed
to the actions of the proposed Te Ture Whenua Māori Bill ? Not at all, not at all, not at
all!

items.speaker: So this is really the question to Government
items.text: what are you , then, to the Māori
people—what are you, then, to the Māori people? What my colleague Nanaia Mahuta is
saying is true: “So what is the benefit for you and me, the Māori?”. We see what the
statistics state: Māori people are still impoverished; Māori land c ontinues to be lost;
the Māori language is diminishing. Look at imprisonment: the majority of prisoners in
the prisons are Māori. Consider the statistics in the health world: there you are; Māori
is down. So to respond to the address by a member who has ju st taken a seat in our

items.speaker: House
items.text: shucks, mate, what then is the benefit for you and me, the Māori? I must say
none at all! None at all! None at all! Therefore, I stand to oppose the Prime Minister’s
statement at the beginning of this year, because I have spok en about the statistics and
the nefarious actions of this Government. I recall a saying by my ancestor, who said: “I
heard, but I didn’t hear; I saw, but I didn’t see.” That is what this Government has done
to my Māori people.
I have talked about the impoverishment. I have just completed a series of conferences
in the city of Auckland. The majority of the conversation is saying that we continue to be
poor. I think about Te Wharekura o Manurewa. It has been waiting a long time for the
Minister of Education to agree to such a school being established at Manurewa, and for
what reason? The Māori language. And why? For the welfare of you and me, the Māori
people! In conclusion, I have witnessed Government representatives who have no
regard to this Māori lang uage, which belongs to you and me. Finally, let the poi fly! I
9270 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
am overjoyed that the question of males performing the poi at the festival to be held this
month has been settled. Mr Assistant Speaker, acknowledgments to you and to us all.]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the Hon Phil Goff —5
minutes.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: In my brief 5 minutes tonight, I want to
focus on a very special group of New Zealanders. They make up about 35 percent of our
population. They make up 35 percent of our production. Do not come to Auckland —
Auckland is coming to you. These are Aucklanders, and we are growing by 800 people
a week—40,000 people a year.
Compared with the problems of some parts of New Zealand, having the problem of
growth is probably a good problem to have. But I would rather have growth with a
Government committed to working in partnership with Auckland City to provi de the
infrastructure that enables that growth to be properly dealt with. Sadly, that is not
happening. We do not have a regional development policy in New Zealand that works. I
challenge any member of the Government or the Opposition to tell me one —one—
regional development policy that works, other than housing unaffordability and
congestion in Auckland, which drives people out of Auckland. I do not think that is a
satisfactory regional development policy. We do not have a policy that tries to match
population growth to the infrastructure that serves it. Once upon a time we would tweak
the pointing system for immigration. We would lower the threshold if we wanted more
people coming; we would raise it if we wanted less. But the Government knows that the
only thing that is sustaining growth in New Zealand is immigration at the moment, so it
is allowing that immigration to come through at the speed that it will.
Now, I am in favour of immigration. I think the immigrants to New Zealand —and
we are all immigrants t o New Zealand, actually, at some point in history —really add
strength and diversity, and make a huge contribution to New Zealand socially,
economically, and culturally. But I worry about the impact of growth that the
Government is not addressing. I worry a bout the road congestion that makes it almost
impossible to get around Auckland at peak hours. The Productivity Commission says
that it costs us $1.5 billion a year in lost time alone because of traffic congestion in
Auckland—$1.5 billion. The New Zealand Council for Infrastructure Development puts
it at $3 billion. That is like taking $3 billion a year and tipping it down the drain,
because in the lost productivity you have got nothing to show for it. We desperately
need infrastructure that will match the growth.
We had a number of things that were very useful. The City Rail Link was to double
the amount of passenger traffic on rail lines, but for 5 years various Ministers in the
Government opposed that, so when we get it, it will be 5 years late. We had a thing
called a petrol tax for Auckland, which enabled the council to have the money to invest
in transport infrastructure; the Government repealed it. I am really pleased to say that
the Government has done a U -turn on the City Rail Link and is about to do  a U-turn on
road charging legislation —but it is too late. We are building a motorway up the north -
west into Henderson and Te Atatū. It is good that it is being broadened, but there is no
busway there—no separated lane for buses, yet we know that on the No rth Shore it is
the busway that has been the most effective way of getting more people into town from
the North Shore by public transport than we get by private transport. We are not
thinking ahead. At the moment we have got the major Port Future Study tha t we are
looking at to know whether or not we should move the port out of Auckland, like they
did in Sydney. But the Government will not participate in that, so we do not have a
regional or a national strategy for it.
What I am saying to the Government is that we have to have that partnership
between central government and Auckland City if we are to make Auckland work.
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9271
Auckland is a great city. It is the only global city in New Zealand: it is the place where
we can retain New Zealanders and where we can att ract the best talent from overseas.
For New Zealand to succeed, Auckland has got to succeed. My call on the Government
in housing and transport —the two major infrastructure deficit areas —is for the
Government to get off the sidelines and to collaborate wit h Auckland City, so that we
can make Auckland a truly great place for New Zealand and a great place for people to
live.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I thought John Palino sound ed
angry yesterday when he was announcing his candidacy but, compared with that effort,
I am beginning to think he is probably a tutor in seances and transcendental meditation.
What a great time it is to be a New Zealander, what a great time it is to be in
Government, and, I have to say, what a fantastic time it is to live in Hamilton. We have
just enjoyed our annual Hamilton Gardens Arts Festival, and it has been a fabulous
experience as always. There are wonderful things happening in the electorates that
David Bennett and I are lucky enough to represent. We have just had the opening of the
new Rototuna Junior High School —634 foundation pupils began on 4 February. What
an exciting time it is for that community. I congratulate them all. I want to acknowledge
the great advocacy that David Bennett did over many years, and say thank you.
After the boundary changes at the last election, that school is now neighbouring my
electorate; in fact, it is in my electorate, and we are looking forward to the new senior
high school beginning next year as well. While I am mentioning schools, can I
congratulate Pūkete School on the unveiling of its magnificent new pou by the Māori
development Minister, the Hon Te Ururoa Flavell, last week. It is a great historical
monument to our city and to that school community, and I know that the children were
absolutely delighted with it. I want to acknowledge Horsham Downs School, which has
also come into my electorate —I think, Mr Assistant Speaker, from your electorate
recently—on their centennial. Last weekend I had the honour of opening their new
multi-purpose room as they marked that wonderful event. It was great to see so many
former staff and pupils there enjoying the occasion.
All the schools in Hamilton West are in great heart, and I am delighted with the work
that they are doing. I want to acknowledge the p rincipals, the teachers, the boards of
trustees, the parent teacher associations, and, in particular, those wonderfully hard -
working support staff in all our schools, not just in my electorate but all around the
country. What a great job they do and what i mportant work they are undertaking with
our young people.
This year has begun well for New Zealand. The Prime Minister’s statement has
highlighted what a busy, focused, purposeful, and effective Government he is leading.
The signing of the Trans -Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement is excellent news for an
export-dependent country like New Zealand. I have not met a single exporter, producer,
manufacturer, or business owner who is not excited by it, because they all know that the
world does not owe us a livin g; we have to make our own way. We have to grow our
economy, we have to create opportunities to invest and for new jobs to be created.
Every free -trade agreement that New Zealand has ever entered into, from CER right
through to the Chinese and the Korean a greements in more recent times, has shown just
how important free trade is for New Zealand.
I am very proud of the National Government’s announcement last year of the
magnificent marine sanctuary around the Kermadec Islands. I am very proud that
yesterday we announced yet another lift to the minimum wage, because every year since
we came into office we have lifted the minimum wage sustainably, knowing that you
have got to have a balance between what can work for businesses —you do not want to
push them too f ar, where they end up having to lay off staff —but also knowing that
9272 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
those at the bottom end need that extra assistance. I am delighted that we have been able
to boost their earnings. Those who work 40 hours on the minimum wage will have
another $20 in thei r pocket from 1 April. I am hugely proud that we are the first
Government in more than a generation to give a significant lift in benefits, and that is
just around the corner, as well, for people who are on welfare. I am so proud that we are
the Government that has introduced free doctors visits for children under 13.
I am really proud of our rising standards of achievement in all levels of education. I
acknowledge the great work that the Hon Anne Tolley started in that regard in her time
as Minister of Edu cation. Did she not take a lot of flak at the time but, boy, are not the
fruits of her labours being seen now? Well done, Anne Tolley, Hekia Parata, and all
who work in the education system, because it is a partnership and they are all doing it
together. I am incredibly proud that unemployment is now much lower, that mortgage
interest rates are low, and wages are rising well above the rate of inflation.
I am not proud of the negativity of the Opposition. I am not proud that they cannot
acknowledge any of th ese achievements. Soon we will vote down the leader of the
Labour Party’s ridiculous amendment suggesting that the Government has given up
hope on the future, has no plans to prepare New Zealand for the future, and is more
concerned with scoring political points. Pot—kettle—black. What a ridiculous assertion
that is. What abject nonsense from the Leader of the Opposition. In particular, we have
seen it with his decision to place the Labour Party as the “Two -position Party” on the
TPP agreement, turning their backs on their previously proud commitment to free trade.
What a nonsense that is.
And, most recently, his complete lack of statesmanship and integrity in failing to
honour the Labour Party’s policy at the last election to support the process over the fl ag
referendum. We should be now having a discussion leading to a vote that is above petty
politics; that is what we all went into the last election with. Nobody will care who the
Government is when the change happens. Do you think the Canadians talk about that?
Of course they do not, but they are mighty glad that they made the change and they now
have a flag that they are very, very proud of. We should be able to do the same. We
should be honouring our war dead who have the silver fern on their graves, by s aying
that now is the time to make the change. We should be embracing the emblem, and I am
wearing my grandfather’s Boer War badge tonight, which is a silver fern, before we
even had the current flag.

items.speaker: A lot of people say
items.text: “Oh, we have got to keep the origi nal flag.” Well, the original
flag was two flags back. The silver fern is the thing that our sportspeople compete
under, that we are recognised for when we travel around the world, and it is something
we can all embrace and be proud of. I hope New Zealande rs will vote for it. I do not
care who the Government is: let us just get on and make a change that is positive for our
country, because that is what this great country provides us an opportunity to do. If we
do not take it now, we will not get it again in our lifetime.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is an honour to be
speaking in the debate on the Prime Minister’s statement, and it is also an honour to
give the concluding speech in this long process. I cannot say that I have heard all the
speeches over the last couple of weeks, but the ones that I have heard from this side of
the House have been positive, forward -looking, and celebratory, honouring Ne w
Zealanders and talking about a Government that is working hard for all New
Zealanders.
I have to say the speeches that I have heard from the Opposition members pointed
out and have shown very clearly that, actually, during their time in Opposition, the
Labour and Green caucuses have not learnt the lessons of being in Opposition. They are
still working as they were in the mid -2000s, judging everything on inputs. They judge
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9273
everything on how much money you put into something. This Government —because it
came through the global financial crisis, perhaps —has been focused on getting results
for New Zealanders. So it is not how much money you put into something; it is the
effect of that spend and the results that you get for the people of New Zealand. This
Government has learnt those lessons, and that is why it has been so successful.
If you look back on the achievements of this Government, even through a global
financial crisis, we have increased the minimum wage by 27 percent since National
came into Government in 2008. At the same time, we have seen inflation kept to a rise
of 11 percent. So that is a very real difference that those New Zealanders on the
minimum wage have seen in their back pockets. Mortgage interest rates were almost 11
percent when we came i nto Government. Now they are down around the 4 percent
mark. We have seen the economy growing—3 percent growth in the last 12 months. We
have seen the average wage grow by $10,000 since we came into Government. When
we came in, it was $47,000, and now $57,000 is the average wage.
Youth offending and our young people —fewer young people are appearing in the
Youth Court. The number is down by 61 percent since National came into Government.
Under this National Government we have the lowest reported crime rates  that we have
seen in 23 or 24 years. Teenage pregnancies are at a historical low. Participation in early
childhood education is at an all -time high. Never before have we seen so many children
taking part in early childhood education, and never before have  we seen so many kids,
particularly Māori and Pasifika kids, leaving school with a qualification, with National
Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2. That has been hard work by a
lot of teachers, staff members, and boards of trustees acros s the country, and this
Government has supported them all the way. Immunisation rates for Māori and Pasifika
children are at the same rate as for European children. We have never seen that before.
It is a tremendous achievement.
On 1 April this year—a month from today—for the first time in 43 years, people who
have children in their families and who are receiving benefits will get an increase of $25
a week. Twenty -five dollars a week is going to make an enormous difference, and all
the families that I have  been talking to have talked to me about the things that they will
be able to do for their children. Then, for those lower -income working families, of
course, Working for Families is being increased by $12.50 a week, and by $24.50 for
those on the very low incomes.
We have done the research, we have got the evidence, and we have based our
investment of taxpayers’ dollars in the places that we know are going to make the most
difference to New Zealand families. And, what is more, we are working together.
Whether it is the Business Growth Agenda, where we have got Ministers working
together across Government; the regional development team, which is out and about; or
the family violence work that we are doing —and even today with the whole -of-
Government approach to reducing harm from gangs —we are working together, using
good evidence, and using that research. We have been open enough to set ourselves
some targets publicly—targets to show the public that we can get better results for them
and their families —and will report on them openly and regularly. So we are investing
the taxpayers’ money wisely, where we know it will have the greatest effect.
Let me just talk a little bit about what we have done in welfare, and I want to
concentrate on two groups that we know  have the highest long -term liabilities and the
worst outcomes in their life. The first is sole parents. We are seeing that the number of
people receiving the sole parent support has fallen by 23.5 percent over the last 5 years.
There are now almost 42,000  fewer children living in benefit -dependent homes. The

items.speaker: Opposition has often asked
items.text: “Who cares? What difference does that make? Why is that
important?”. Well, it is important because, again, through the evidence and the research
9274 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016
that we have done here on th is side of the House, we know that 48 percent of the
children who are born into a benefit -dependent home will have a Child, Youth and
Family notification before they are 18 —48 percent. Someone will be concerned about
them being either neglected or abused. Almost half of them will not get NCEA level 2.
These are children who are born into benefit -dependent homes. Forty-five percent of
them will be on a benefit themselves before they turn 19 and, unfortunately, 5 percent of
them will have either a community sentence or will be going through the courts and in
jail before they turn 19. So that is why it is important that we help and support their
parents get into work, because that gives not only the parents but their children a better
chance in life.
Then, with young people, we have seen that the 15 to 19 -year-old “neet” rate is the
lowest since records began back in 2004. That has taken an enormous amount of work
right across Government, from education to health, to justice, to the police, and to the
Ministry of Social Development. We have all worked together to make sure that those
young people get the best opportunity that they can.
The Prime Minister talked about the overhaul of Child, Youth and Family. Last year
I appointed an expert panel to lead that co mplete overhaul of Child, Youth and Family
because those children are the most vulnerable in our communities and they deserve to
have the best lives. It is not their fault that they were born into families who abuse them
or neglect them. They deserve to ge t the whole attention of the Government and their
communities to make sure that they can live successful lives.
The panel has reported to me. It has identified during that time four building blocks
of the new system. It has identified that we need a child -centred system. We talk a lot
about it, but when you talk to the kids themselves, they say “Actually, no one talked to
me. Actually, no one listened to me.”, and we do not feel it is a child -centred system.
We need an investment approach. We need to use t hat same evidence and research to
know where we need to put our dollars to get the best effect long term for those kids.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: They’re collecting some evidence and making decisions based on
evidence.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The Opposition does not like any of this because it is
content to sit back and watch these kids be abused, be re -abused, and be revictimised
and continue to live lives where they are not succeeding in life. That member smiles,
but, actually, the statistics are really bad because we know that the statistics tell us that
90 percent of those kids who live in care will end up on a benefit. The statistics tell us
that 80 percent of them will not get NCEA level 2. They deserve better than this, and
this Government is going to deliver it for those kids.
New Zealanders know that this National -led Government—and I want to pay tribute
to our coalition partners, because we cannot do it without them. They have been part of
all the success that we are celebra ting here in the House in the conclusion of this debate
tonight, and we welcome the input that we get from them. New Zealanders know that
this National-led Government is working for them because it is actually delivering for
them. New Zealanders know that this National-led Government is investing their dollars
wisely, based on good research and based on evidence. New Zealanders know that this
National-led Government is addressing the hard issues by addressing and understanding
the drivers: the drivers of cr ime, the drivers of poverty and hardship, and the drivers of
economic growth and prosperity.
New Zealanders have confidence in this Government. They have shown it time and
time again—

Second Reading
