items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call David Seymour—5 minutes.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I rise on behalf of the ACT Party in
opposition to the Building (Earthquake -prone Buildings) Amendment Bill. This debate
has been characterised by overflowing wells of empath y from members around the
House—and it is difficult not to when we recall the tragic losses in Canterbury and
when that city, Christchurch, is still shaking anew, even in the past few days. However,
the warmth in some members’ hearts appears to have drifte d up to their heads into
policy making because, when you make public policy, real empathy is about making it
for people.
The first mistake in this policy process was not to base the policy making on the risks
faced by New Zealanders but to apply an arbitra ry standard of 34 percent of new
building code across the country. What that did, from the point of view of individual
New Zealanders, was it meant that the costs and benefits of applying this policy were
vastly different for the risks that New Zealanders face as individuals, and also vastly
different in terms of cost -benefit analysis between different regions of New Zealand. In
fact, some analysis of the initial bill said that the Auckland population would be
spending 3,000 times more to save a life than p eople in Wellington. Minister Nick
Smith made a very revealing comment in his speech to this second reading. He said that
even as an engineer, he was surprised at how much variability there is to earthquake risk
across New Zealand. With respect, only a member from the South Island could say that.
We Aucklanders know that although, for our excesses and sins, we may well one day
drown in runs of lava from our many volcanoes, the risk of an earthquake in our part of
the country is practically nil.
9276 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 1 Mar 2016
The Minister  got pushed back hard, and he introduced a differential level of
strengthening for different parts of the country. He said: “It’s OK. We’ll exclude some
buildings and some structures.”, and that was admirable. He said that we would have
more time—up to 50 years—to strengthen in low-risk areas. But it raises the question: if
it is not important to do this for the next 50 years, then how urgent and how important is
this strengthening overall? The bill was somewhat improved, but according to the
regulatory impact statement for the bill in its new state, the net present value for this
particular piece of legislation is negative three-quarters of a billion dollars. In Auckland,
even just to find out whether a particular building complies with the requirements of the
legislation is estimated to cost $10,000 to $20,000 per building.
If we were making empathic public policy, we would be highly focused on ensuring
that the amount of money spent and the resources that go into earthquake -strengthening
are commensurate with the price that we are prepared to pay to avoid and mitigate other
risks. And yet, in Auckland we will be spending money on earthquake strengthening
when the risks that we face by being in those buildings are hundreds and thousands and
tens of thousands  of times lower than the risks that we face every day in the course of
riding bikes, driving cars, and flying planes. GNS Science was commissioned by the
Auckland Council, and it suggested that in Auckland this legislation might reduce
deaths over 10,000 years by three lives. It would save only three lives.
There is a very simple way that this bill could be enhanced and could be passed, and
that would simply be to exempt the low -risk areas that have already been identified in
the enhanced bill. Take away th ose $10,000 and $20,000 costs that the Minister has
admitted are not addressing any urgent concern—because he says he has got 50 years to
do it—and that would be a bill that the ACT Party could support. But right now it is an
unempathic bill, which does no t deal with the risks faced by New Zealanders but seeks
to preserve an arbitrary standard at all costs. Thank you.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I stand to take a very short call on this piece of
legislation, but before I do I just want to pay tribute to the late and great Dr Ranginui
Walker—moe mai, moe mai, moe mai e koro.
As I said, I stand to take a very short call on this piece of legislation. It has some key
changes in it that we have heard before, but I just want to reiterate those. One of the key
changes is to do with national time frames. It implements a national time frame. That
actually identifies the risk level of buildings —low risk, medium risk, and high risk —
with high risk giving councils 5 ye ars to do the assessment on these buildings and 15
years to strengthen them; medium -risk buildings having 10 years for identification and
assessment of these buildings, with a 25 -year strengthening period; and for low -risk
buildings it is 15 years for iden tification and assessment and 35 years to strengthen the
buildings.
This bill also addresses areas around unreinforced masonry. Those are things like
facades, parapets, and verandahs. It makes sure that, once that assessment has been
made, those areas are  reinforced as quickly as possible. Those are the areas that fell in
the earthquake in 2011, and up to 35 people died because of that. We need to address
those areas very quickly.
The bill also identifies key buildings like schools and universities and ho spitals, and
makes sure that those that have been assessed as medium to high risk are upgraded in
half the time that other buildings in the area would be.
This legislation also identifies category 1 historic buildings and allows them to have
a longer peri od for strengthening, just because of their character and the types of
buildings that they are, and their historic significance to the region.
This is a good bill. It is a bill that addresses a lot of the issues around the earthquake -
prone area that exist s in this country, within the Ring of Fire. So, along with all my
1 Mar 2016 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 9277
colleagues here in National and across the House, I support the bill at its second
reading. Thank you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Firstly, I just want to pull up
the member from ACT, David Seymour, on a matter of geology. He does not realise
that in a volcanic region like Auckland, when the volcanoes explode, it will have an
impact on the land. I would re commend to the member from ACT that what he should
do is go to where the children of Auckland go to find out about geology and
volcanology, and that is the museum at the Auckland Domain. They have a very good
exhibit there—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Isn’t Mount Eden—isn’t that in his electorate?

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Yes. They have a very good exhibit there that actually shows
you the impact on buildings of a volcano exploding. There are lots of buildings in
Auckland that will be impacted if one of the many volcanoes —and, let us face it, there
are, what, seven, nine volcanoes in Auckland—happened to explode.
However, we are here to talk about the Building (Earthquake -prone Buildings)
Amendment Bill. As the previous speaker, Joanne Hayes, discussed, it is around
amending the Building Act to ensure that we deal with earthquake -prone buildings as a
result of what has happened, the earthquake sequence, in Canterbury. There are some
time frames in which to put that in place, and also there are some definitions around risk
and what types of buildings will be covered. This bill will have a huge impact on the
territorial authorities; there is no doubt about that. But there are some specific issues I
want to deal with.
We know that it is impractica ble to deal with all the buildings. However, this bill
actually excludes particular buildings, such as farm buildings, retaining walls, and other
such structures that will not pose a risk to human life should they come down in an
earthquake. We know, also,  that there are some things that are not covered in this bill
that, actually, were impacted in the Canterbury earthquake sequence.
One of the things that I really hope does get covered off is poor engineering. We
know that with the CTV Building, for examp le, no one has really taken responsibility
for the poor engineering that caused the deaths of all those people in that particular
building. That was, really, a failure of engineering, and I do not believe that we can
really continue without actually having  some way of determining whom to hold
responsible for that. I would hope that this bill actually takes account of that.
There are some priority buildings that are included in this bill: hospital and
emergency facilities, of course; certainly educational facilities; and parts of buildings
that are reinforced —such as parapets —and that could fall in an earthquake. Actually,
some of these did fall, and some of these did cause deaths in the earthquake sequence,
particularly in the 22 February quake. There are some issues that are not addressed in
here that we are fully cognisant of in Canterbury, and those are things such as the risks
that become apparent from building materials once buildings either come down or are
demolished—and I am speaking specifically about the risk of asbestos, which is quite a
risk when we are demolishing buildings.
But what I want to do, particularly, is I want to honour a particular person for whom,
if this bill was in place and if our territorial authority had enacted what it should have
done and assessed buildings —and assessed this particular building —as being risky,
then she would not have died. That is Mrs Maureen Valerie Fletcher. Mrs Fletcher is the
mother and mother -in-law of very dear friends of mine, and she was 74 when she
passed away, when a verandah of a cafe that she was having a cup of tea at collapsed on
top of her during the earthquakes. What is particularly sad about Mrs Fletcher’s case is
that she was unidentified for a couple of weeks. There were 2 weeks in which her
family had not heard from her and they had no idea that she had actually perished. What
9278 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 1 Mar 2016
had happened was her body was tak en out of the building where she died, but it was
misidentified.
There was a family in Christchurch who thought their mother had passed away, and
there was a family —my friends—in Auckland who had no idea that their mother had
passed away. So for 2 weeks m y friends were perplexed about what had happened to
their mother. They travelled to Christchurch, spent a lot of time on the ground, and
spent a lot of time with the emergency services trying to identify what had happened.
When the mistaken identification did actually come to light, of course it meant that
another family realised that their loved one was safe and, actually, in a rest home in
Auckland; and my friends, of course, realised that their mother had passed away.
Why I bring this up is that this bill is about saving lives. If this bill had been in place,
if the Christchurch City Council had been able to assess its buildings and assess that
building with the verandah as unsafe, Mrs Maureen Valerie Fletcher might not have
died. That is what this bill is about, Mr Seymour. It is about ensuring that no one else is
put at risk, because we can do something about that. It is about ensuring —do not shake
your head, Mr Seymour —that there are no further families that have to go through the
ordeal that the Fletc hers had to go through while they waited to see where their mother
was. It is not something to shake your head about, Mr Seymour.
This impacted 187 families directly, who lost people in Canterbury, but it also
impacted the whole country. Even as recently as a couple of hours ago, we are still
experiencing aftershocks in Canterbury. Every time we have an aftershock or a major
quake—we had a 5.7 on Valentine’s Day —what does that do to the structures that are
already weakened by the severe force that has been  impacted upon them? This is not a
laughing matter, Mr Seymour, and it is an absolute responsibility of this Government
and of the territorial authorities, the councils around this country, to make sure they get
it right so that people in Auckland and Well ington and Tauranga do not have to go
through the same kinds of dreadful, dreadful things that have happened to the people of
Canterbury.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: What, with volcano-strengthened buildings?

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: We do not wi sh that upon anyone, especially the people in
Epsom, if they are represented by someone who is as uncaring as you.
We can do something about this, and we should. I am getting quite emotional about
this, because people did lose their lives. This is a bill t hat will actually impact on the
lives of people and ensure that they do not have to suffer the way 187 families have had
to. Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Kia ora e Te Mana Whaka wā. I stand to take a short
call on the Building (Earthquake -prone Buildings) Amendment Bill, and agree with the
previous speaker, Poto Williams.
In Christchurch we have just had the fifth anniversary. The latest earthquake was on
Monday morning, early, about 3 o’clock, and it was right under my house, because that
is where the epicentre was, in Cashmere View Street. What we are seeing here is that
there is a continuous flow of aftershocks, even after 5 years. So I want to congratulate
the Minister for Bui lding and Housing because at least we are being very, very
considered here in this bill. It is not just in Christchurch. New Zealand is a young
country; there is a lot of seismic risk right across Aotearoa. This bill does address
something that people from  Christchurch—those who are here now from Christchurch
would never want to see anything like what happened in our city. So this bill really is a
catalyst, in a lot of ways, to address the whole situation of earthquake -prone buildings
across New Zealand.
During the submissions process we heard from a lot of submitters, a lot of local
bodies, and a lot of councils. We even heard from people like Ann Brower, who was
1 Mar 2016 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 9279
injured during the earthquakes. Listening to these submissions explains why there were
a number of changes that were made. I think one of the main changes is actually about
the varying timetables for strengthening the relative earthquake -risk buildings, from
high to medium to low. The reason for that is that we heard from councils right across
New Zealand during the submissions process the fact that we needed to categorise these
high-risk areas, medium, and low. It is in all fairness, because there are obviously huge
costs that are related to identifying these buildings. We had to do it and put a sy stem in
place that was really related to the various risk factors right across the country. So that
was the first one.
The next change was that looking at the bill before, we then came up with a situation,
again from listening to the submissions, about th e prioritisation of public buildings,
particularly buildings used for education, hospitals, and emergency services. The one
thing, too, that came out of this —and this was particularly from Ann Brower’s
submission—is that there are those buildings that had facades and parapets that were
dangerous and that did cause a lot of injury, and in some cases death. So it was during
that prioritisation part of the bill that we thought it was important to make that change.
The other change was the fact that we needed t o categorise, also, other buildings right
across, particularly by reducing the number of buildings covered —farms, retaining
walls, monuments, walls, and all of that.
Looking at this bill, I say it is very timely. It is a bill that I and all my colleagues,
particularly on this side of the House, recommend and support. Hopefully this bill can
go through and become legislation. Kia ora.
A party vote  was called for on the question,  That the Building (Earthquake -prone
Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
Ayes 120
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand
First 12; Māori Party 2; United Future 1.
Noes 1
ACT New Zealand 1.
Bill read a second time.
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Health
items.text: I move, That the Radiation Safety Bill be now read a third time. As
the House has heard during the passage of this bill, it will repeal and replace the
Radiation Protection Act 1965 and its regulations, providing a much -needed update to
our 50 -year-old legislation in this area. The bill introduces best -practice principles in
radiation safety into New Zealand law and enhances security measures, which will
provide a means for New Zealand to meet its international obligations relating to
radioactive material. In doing so, the bill meets  the stated purpose of establishing a
legislative framework to protect the health and safety of people and to protect the
environment from the harmful effects of ionising radiation, while allowing for its safe
and beneficial use.
It is fair to say that this is a carefully considered bill. Public consultation on radiation
protection legislation began in 2002, and as a result, in 2004, the Government decided
that there was an overall benefit in developing new legislation. I am advised that many
technical details, including the overall scope of the 2004 decision, were grappled with at
this early stage. The policy informing the bill was reconsidered in some detail, and in
9280 Radiation Safety Bill 1 Mar 2016
2009 the Government agreed to a refined set of instructions for the new legislation.
From there, as you might imagine for a bill of this nature, a considerable amount of
science advice and review has occurred. In addition, the emergency provisions of the
bill have received input, and even scenario testing, from agencies such as the New
Zealand Fire Service, the New Zealand Police, and the New Zealand Defence Force.
Also during this period, care has been taken to ensure that New Zealand’s requirements
under the international agreements mentioned in clause 3B were incorporated into the
bill.
The Health Committee made considerable improvements to the bill. I would like to
thank the committee for its work in grappling with the content of both the bill and the
science and technicalities of the phenomenon of radiation itself. Thanks are also due to
submitters on the bill and the Regulations Review Committee for their high -quality
input during the Health Committee’s consideration of the bill. Supplementary Order
Paper 131, which Jonathan Coleman lodged, made some further minor adjustments to
wording, to allow the provisions of the bill to operate as originally intended.
Regulations and codes of practice are being developed to support the bill once it
comes into force. The bill also requires a central register of radiation sources to be
established. A re gister and codes of safe practice are already in use under current
legislation and will be upgraded to accommodate the requirements of the bill.
The bill provides for a high degree of regulation, insists on very high compliance
standards and rates, and shows very little tolerance for safety and security practices that
fall short of these expectations. However, at its core, the bill allows for the benefits of
radiation use to be made available to New Zealanders across the fields of medicine and
other health services, animal health, science and research, and industry.
It is clear that all members have recognised this aim as worthy, and the opportunity
to update this legislation is timely. I want to thank all members for their support.
There is so much more to say about this exciting bill. I do have more time on the
clock and I would like to use it on this bill, but I know that there are many other
members who want to have their say. And so I am pleased to be advancing this much -
awaited advance to our legislation, and to commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I realise that the title of this
bill is quite boring —the Radiation Safety Bill —but that must h ave been the most tired,
weary, boring speech an acting Minister has made in this House. And it was a real
disappointment that Mr Bridges could not lift himself up and be as excited about the
passage of this bill as those of us who have been on the Health Committee, have heard
the submissions, and have come into this House and supported a major change that is
needed in this area.
You see, it is 50 years since the original Act was put in place, and so we are
changing a law that is 50 years old. So the members of the select committee—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Was the member there?

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: No, I was not there. I was not there, but I have to say that
the member looks like he might have been there. He could well have been there. The
original legislation is 50 years old, and we in the select committee have worked very
hard to get the bill through our committee and into the House. In fact, the genesis of this
bill was not 50 years ago —when I was not there —but it was, in fact, when I  was the
Minister of Health that I started the review—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Some 10 years earlier.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —of this Act. Oh, a very good interjection comes from the
Minister, because it is 11 years since I was the Minister of Health, although on a daily
basis you would think I still had the job if you listen to Dr Coleman. If you listen to Dr
Coleman, everything that ever happens in health is my responsibility. But I have to say
that 11 years ago, when I was the  Minister of Health, I started the review. So now, in
01 Mar 2016 Radiation Safety Bill 9281
National’s eighth year of Government, we have finally got around to passing the
legislation. So congratulations to us all—

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: The busy Government.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Busy committee, Mr Bishop—busy committee. Give credit
where it is due.
This Radiation Safety Bill replaces the Radiation Protection Act 1965. The purpose
of the Act is for us to meet our international obligations relating to radiation protection,
radiation safety and security, and nuclear non -proliferation under a range of
international treaties.
We acknowledged that we needed to update this legislation, and we needed to keep
pace with technological changes, because think back to 1965, those of you who can
think back that far—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Not Mr Bridges. He was not even in short pants then. But

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Annette had already been a Minister for several years.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: No, I think I might have j ust left school, Mr Bridges, and I
can remember the first time I did see television. But think forward 50 years on and you
will see that there have been a lot of technological changes, and we needed to make the
changes in this legislation.
I think the bil l has got the wrong name, though, and I did put forward during the
Committee stage Supplementary Order Paper 140 —which I know my good friends
opposite on the Health Committee would love to have supported —because I think it
should have been called the “Ionising Radiation Safety Bill”.
I wonder whether Mr Bridges, who made the previous speech, knows the difference
between ionising radiation and non -ionising radiation, because I am happy to give a
little lecture on what the difference is and on why this bill s hould have been called the
“Ionising Radiation Safety Bill”. People do not know the difference, and we found that
out at the select committee when we got submissions from people who thought they
were talking about non-ionising radiation. So for Mr Bridges, who said he knows but he
has given no indication in his speech that he understood it at all, ionising radiation is
high-energy radiation and includes X -rays, alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma
rays that have ionising capability. Non -ionising radiation is electromagnetic energy and
includes laser lights, electromagnetic fields, radio waves, cellphone towers, Wi -Fi,
microwave ovens, ultraviolet tanning machines, and power lines.
So, Mr Bridges, they are non -ionising and, unfortunately, some of those  people who
came to our committee thought that we should, in fact, be legislating for them. They are
regulated under standards, not under legislation. So I think it was important that, in fact,
we gave this bill that title so that there was no misunderstan ding about what we were
doing. I know that given the opportunity, Mr Simon O’Connor and others on the
committee would have voted for my Supplementary Order Paper. But the Minister in
the chair, who never said a word during the Committee stage, did not say a peep and did
not support my Supplementary Order Paper. So—

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Bulldust.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: No, it was not bulldust, Mr Bishop —it certainly was not.
One of the reasons I thought it was important that we did give it the proper title is that
the World Health Organization, in respect of the public health risk posed by non -
ionising radiation, has said that the evidence is very weak and that, in fact, if you
comply with current limits, it has no effects on health.
Debate interrupted.

TUESDAY, 1 MARCH 2016 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
Australia—Electoral Matters Committee of the Victoria Legislative Assembly 
Mr SPEAKER : Honourable members, I am sure that members would wish to 
welcome members of the Electoral Matters Committee of the Victoria Legislative 
Assembly, led by Chairperson the honourable Louise Asher, who are present in the 
gallery. 
MOTIONS 
Fiji—Tropical Cyclone Winston 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I seek leave to move a motion without 
notice on Tropical Cyclone Winston. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I move, That the House express its support for the people and 
Government of Fiji and other Pacific neighbours affected by Tropical Cyclone Winston . 
During the weekend of 20 and 21 February, Cyclone Winston cut a path of destruction 
through Fiji, resulting in loss of life and significant loss of property and crops. Cyclone 
Winston was designated a category 5 cyclone, the strongest cyclone to make landfall in 
Fiji, with sustained winds reaching over 300 kilometres  per hour. In some villages that 
the eye of the storm passed directly over, the devastation is near -complete. It has been 
assessed that up to 40 percent of Fiji’s population has been impacted by the cyclone. 
In the immediate aftermath of Cyclone Winston, N ew Zealand quickly understood 
that significant resources would be required to help Fiji. Our early offer of P3 Orion 
flights to undertake aerial damage assessment was accepted, and over the past 10 days 
the P3 Orion has undertaken four flights. The reports  and imagery following were 
valuable in assessing where relief is needed most. A C -130 Hercules has also made a 
number of flights to Fiji, taking much -needed relief supplies. To date, over 160 tonnes 
of priority emergency goods have been provided to Fiji, including food, construction 
supplies, generators, tents, tarpaulins, blankets, and shelter kits, as well as water and 
sanitation kits. More Hercules flights are planned for this week. 
Last week an Air Force 757 flew a team of army engineers and urban sear ch and 
rescue personnel to Fiji, and they are now working alongside Fijian partners to bring 
immediate relief to communities, including repairing schools and public infrastructure 
and clearing debris. A New Zealand Air Force King Air has also been made ava ilable to 
the Government of Fiji to enable its officials and medical teams to travel to remote 
villages. A New Zealand medical assistance team is also in Fiji, supporting the Fijian 
Government in undertaking assessments and providing primary health support  to those 
affected. On Sunday our navy’s offshore patrol vessel HMNZS Wellington arrived in 
Suva, and HMNZS Canterbury is also expected to dock tomorrow, carrying nearly 90 
tonnes of relief and building supplies and helicopters. By the end of this week, th ere 
will be close to 400 New Zealand personnel in Fiji doing what New Zealand does 
best—getting out on to the ground and helping our Pacific neighbours in their time of 
need. 
9196 Motions 1 Mar 2016 
 
Our already established aid programme in Fiji has been bolstered in the wake of 
Cyclone Winston. Our total financial contribution to the cyclone response to date stands 
at $4.7 million. The New Zealand public has been generous, and many companies have 
also made offers of assistance. The Fijian community here is rallying its support fo r its 
friends and family back home. New Zealand’s response to Cyclone Winston is shaping 
up to be our largest humanitarian response in the Pacific. Yesterday the Minister of 
Foreign Affairs, Murray McCully, travelled to Fiji to see first-hand the wreckage caused 
by Cyclone Winston. Mr McCully flew over some of the devastated areas and has told 
me about the widespread damage to housing, the scarring of the landscape, and the loss 
of crops. During the visit Minister McCully met with the Fijian Minister for Fo reign 
Affairs and also with the Minister of agriculture and national disaster management. 
Both have expressed their gratitude and appreciation for the swift and generous 
response from New Zealand. 
A strong bond exists between the people of Fiji and the peo ple of New Zealand. The 
thoughts and sympathies of all New Zealanders and of this House are with the people of 
Fiji during this time. The Fijian people are resilient and they will overcome this event, 
and in time they will recover. They can be assured that  New Zealand will continue to 
work with them and support them through the relief, recovery, and rebuild phases. 
ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) : On behalf of the Opposition,  the 
Labour Party, I would like to join and support the Government in its resolution before 
the House today in sending our thoughts and sympathies to the people of Fiji following 
the loss of lives and the destruction caused by Cyclone Winston, and to ackno wledge 
the contribution that the Government has made on behalf of the people of New Zealand 
and, indeed, the contribution coming from the Fijian community also resident in New 
Zealand.  
Cyclone Winston was the largest and strongest cyclone ever recorded in  the southern 
hemisphere. Clearly, Fiji has suffered significant damage: in some areas entire villages 
have been flattened. The geographic distances and the remoteness of some areas 
involved make it hard to assess the full impact of the cyclone but we know  it has been 
catastrophic, and it is reassuring —at least from a New Zealander’s point of view —to 
see the role and contribution that the New Zealand personnel are making in making the 
assessments and assisting in the recovery. The number of people in emerge ncy shelters 
doubled almost every day last week, peaking at almost one -twentieth of Fiji’s entire 
population. According to Unicef, 51,000 people are still in shelters. We know it could 
be weeks before electricity is restored to some areas. 
New Zealand, as the Prime Minister has said, stands side by side with the people of 
Fiji, and we will do whatever is required to help them through this disaster and the years 
of recovery ahead. 
JAMES SHAW (Co -Leader—Green): Our hearts do go out to the people of Fiji. 
Tropical Cyclone Winston was, as has been mentioned, the strongest storm in recorded 
history in our hemisphere. Wind speeds topped 320 kilometres an hour; whole forests 
were stripped of their foliage; and schools, hospitals, and houses were flattened. More 
than 40 people are dead and thousands are now homeless. 
Personally, I have found it impossible not to be moved by the images of children 
standing by their wrecked homes and the wreckage of entire comm unities lying 
scattered on those famously beautiful Fijian shores. I thank the National Government 
for its immediate and its substantive response in the aftermath. Our close ties to Fiji 
make this unlike many global catastrophes, and it is heartening to kn ow that those ties 
are now moving thousands of New Zealanders to give generously to our brothers and 
sisters now suffering in Fiji. 
1 Mar 2016 Motions 9197 
 
There is another way that New Zealanders and the Government can respond to this 
cyclone and to others like it. It is no coin cidence that this was the strongest cyclone 
recorded in our hemisphere or that this was one of many record -breaking storms that 
have occurred in recent times. As a nation, we need to start facing the truth that climate 
change is making tropical storms like  Cyclone Winston more ferocious. As New 
Zealanders we are the fifth -highest emitter per capita of climate pollution. Since we 
committed to reduce our climate change emissions in 1990, and under successive 
Governments, New Zealand’s net emissions have risen  by 42 percent, and the Ministry 
for the Environment projects another 50 percent increase by 2030 if we keep doing what 
we are doing. We as a nation are not properly reckoning with the fact that our actions 
are hurting those people in the Pacific who are t he most vulnerable to the impacts of the 
pollution that we are adding to. If we really want to help the Pacific, our climate 
emissions should be going down, not up. 
New Zealanders are getting in behind the recovery effort in Fiji. The Government 
has provided financial aid and deployed Defence Force resources and personnel to help. 
The Green Party supports these efforts, but along with that desperately needed and 
immediate aid, the next most compassionate thing that we can do for Fiji now is to 
listen to the pleas of Pacific Island leaders and commit to taking real action on climate 
change. While we wring our hands and we fret at how expensive it might be for New 
Zealand to do anything about climate change, we ought to recognise that the cost to our 
Pacific neighbours of our doing nothing is now being measured in human lives. Thank 
you. 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First): At times such as this it does not 
matter what one’s political persuasion is or—dare one say it—what one’s name is. New 
Zealand First joins with our political opponents in expressing our regret for what has 
happened, as well as our best wishes and support for the Fijian nation and people as 
they begin the long road to recovery from this terrible event. This is not a time to 
discuss why it may have happened, but we are very mindful that there needs to be a 
discussion as to why it is happening. We are sure that the New Zealand public will show 
their characteristic  generosity in giving aid and financial support to our Pacific 
neighbours. 
MARAMA FOX (Co -Leader—Māori Party): The Māori Party would like to add 
its voice to the sympathies that have been off ered to the people of Fiji who have lost 
loved ones at this time. Last week, as the cyclone looked like it was going to bypass it, 
and then made a U -turn to come back towards Fiji, our close family friends were on a 
flight to Fiji and landed the day before  the cyclone arrived. They found themselves in a 
place of utter devastation. They were there to visit with their family members and also 
to witness the rededication of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter -Day Saints temple. 
They travelled for some hours th rough the devastation, to check that their family were 
OK. They report that the majority of the people in the village and the families that were 
there are subsistence-living. What they gather and what they grow is what they eat, and, 
thereby, looking at th e devastation of the crops and the people and the way that they 
were affected, there will need to be ongoing support from our Government, and we 
recognise the generosity of our Government and of the New Zealand people in the 
Fijian community here. 
But that support will need to be ongoing for some time, until crops can be replanted; 
until life can go back to normal. They found themselves —tourists in Fiji —being cared 
for by Fijian people who, while looking after them, had no home of their own to speak 
of. So I want to acknowledge the resilience of the Fijian people to gather together in 
communities, to pick up, and to start again. They are already clearing this ground for 
crops. They are already rebuilding shelter to live in. We offer our support and our 
9198 Motions 1 Mar 2016 
 
sympathies to them, and recognise their strength and courage. I have some pretty poorly 
pronounced words in Fijian that I would like to offer, and this comes from the high 
commission. 
Kei mami duavata kei kemuni, kei na nomu ni vanua ena gauna dredre ni lako 
curuma tiko. Mo ni tu vaka kaukauwa tiko, me rawa ni tarai cake tale o Viti lomani. 
Thank you. 
DAVID SEYMOUR (Leader —ACT): On behalf of the ACT Party I would like to 
join other leaders in expressing heartfelt sympathy for the people of Fiji, particularly 
those who lost their lives and lost loved ones. I would also like to wish safe passage to 
the New Zealand Defence Force per sonnel assisting in the recovery from this disaster, 
and acknowledge the very generous response by many New Zealanders who have 
responded by voluntarily giving aid to assist in that recovery. Thank you. 
Motion agreed to. 
OBITUARIES 
Dr Ranginui Walker DCNZM 
MARAMA FOX (Co -Leader—Māori Party) : I seek leave to move a motion 
without notice and without debate on the passing of Dr Ranginui Walker. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
MARAMA FOX: I move, That this House acknowledge the passing of Dr Ranginui 
Walker, who was not only a great statesman but a distinguish ed scholar, an 
inspirational mentor, and a champion of the people . E te rangatira, te tōtara haemata, 
moe mai rā. 
[Esteemed leader, rest there, the strongly growing tōtara.] 
Motion agreed to. 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economic Outlook—Reports 
1. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister of Finance : How 
does the outlook for the New Zealand economy compare with other developed 
countries? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Reasonably good. New Zealand 
businesses are confident and backing themselves, despite some global uncertainty. 
Exporters who were forced to become more efficient when the exchange rate was 
around 88c are now able to reap the rewards of a much lower exchan ge rate. The 
manufacturing sector has notched up 40 straight months of expansion, and the services 
sector, which makes up 70 percent of the economy, has been growing at the fastest level 
in 7 years. Treasury forecasts that growth will be around 3 percent over the next 2 years, 
similar to Australia and a bit faster than the US, Canada, and the UK. 
Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi : How is the positive economic outlook translating into 
more jobs and higher income for New Zealand families? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : In the last year the annual average wage increased by 3.1 
percent, much faster than inflation, and by 2020, at moderate rates of increase, it will 
reach over $63,000. Against this background, the Government announced an increa se in 
the minimum wage yesterday, up 50c an hour to $15.25 an hour, which will directly 
1 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9199 
 
benefit over 150,000 workers. This 3.4 percent increase in the minimum wage is 
significantly more than the cost of living increase, which is 0.1 percent.  
Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi: What risks are there to New Zealand’s economic outlook? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : With reasonable pace of growth and real wage rises for 
many New Zealanders, domestic results are reasonably strong despite ongoi ng wobbles 
in the global economy. There is uncertainty around the impact of US interest rate hikes, 
risks around European banks, and always some uncertainty about the nature of the 
changes in the Chinese economy. However, New Zealand is relatively well pos itioned 
to deal with what we would regard as the normal spread of risk in the global economy.  
Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi : What steps is the Government taking to mitigate risk and 
continue to support our growing economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : One way this Government and previous Governments have 
taken steps to mitigate risks is through the negotiation of a network of free -trade 
agreements. The importance of the Trans -Pacific Partnership agreement is so high 
because it gives us better access to 800 million customers in 11 countries and accounts 
for 36 percent of the global economy. We believe the benefits that have been calculated 
for this agreement are conservative, based on the success of the most recent free -trade 
agreement negotiated by the previous Labour Government, the Chinese free -trade 
agreement.  
Housing, Rental—Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill 
2. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister for Building and 
Housing: Will the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill guarantee that no New 
Zealand renter will live in a cold, damp, mouldy house that makes them sick; if not, 
why not? 
Hon Dr NICK SMITH (Minister for Building and Housing) : This bill will make 
180,000 homes warmer, drier, and safer without imposing excessive compliance costs 
on landlords that would inevitably be passed on to tenants. The bill req uires that all 
rental properties have a smoke alarm by 1 July this year and that they are progressively 
insulated over a period of 3 years. No bill provides an absolute guarantee; it is as foolish 
as pretending that our criminal laws prevent all murders or  that our road safety laws 
prevent all motor accidents. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Can I just, before I call the member, mention the level of 
interjection. We have been away for a week, so I would expect some level of 
interjection, but if it is going to be disruptive then I will start naming members, 
mentioning their names, and then, if it continues beyond that, I will, with regret, be 
asking some members to leave. 
Metiria Turei: Will the Minister take the advice of the C hild Poverty Action Group 
and include a rentals warrant of fitness in the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill to 
provide a more comprehensive improvement in the warmth, the dryness, and safety of 
rental houses? 
Hon Dr NICK SMITH : There  are two problems with the warrant of fitness 
proposal. I am advised by officials that it would cost $225 per home, or $100 million 
per year, just for the compliance and the administration, without fixing a single house. 
The second concern I have is the pedantic nature of having “Clipboard Charlies” putting 
in unreasonable requirements. For instance, if I look at the member’s own bill, it would 
assess my Beehive office as unsafe, because I do not have a safety strip on my window 
or my flat, and I do not think that is reasonable. The third part is, of course, that any cost 
that you impose actually goes on to rents, and if you are going to put $225 on the cost of 
every rental property in New Zealand, that is actually a cost that will impact on the very 
families that we should be helping. 
9200 Oral Questions 1 Mar 2016 
 
Metiria Turei: What, then, is the cost of the lives of the 15 children who die each 
year from poor housing and the 42,000 child admissions to hospital each year from 
cold, damp housing and poverty? 
Hon Dr NICK SMITH : This Government has made more progress on getting our 
homes insulated than any other Government in history. That is why we have a bill 
before the House that is going to require all homes to be insulated by 1 July 2019 and to 
require a smoke alarm, because there are too many New Zealanders who die 
unnecessarily as a consequence of the lack of those things. What we are not going to do 
is impose a massive bureaucracy that will impose costs on the very families that we are 
trying to help. 
Metiria Turei: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister referred to the cost 
of a warrant of fitness scheme. I asked him the financial cost of the deaths of 15 
children and the 42,000 child hospital admissions. He did not answer that question— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! And nor could you expect a Minister to do that. When you 
consider that it is a supplementary question, I do not think the member could rightfully 
expect the Minister to put a dollar value on to 15 deaths an d what I think were 40,000 
hospital admissions. The question was without doubt addressed. 
Metiria Turei: Has the Minister sought any advice on the cost of 15 child deaths and 
the 42,000 child admissions to hospital caused every year by cold, damp housing? 
Hon Dr NICK SMITH: Yes, I have. There has been extensive cost -benefit analysis 
on the Government proposals. The analyses showed that a warrant of fitness imposed 
more cost than benefit, and that the proposal that we have in the bill is the best way in 
which we can address the very issues that the member is concerned about. 
Joanne Hayes: What progress has been made in improving home insulation over the 
past 15 years?

mortgage, they can pay the power bill, they can buy the groceries from the supermarket, 
they can put food on the table for their kids, and they can put a roof over their heads. 
That is the hope that we have for New Zealand; that is the Kiwi Dream that we believe 
in on this side of the House —the Kiwi Dream that has been slipping ever so further 
away from the grasp of ordinary New Zealanders every single one of the 7 long years 
that the National Party has been in power. 
On this side of the House, we are interested in what is happening with the future of 
work. We are interested in ensuring that the future of work delivers for working people. 
On the other side of the House they laugh at us for having a Future of W ork 
Commission. They laugh at us for bringing people like Guy Standing and Robert Reich 
to New Zealand to actually talk about the challenges of the future of work, the 
challenges of greater automation, the challenges of a greater number of people working 
in contracting situations rather than in employment situations, the challenges of 
ensuring that the future of work actually delivers for people, that it results in higher 
wages, that it results in stable incomes, and it results in people being able to live the 
Kiwi Dream—being able to own their own home, being able to have a life outside of 
work. Those are the sorts of things that we are focused on, and that is what National 
members laugh at us for. Well, they can laugh as much as they like; we will continue  to 
focus on the Kiwi Dream. 
David Bennett can say as much as he likes that more people are employed. Actually, 
the number of people unemployed is still higher today than it was when the National 
Government came to office. The few people who have been able  to pick up extra work 
are picking up part -time work, or casual agreements, or zero -hour contracts—insecure 
work that does not pay the bills and does not give people the security they need to be 
able to lead a decent life—and National is happy with that. W ell, we are not happy with 
that on this side of the House. We are unsatisfied with that. We think New Zealand can 
do better. Just because National has given up on the Kiwi Dream does not mean that the 
rest of us have to give up on the Kiwi Dream. So, yes, we are looking at the future of 
work. We are looking at how we ensure that productivity gains and the wealth that this 
country generates can be shared fairly, so that a hard day’s work does result in a good 
day’s pay and actually means that you can have th at Kiwi Dream and you can feed your 
family and you can live a reasonable life. That is what people expect from living in New 
Zealand, and it is slipping away under the National Government.  
So we will look at things like how we ensure that people who are i n contracting 
situations get the minimum rights that we should expect for everybody who works in 
New Zealand, like getting the minimum wage. The Government can crow about putting 
the minimum wage up by a meagre amount —it has finally hit $15 an hour, 6 or 7  years 
after the Labour Party first said that we should have a minimum wage of $15 an hour. 
That is great, except for the fact that there are thousands of people who work in New 
Zealand who do not get the minimum wage because they are not employees and the y 
are not entitled to those basic minimums. There are thousands of New Zealanders who 
do not get all the other basic rights that ordinary working people should be able to rely 
on in New Zealand —and do you know what? National is OK with that too. Well, on 
this side of the House we think we can do better. 
So our Future of Work Commission will look at things like how we expand 
collective bargaining so that people who are in contracting arrangements can get the 
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9227 
 
benefits of joining a union and bargaining collect ively, and using their collective power 
to get fair wages and a fair income, so that they can live a decent life. Those are the 
sorts of things that we are interested in on this side of the House. Those are the sorts of 
things that National laughs at. 
One of the things that we believe should be part of the Kiwi Dream is being able to 
rely on our health care system to deliver when we need it. When you go to hospital you 
should be able to expect to get the care that you need. I am hearing overwhelmingly 
from people in my electorate and from people across the country, actually, that our 
health system is failing. That is what we get when National fails to fund the health 
system properly. OK, the Prime Minister can stand up and say that the health budget has 
gone up every year. That is true. But the question is: has the health budget moved 
sufficiently to cover the costs of inflation and population growth? No, it has not. 
In fact, $1.7 billion is missing from our health system, and that shows up in events 
like the one I experienced a couple of weeks ago when I drove for 2 hours to take my 
father from Palmerston North to Wellington Regional Hospital for an appointment that 
was pre -arranged—only to be told when we walked through the doors: “No, your 
appointment is no t going ahead.” Why did we not hear about the fact that that 
appointment was not going ahead before we left Palmerston North and drove all the 
way to Wellington? Because the booking clerk was so tired of calling my father and 
cancelling his appointments that they were too embarrassed to make that phone call, and 
they put it back on whomever it was who made the decision to cancel my father’s 
appointment one more time, and that phone call never happened. 
That, to me, demonstrates a health system that is sick,  and it has become sick under 
this National Government because National refuses to fund health care. It refuses to pay 
our health professionals properly, and it refuses to provide the resources so that our 
health system can absorb one or two urgent cases a nd still provide the routine cases —
which they had booked people in for, written to them about, told them to come to 
hospital, and make a 2 -hour journey, or longer in some cases —and when people walk 
through the door, they are told that “No, your appointment  is not going ahead today, 
because we don’t have the resources to provide that appointment that we promised you 
were going to get.” That broken promise is delivered to us by National and Jonathan 
Coleman refusing to fund the health system properly. 
I received a letter that one of my constituents got from our local primary health 
organisation. This constituent had been referred to the primary health organisation by 
their GP and the referral was for a mild to moderate mental health condition. They were 
told that they did not meet the criteria, not because their condition was not sufficiently 
acute for the primary health organisation to take them on —no, they did not meet the 
criteria because the primary health organisation has the resources to provide for only 
mild to moderate mental health treatment for Māori, Pasifika, community services card 
holders, and people between the ages of 10 and 24. I will give the organisation credit —
it was absolutely honest about that. It did not say: “You don’t meet our crite ria because 
you are not acute enough, because you don’t have an illness, because we don’t think 
you need to be treated.” They said: “You don’t meet our criteria because you’re not 
Māori, Pasifika, a community services card holder, or a person between the a ges of 10 
and 24.” 
Our health system is sick if we cannot respond to the people who need treatment. 
This person could very well have received low -level treatment for a mild illness and 
saved the health system a lot of money. My concern is twofold: this per son will become 
sicker because they are not getting the treatment they require, and that bothers me 
greatly. But another thing bothers me, and that is that they may very well end up in the 
mental health ward at the hospital with a more acute condition that  is more detrimental 
9228 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016 
 
to them and also more costly for our health system. That is what is wrong with our 
health system—it is short-sighted, it is under -resourced, and it is underfunded, and that 
is thanks to this National Government. 
None of this lives up to the Kiwi Dream. None of this lives up to what it means to be 
a New Zealander. It is certainly not how I was brought up as a youngster in New 
Zealand—I was led to believe that this was the best country in the world to grow up in. 
But now it is a country where it is almost impossible to find a job, and when you do find 
a job you are likely to be underpaid and to have too few hours to make ends meet. It is a 
place where the Government laughs at people who say we need to focus on the future of 
work and we need to make sure that people are prepared to engage in the future of work 
to get a decent income. And it is a country where you get turned away from the hospital 
even when you have an appointment. That is not the Kiwi Dream. That is the nightmare 
of John Key’s National Government. 
Dr SHANE RETI (National —Whangarei): The Prime Minister’s statement of 9 
February outlines the current and future initiatives as this Government looks to continue 
to build a resilient and competitive economy and do a good job for New Zealanders. 
The underlying fiscal strategy that was enunciated is to have a tight rein on spending, to 
pay down Government debt, and then to return excess revenue to taxpayers. In return, 
we expect results in efficiencies from our public services. This strategy is giving us 
projected economic growth of 2.7 percen t over the next 5 years, and this position does 
well against GDP growth in other major OECD countries like Australia, the US, and 
Japan.  
At a national level, then, the economic outlook is stable, with steady hands on the 
tiller. Where we can policy influe nce key local drivers, such as interest rates, the 
Consumers Price Index, and inflation, we do so in the long -term interest and with the 
best information we have to hand. By definition, then, we have less influence on 
offshore factors, and this is where a resilient and multifaceted economy provides the 
best solution, yet, at the same time, recognises the not insignificant contribution by New 
Zealand to mitigate some of those global risks through our voice in forums such as the 
United Nations Security Counci l. At a macroeconomic level, then, the positive growth 
in a steady and stable economy is good.  
At a regional level, this Government recognised the importance of the regions, and 
the regional growth programme specifically focuses on five regions to identif y growth 
opportunities: Northland, the Bay of Plenty, the East Coast, Manawatū -Whanganui, and 
the West Coast. This programme is a collaboration between the Ministry of Business, 
Innovation and Employment and the Ministry for Primary Industries, together with local 
businesses, iwi, and councils. Last year in Northland we had the regional growth 
strategy at the beginning of the year, which identified the scope of the opportunities, 
and this year, a few weeks ago, we had the regional action plan identifying 58  
opportunities for Northland.  
Why Northland? Well, you know, we acknowledge the challenges. We are not afraid; 
we do not avoid them. We acknowledge the challenges that are currently confronting 
dairy, and we are working hard to do what we can about that. We also acknowledge the 
challenges that Northland has in underperforming compared with other regions. So we 
are not afraid to address those issues. In fact, the action plan, with its 58 points, 
identifies and prioritises what those actions might be.  
I would like to look at two of the significant actions in that plan for Northland. First 
of all, there is the road of national significance. The road of national significance is 
absolutely critical for Northland. It is part of a nationwide investment in roading  for 
roads of national significance at $4.5 billion. There are projections of 35,000 jobs as 
part of that package. Northland was very pleased to hear the scoping out of the four-lane 
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9229 
 
highway from Auckland to Northland, the “Northland corridor”. That is rea l progress 
and, even better, it is an example of regional investments moving off the blackboard, off 
the plan, and becoming real and tangible.  
In fact, Northlanders can see how real and tangible this investment is right now. As 
they come over the top of the Brynderwyns there is probably a kilometre of cones as the 
north side of the Brynderwyns is straightened out and the safety profile improved. 
Another 15 to 20 minutes’ drive on, you will come to the Kensington roundabout, 
which is about to commence —a significant piece of work on State Highway 1, which 
will also improve feeder roads into that area. Another 15 to 20 minutes on, on State 
Highway 1 at Hikurangi there are several hundred metres of cones where the highway is 
being upgraded, there and many other areas of roading investment as well.  
I would like to take one other example from the action plan: Hundertwasser Art 
Centre. It is another example of actually deploying an action —taking it off the 
blackboard and making it real. There is $4 million for the  Hundertwasser and the 
Wairau Māori Art Centre. In 1973 Frederick Hundertwasser came to New Zealand. He 
was an established international artist when he did. He gained New Zealand citizenship, 
lived in Northland where his artwork was prolific and was influe nced by living in 
Northland, by living in New Zealand, and by living with Māoridom. I challenge a 
search for any other international artist who came to New Zealand with that reputation 
and has done the same. Stan Semenoff, Phil Halse, and others have led t he 
Hundertwasser challenge and over many years others have contributed. It is a real

pocket—$4 million of proof and evidence right there. Thank you. 
TODD MULLER (National—Bay of Plenty): I would like to take a leaf out of Bill 
English’s book, actually, and spend just a moment reflecting on some of the Opposition 
response to the Prime Minister’s stateme nt and particularly to its members’ discussion 
on the future of work. One of the things that I would like to draw out is how they 
particularly reinforce that the future is going to be a period of unprecedented change; we 
are going to have significant globa lisation, technological connectivity and disruption, 
and massive turmoil. In fact, it is a huge opportunity for both capital and labour —and 
they talk about a huge free flow of ideas and talent and investment. 
So with that as a basic premise, I find it extr aordinary that the policy response of the 
Labour Party to that future is to contract out of the very trading bloc that has been 
established to maximise the opportunity for this country to be able to participate in this 
future. It is a trading bloc that har dwires innovative businesses to over 40 percent of 
world trade: 800 million consumers. It is a trading bloc that creates a framework to be 
able to deal with the issues of intellectual property and services and investment into the 
future that other countrie s are lining up to join. It is a trading bloc that will exceed the 
expectations of the national investment analysis. That is a future that this Government 
wants to be a part of and the Opposition wants to withdraw from, and I think it is very 
flawed thinking indeed.  
The other policy that Opposition members then put on the table is one that increases 
the subsidies for those who want to retrain. I respectfully put forward that that is 
precisely the wrong question to be asking. The real question here is wheth er we are 
teaching the right vocational and tertiary courses to enable people to have the skills and 
resilience to be able to be successful in that future economy. In my view, this 
Government has a fantastic track record in investment, particularly across vocational 
and tertiary areas both in terms of their prioritisations of ICT graduates, STEM funding,

changing world, lo oking out 5, 10, 15, 20 years, it is as much about attitude as it is 
9230 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016 
 
about technical competency. In my opinion, a party that—as we do—talks to that future,

SUE MORONEY (Labour) : The Kiwi Dream —it is not too m uch to ask. I think 
that the National Party has forgotten about the basic needs of New Zealanders: 
somewhere safe to live; hopefully, a place that you can call home, that you can own. 
That is not too much to ask. Basic needs include security for the people  we love, a 
chance to enjoy the outdoors and the environment that we care about, and a job —a 
decent, secure job—that gives us the time, the money, and the safety to lead a fulfilling 
life with those we care about. It is a simple concept —the Kiwi Dream —but for an 
increasing number of New Zealanders it is getting completely outside of their reach 
under this National Government.  
I was hoping to hear something inspirational from the Prime Minister’s statement 
that might change that situation, but a couple of weeks after the Prime Minister stood up 
and gave his statement, you know, I cannot name one exciting thing that he said, and I 
do not think any New Zealander can. What was the transformational thing that the 
Prime Minister came out with in his speech that w ill improve people’s lives? That is 
what we are charged with: we are charged with improving people’s lives, not handing 
out the same old misery that is stopping thousands of New Zealand families and 
children from achieving that simple Kiwi Dream. That is w hat we are here to try to 
secure. It is out of reach for far too many New Zealanders under this Government.  
My generation of parents is facing the sad situation of being the first generation ever 
to look at our children and know that they are going to be worse off than we were. That 
has not happened before. I think all parents aspire to know that their children’s lives are 
going to be better than theirs. But we are facing down the barrel of being the first 
generation who will not be able to look our childr en in the eye and say that, because 
they face increasing housing costs and their chances of actually owning their own home 
are becoming a distant, distant memory. They face increasing debt for everything that 
they are engaged with—for their education, and for just simply being allowed to live on 
this planet and participate in life in New Zealand. They are under growing amounts of 
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9231 
 
debt. The life expectation of the generation below us is below the life expectation for 
my generation.  
That is a dreadful situat ion for any parent to have to contemplate. Also, our children 
face increasingly insecure jobs. That is what they are facing under this National 
Government. It is only the Labour Party that is concerned enough about that prospect 
that we are doing the hard work and the thinking and the policy making around what the 
future of the workforce needs to look like, to actually make it more secure for people, to 
ensure that the workforce and the labour market work for people.  
I listened to the sad contributions from the last couple of National MPs. Todd Muller, 
who has just resumed his seat, said that our entire success is going to be measured on 
how connected we are to the world. No, Mr Muller, our success will be rated on how 
people’s lives are. We have an economy  to serve the people; not the people to serve the 
economy. They have got it completely the wrong way round. That is what I think was at 
the basis of the Prime Minister’s statement that was so disappointing and did not bring 
forward any of the inspiration, any of the vision, that New Zealanders are desperately 
crying out for.  
Under National, the Kiwi Dream is slipping away. National members are too 
distracted on working out how to get rid of our flag, for goodness’ sake! They are so 
distracted on how to get rid of our flag that they had a crisis meeting about it. They had 
a crisis meeting on how to get rid of our national flag when they should have been 
having a crisis meeting on how to lift out of poverty the increasing number of children 
who are slipping i nto poverty under National’s reign. That should have been what the 
crisis meeting was about; not about getting rid of our flag. So the Government has 
completely got its priorities upside down.  
On this side of the House we are connected to the Kiwi Dream, and we are 
determined to deliver that. I want to talk about a few aspects that we are taking charge 
of. Extending paid parental leave is one aspect. If the Kiwi Dream starts anywhere it 
starts in those first early days and months of a child’s life. Getting  that right, getting the 
support, getting the security, getting the attachment between parent and baby —there 
should be no greater priority than that. That is where the Kiwi Dream starts. If it goes 
wrong in those early months, what all the research and evi dence tell us is that we as 
taxpayers will pay for that, over and over and over again. When that child cannot learn, 
when that child ends up in hospital, when that child is not going to school because of 
health problems, when that child is disconnected from their caregiver, from their parent, 
then we all pay, over and over again, for the bad outcomes of that.  
On this side of the House, and with the support of other wise parties, what we know 
is that this sort of investment is the type of thing that the Pri me Minister should have 
been talking about. He should have been agreeing to extend paid parental leave to 26 
weeks. But was he doing that? No. Instead, he is talking about putting a veto on it, to go 
against the will of this Parliament and to go against th e will of the majority of New 
Zealanders, to put a stop to getting the start to the Kiwi Dream. That is what the Prime 
Minister is focused on; not on dealing with the issues that matter to New Zealanders.  
Decent jobs—that is what this side of the House is  focused on. We know that having 
a decent job is fundamental to being able to secure the rest of the Kiwi Dream. It is 
fundamental to that. But under this Government, zero-hour contracts are what have been 
going on. People have to put their lives on hold, just sit and wait for a phone call that 
may never come, to give them a little bit of extra money so that they can put food on the 
table. For far too many of our families those jobs mean not only that can they not 
participate in their community but also tha t they cannot do the basic thing of putting 
food on the table. We are a food-producing nation, and 27 percent of our children live in 
poverty. Too many of our children go to school hungry, in a food -producing nation. 
9232 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016 
 
How can we get it so wrong? How can tha t be? Did the Prime Minister address that at 
all in his statement? There was not one measure —not one measure —to reduce child 
poverty. There was not one measure to secure decent jobs. There was not one measure 
that actually deals with the day -to-day pressures that New Zealand families are facing, 
and it is very, very disappointing.  
Another part of a decent job is the good old Kiwi adage that you get a fair day’s pay

idea that it has got in this space. Well, it is not acceptable and it needs addressing.  
In the final part of this speech I want to talk a little bit about transport and its r ole in 
the Kiwi Dream. I can tell you that sitting on the Auckland motorway for hours on end 
is not part of the Kiwi Dream. That Government has presided over increasing volumes 
on the Auckland motorway, without people getting anywhere. It has spent $2.3 bi llion 
on the Waikato Expressway. That was money, funding, set aside by a Labour 
Government to do exactly that. We agree with the Waikato Expressway, but what the 
Government has managed to do is to squander that $2.3 billion. It now takes longer than 
ever to get from central Hamilton to central Auckland. It now takes longer than ever. It 
used to take an hour and a half 
Hamiltonians now have to put aside 3 hours to get from central Hamilton to central 
Auckland, and that is after the Government has spent $2.3 billion on the Waikato 
Expressway. Why? Because it did not do the public transport part that needed to go 
alongside that, to make it work. The Government has ignored the needs of public 
transport in Auckland, and now what we are doing, with the Waikato Exp ressway, is we 
are feeding a greater volume of traffic faster to get to the “great southern car -park” and 
sit there for longer. That is what the National Government has managed to achieve. It is 
not good for productivity. It is not good for family life. 
Because of the housing crisis in Auckland, which the Government has failed to fix, 
we have got people moving to Hamilton, living there, but returning to their jobs every 
day in Auckland. They are going on that motorway, sitting there for hours on end, doing 
a full day’s work, and doing it again at the other end of the day. They are becoming 
unsafe on the roads, and when they get home they are feeling stressed with their 
families. That is not the Kiwi Dream. It is not working under this Government.

DENISE ROCHE (Green): Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. I rise to take the final 
call for the Greens on the Prime Minister’s statement, and I want to address the four 
priorities that he outlined. They were to responsibly manage the Government’s finances, 
to build a more competitive and productive economy, to deliver better public services to 
New Zealanders, and to support the rebuilding of Christchurch.  
I applaud the Government’s small army of public relations and communications staff 
for being able to spin this Government’s appalling record on these issues into some kind 
of achievement. National has promised to responsibly manage the Government’s 
finance. The reality is that it has increased New Zealand’s public debt to $120 billion. A 
legacy of National’s poor economic ma nagement is tax cuts to its rich mates and 
giveaways to dodgy corporates. It promised to build a more competitive and productive 
economy; instead, it built an economy that was built on property speculation —ask 
anyone in Auckland —and on casino capitalism an d on unsustainable practices. It has 
1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9235 
 
failed to meaningfully diversify the economy and implement a vision towards a greener 
and more sustainable economy.  
Our trading fortunes seem to rise and fall with the dairy prices, and we see, as the 
result of this, f arms carrying nearly $60 billion in debt, with dairy farms carrying $40 
billion of that debt. Nearly one in 10 farmers is under financial stress. The 
Government’s single -minded focus on bigger, more intensive farming endangers our 
fragile ecosystems. It pr essures farmers into intensifying, and it undermines New 
Zealand’s No. 1 strength: our “clean, green” reputation.  
This Government claims to have provided Better Public Services. It has certainly 
been very good at delivering public services to further priv ate interests—to places like 
Serco, Skycity, and, let us not forget, charter schools —and it has certainly been very 
good at replacing democratically elected bodies in favour of appointed cronies. We see

Currently there are 129 days of waiting time to get a State house if you are in urgent

to help the Government fudge the books with its creative accounting. The Government’s 
hard-line ideology is pressuring our hard -working public servants. Our nurses and 
doctors are having to cope with nearly $2 billion —$2 billion —in underfu nding, our 
universities are slipping in the world rankings, and our Department of Conservation is 
struggling to fulfil its core responsibilities due to budget cuts.  
The reality on the ground was exposed a couple of weeks ago by the Salvation 
Army’s report. In it, it says—and as we know—that there are still 220,000 kids living in 
poverty, there are still 150,000 notifications for potential child abuse this year, and there 
are over 55,000 food parcels being provided by the Salvation Army. Only on “Planet 
Key” can the number of kids remaining in poverty increase despite the economy 
growing 12 percent since 2010.  
The reality about our Public Service is that it cannot continue to struggle with 
underfunding. Political reporter Andrea Vance was correct: instead o f having Better 
Public Services, we have “Bitter Public Services”. Despite the Government’s glossy 
public relations, our hard -working teachers, nurses, doctors, and police are bearing the 
cost of having to do much, much more with less, and that means that our most 
vulnerable—our kids, kids living in poverty, regional New Zealand, and our new 
migrants—are bearing the costs of these stealth cuts.  
Let me just talk a little bit about Christchurch and the promises there. My colleagues 
from Christchurch have already touched on this, but allow me to ask the question once 
more: how can the Government be listing its rebuilding of Christchurch as an 
achievement and then, several days later, slash the funding for mental health services in 
the area? Rebuilding is more than replacing bricks and mortar. It is about supporting 
people who have been hurt and are facing losses, it is about wrapping support around 
the vulnerable and vulnerable communities, and it is about acknowledging that the loss 
of friends, family, businesses, and ways of life can be painful and difficult and that it 
requires help. I pay tribute to the incredible resilience, courage, and fortitud e of the 
people of Christchurch, and I condemn this Government, which by its actions is failing 
the people of Christchurch and the people of New Zealand.  
The Government has repeatedly promised a brighter future for New Zealand, but it 
has always talked a better game than it has been prepared to deliver. For ordinary 
working New Zealanders, we have gone backwards in terms of rights at work, we have 
gone backwards in terms of the work climate where lots and lots of public servants feel 
bullied and fearful, a nd we have gone backwards about zero -hour contracts. The Prime 
Minister promised a brighter future for New Zealanders, but, actually, he has left every 
9236 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1 Mar 2016 
 
New Zealander in the dark. The recent increase of the minimum wage to $15.25 an hour 
and the gap between  that and the living wage of $19.80 reflect that reality. Since 2009 
the highest-paid third of New Zealanders have seen their incomes increase eight times 
as much as the lowest-paid third.  
Last year the Government promised to outlaw zero -hour contracts, b ut instead of

It is interesting to note what the Prime Minister did not talk about. Not once did the

Prime Minister address the growing gap between the haves and have -nots in this

progressive Prime Minister would have talked about child poverty and supported 
measures to fix it, like our breakfast in schools bill —the Government could have 
supported that —and like, maybe, decent incomes for families. A progressive Prime 
Minister would have talked about how climate change is the greatest challenge we face, 
but it is a lso an opportunity for New Zealand to become world leaders in a new, high -
value, cleantech, low-carbon economy. A progressive Prime Minister would have talked 
about how we can have an economy that works for everyone, not just the very rich, and 
a progressive Government with the Greens in it would do more than just talk and spin.  
We would act on these issues and make sure that every single child in New Zealand 
is cared for and lives in a warm, dry home. We would make sure ordinary New 
Zealanders would get a  fair deal at work and a fair share of the benefits of a smart, 
thriving green economy that works for everyone. We would make sure that we have 
rivers we can swim in and vibrant green cities and townships with fast, affordable, clean 
public transport. An Aotearoa with the Green Party at the heart of Government will be a 
much kinder place, and certainly we would deliver a lot better than what this 
Government has.

to the Opposition you will hear a completely different level of slogans and a completely

When it co mes to infrastructure, we were handed a massive deficit. I am Associate 
Minister of Education. Let me walk you through the numbers. We were handed leaky

to not just the people of central Auckland benefiting; it is the people of west  Auckland

The last speaker, Minister Nikki Kaye, talked about the Prime Minister’s statement 
and the vision and the great words and the great slogans that were in it. She talked —and 
I wrote it down —about “a Government that cares”. She talked about “a compassionate 
Government”. But there was one word and one phrase that did not appear in the Prime

1 Mar 2016 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 9239 
 
petition. People sat in the gallery watching the to -ing and fro-ing of question time, and

opportunity for them to make a choice and literally —literally for those people —save 
their lives.
